To enhance data efficiency in speech recognition, a significant amount of research has focused on multi-modal training methods combining text information with speech data. These methods typically involve two phases of learning: initial training in a bidirectional mode and subsequent speech-only training. This work challenges the common practice of restricting the attention to either the text or speech input during multi-modal training by introducing a novel approach with a bidirectional attention mechanism. This mechanism allows the network to learn from both inputs simultaneously and produces a range of attention weights that are leveraged through two sets of transformation matrices. Notably, this approach yields significant gains of 1.37% word error rate when tested on the Librispeech corpus and 3.04% relative improvement when the dataset is limited to 100 hours, outperforming strong baselines, including transfer learning and multi-stage models. The proposed method is also compared to other attention schemes, demonstrating its effectiveness, and is found to facilitate learning without the need for speech-only fine-tuning, resulting in no degradation when tested on unseen data. The model architecture is also examined in terms of its interpretability, with attention weights providing valuable insights into the learning process. The proposed approach is found to be particularly effective when there is limited data available. The code for this research is made available at https://github.com/seyoon/yoon-2021-speech-text-paper, and the model weights can be downloaded from https://seyoon.github.io/2021/09/01/speech-text-models.html. The findings of this research are also presented in the form of slides at https://seyoon.github.io/2021/09/01/speech-text-slides.html. Additionally, a follow-up study has been conducted to explore the potential of this model for data efficiency in other tasks such as speech synthesis and music generation, with the code available at https://github.com/seyoon/yoon-2022-speech-text-extended. This paper investigates the long-term behavior of uniform parking functions as they are randomly and independently added to a growing set. We show that the distribution of the locations of these functions within a set of n elements converges to a specific, probability-driven pattern as n increases without limit. The probability of any element k being chosen to store a function before any other element is in proportion to the difference between the square of k and the square of the next lowest element, resulting in a storage pattern that prioritizes the middle elements most heavily. A crucial aspect of our method involves establishing an alternate yet equivalent definition for the sequence in which uniform parking functions are placed, making it possible to analyze this problem using a recursive approach that utilizes the concept of a 'pebble system'. As a result, we are able to derive not only the proposed storage pattern but also explicit, general formulas for the probability of any element k being chosen over any element that is one unit lower, as well as the expected location of any particular function within the sequence in a set of n elements. These formulas reveal an intriguing, almost but not quite arithmetic progression to the set of probabilities for any given level. We also investigate another property of uniform parking functions, where we examine the asymptotic behavior of the number of functions whose most preferred location is a specific position. As part of this investigation, we develop formulas for this particular property as well. Interestingly, these formulas follow a different but very similar distribution that is more closely aligned with a specific sequence that is based on the square of the elements rather than their linear progression. Consequently, in a set of n elements, the position that is most preferred over all other positions will be the one that is at the center of that set with a high degree of certainty. A very intuitive and visual way to understand both of these properties is through the use of a line graph where the x-axis represents the sequence in which the functions are placed and the y-axis represents the number of functions that are located at any particular point within that sequence. When this line graph is plotted for any set of n elements, it will form a perfect bell-shaped curve that resembles a normal distribution. A key aspect of this line graph is that it will have n/3 as the midpoint and will maintain a specific, proportional relationship with a normal distribution as n increases without limit. This proportionate relationship will allow us to use the one-third rule as a general guideline to understand and predict the behavior of uniform parking functions within any set of n elements even when n is extremely large. We investigate the conductance of superconducting niobium nitride nanowires using a gate voltage. As the gate voltage moves through critical points, the conductance exhibits notable variations, which can be controlled with an external voltage. By comparing our experimental results to theoretical predictions, we find that the conduction of these nanowires can be explained by the phenomenon of quantum phase-flips when the capacitance of the gate is sufficiently large. However, when the gate's capacitance is too small, the behavior of the nanowires is instead controlled by a Coulomb blockade that is also sensitive to the critical points. This equivalence of these two scenarios occurs when the charging energy is equal to the energy of a single photon, a critical distance that must be reached in order to observe the desired behavior. As a result, the desired coherent quantum phase-flip phenomenon is challenging to achieve in experiments involving thin superconducting wires. This study sheds light on the need for extensive analysis of a system's capacitance and resistance in order to accurately interpret observations of coherent quantum phase-flip events. Furthermore, the concept of using critical points to distinguish between the two scenarios provides a practical method for distinguishing quantum phase-flip and Coulomb blockade phenomena. This research provides a foundation for exploring the combination of quantum phase-flip and Josephson effects in enclosed spaces using a gate voltage, a phenomenon that could be used to develop highly precise voltage standards. As a result of the challenges involved in achieving this phenomenon, there is a need for further theoretical analysis using a comprehensive model that incorporates multiple capacitances and resistances, as well as a proposal for a new experimental technique that incorporates time-differential resistance measurements, which could provide insights that will be crucial in advancing the development of precise voltage standards. Furthermore, the study highlights the potential for observing coherent Josephson effects in an out-of-equilibrium setup, and the findings suggest that further investigation is necessary to fully understand the behavior of superconducting nanowires and to develop the theoretical framework necessary for interpreting the results. As a result, the study proposes a new experimental technique that incorporates time-differential resistance measurements, which could provide the necessary insights to drive the development of precise voltage standards and to advance our understanding of the complex phenomena involved. However, there has been limited research on this particular object due to a lack of high-quality near-infrared spectra. GJ 229B is unique in that it is one of the coolest objects in a binary system, and its proximity to the Sun makes it ideal for further study. We analyzed the object's evolution under different scenarios of irradiation from its host star, and results from dust models suggest that GJ 229B's low luminosity could be a product of its being an L-type main-sequence object rather than a T-type one. We also explored possible detection pathways for the object using current and upcoming observational facilities. Notably, the SPICA telescope offers the highest sensitivity for detecting its molecular emission, while a binary microlensing event in 2025 presents an opportunity for direct magnification of the object's light. We conclude by highlighting the code's potential in retrieving the complete spectral range of this T-dwarf and its host star system through a binary analysis, and we anticipate it to be a valuable tool in the scientific community for the study of this particular object and similar binary systems involving a T-dwarf companion. Furthermore, we outline the code's capacity to handle a range of observational data, from existing archives to upcoming observations, and its ability to make predictions for current and future facilities, as well as a forecasted detection of the object's oxygen line with the SPICA telescope, above the detection limit of 5σ. Ultimately, we aim to position the code as a key instrument for any research related to GJ 229B and similar T-dwarf binaries. View video prediction tackles the challenge of forecasting a sequence of views that are significantly different from previous observations, based on a single frame or short sequence. Unlike most approaches that focus on consecutive view increments, the existing methods fail to capture the unique characteristics of new view predictions. Existing models, despite being effective for consecutive view predictions, produce unsatisfactory results for new views, often producing inaccurate forecasts that diverge significantly from actual outcomes. This discrepancy suggests that new view predictions require unique capabilities, distinct from those for consecutive view predictions. To address this, we propose a dual representation framework that differs from the standard two-stream approach used in most view prediction models. The proposed framework divides the prediction process into two concurrent tasks: forecasting new views and predicting views that are similar to previous ones. The two learned representations are then combined using a weighted method, with the weighted fraction representing the likelihood of each representation. However, unlike standard approaches that fix the weighted fraction, our method trains it as a variable, obtaining the optimal weighted fraction during training. This is achieved by treating the weighted fraction as a part of the model's parameters. To validate our approach, we conducted extensive experiments on the CMU Panoptic Video Dataset, comparing our method to state-of-the-art models that focus on consecutive view predictions. The results show that our approach delivers significantly better performance, with an average improvement of 12.14% in prediction accuracy for new views. To facilitate thorough evaluation and comparison, we introduced a new strict view classification benchmark, along with a detailed analysis of each view prediction example in conjunction with its corresponding classification label. This allows us to provide a quantitative assessment of prediction accuracy in relation to view angle, obtaining a score of 0.346 for our method, with an average of 0.346 for easy views and 0.294 for new views, and significantly lower scores for method-specific evaluations. The comprehensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing methods, with a notable performance gap of at least 10% in new view prediction scenarios. The proposed dual representation framework, along with the new view classification labels and the CMU Panoptic Video Dataset, are now available for public access through the project website. This marks the first time a view prediction approach has outperformed consecutive view prediction models with a significant margin of 12%, achieving an accurate prediction score of 0.294 for new views, with the resulting models and data now available for further research and improvement. We examine the validity of using a constant mixing model to analyze airborne pathogen transmission within an urban bus. Unlike real-world situations where people mix according to the bus's seating layout, this model assumes random mixing without regard to physical constraints. In comparing these two approaches, we run computer simulations based on actual data collected from an urban bus, including factors such as passenger flow, ventilation, and physical distancing. Our findings show that while the constant mixing model can provide qualitative insights, it does not accurately capture the spread of disease in an urban bus setting. Specifically, we discovered that the constant mixing model overestimates the transmission rate by up to tenfold, highlighting the need to use more realistic modeling methods that take into account the physical layout of buses and other confined spaces. We also explore how various ventilation rates affect disease transmission in these environments and find that it has a relatively minor impact compared to other factors. To facilitate further comparison studies, we developed an open-source tool that allows researchers to easily assess the spread of disease in urban bus settings utilizing various modeling approaches. We hope this research will contribute to the development of more effective strategies for containing the spread of airborne pathogens within urban buses and other public transportation. In addition, we discuss the implications of our findings for the design of bus seating layouts with the goal of slowing down disease transmission in real-world settings. Furthermore, we highlight the value of combining computational modeling with experimental data collection in informing policy decisions and the development of more practical public health interventions. Finally, we discuss the broader applicability of our research to the broader context of epidemiological modeling in complex networks and call for further exploration of how to integrate physical constraints into these types of models. We also discuss the role of ventilation rates as key factors in disease transmission and propose that they be given more consideration in future modeling studies. To this end, we suggest that future modeling studies incorporate a more nuanced view of ventilation rates that takes into account the unique factors at play in urban bus settings and other confined environments. We conclude by emphasizing the need for a more holistic approach to understanding disease transmission that considers not only individual behavior but also the broader environmental context in which transmission occurs. We believe that this research lays the groundwork for a more comprehensive exploration of these factors in urban bus settings and other public transportation settings and call on other researchers to build on this foundation by exploring additional factors that contribute to disease transmission in these types of environments. A cryptographic technique known as functional encryption enables users to efficiently compute outcomes of specific functions while keeping the underlying input data private. One of the most well-known functional encryption methods is keyless functional encryption, where a user can perform computations without needing an encryption key. In this study, we introduce the initial concept of keyless functional encryption for classical messages transmitted in Gaussian noise channels, a fundamental and broadly applicable cryptographic framework. Leveraging an existing scheme designed for binary inputs and additive white Gaussian noise channels, we developed a method to extend its security guarantees to include manipulations of signal power and possibly adaptive attacks, all without the need for an encryption key. This new keyless functional encryption framework can be used to securely enable various applications, such as secure computation for privacy-preserving classification and securely outsourcing encrypted storage, both with power-controllable and uncontrolled attacks. Our findings demonstrate that this new keyless functional encryption framework offers superior performance over its key-based counterpart, featuring significantly lower encrypted message lengths with comparable computation costs. This improvement in efficiency enables secure computation for a wider range of signal power levels and reduces the risk of power-controllable attacks in protocols employing random padding. Our proposed approach also facilitates the integration of physical layer characteristics into cryptographic constructions, a novel contribution that could contribute to the design of secure end-to-end communication systems protecting against various types of attacks, including both unbounded and bounded physical attacks, spanning from passive observation to active jamming and manipulation of signal power. The spin-orbit proximity effect, a phenomenon where a strong spin-orbit material's influence on a nearby ferromagnetic layer causes magnetic polarization to extend beyond the ferromagnetic interface, has been observed in various combinations of materials. Our research focuses on the Bi/Co system to explore this effect, specifically on the ferromagnetic resonance of Co nanowires when coated with a thin layer of Bi. By conducting in-depth analyses of FMR spectra with different Bi thicknesses, our findings show that the Bi layer causes a reduction in the gyromagnetic ratio ($\gamma$) and the ferromagnetic resonance field ($H_r$), while the FMR line width remains unaffected. Notably, these changes are most pronounced when the Bi layer is 2-3 nanometers thick. To understand these observations, our theoretical model incorporates the role of interface interactions in Bi layers, with proposed mechanisms for spin accumulation and orbital interaction with Co nanowires. Based on this framework, we identified the most critical interface that influences Bi's behavior, specifically the Co-Bi interface over the air Bi surface. By considering these interface interactions, our model is able to accurately predict the observed $\gamma$ and $H_r$ variations with Bi layer thickness. Furthermore, our results indicate that the Bi layer causes a reduction in Co's anisotropy constant ($K$), while introducing a bi-anisotropy constant ($B$), which together provide valuable insights into the Bi/Co system's magnetic properties. Based on these findings, our model proposes a possible increase in the Bi layer's orbital potential ($\lambda$) as the underlying reason for these effects, which could potentially be validated through future experimental measurements of the Bi layer itself. By understanding the Bi/Co system's proximity effect, our research paves the way for exploring other spin-orbit proximity systems, which could hold the key to developing novel functional materials through the manipulation of their magnetic and orbital properties. Additionally, our work highlights the significance of interface interactions in proximity effects, which could be optimized further by controlling the interface quality, layer thickness, and material combinations. Adapting online services and products for individual needs is known as customization. While it has the potential to enhance user experience, over-targeting may lead to privacy concerns. A survey of N=1091 participants was conducted to investigate the complex relationship between customization, privacy, and user behavior. Our research revealed that customization can boost user satisfaction but may harm acceptance if done excessively. This acceptance drop-off effects was found to be more pronounced in individuals who value privacy. Moreover, those with higher self-awareness tend to appreciate customization more. Our findings suggest that companies can raise customer satisfaction through customization but must balance this with respect for users' desire for privacy. Our survey also uncovered the concept of an "privacy self-awareness spectrum" which could guide further research into the customization-privacy behavior of individuals. Ultimately, our results provide insights for companies to customize their offerings while protecting users' privacy and promoting positive user experiences. Full-scale replication of existing research along with new insights are presented in this study. Our survey offers a middle ground where customization is beneficial for satisfaction but detrimental to acceptance if taken too far. This study examines the relevance of centering theory in evaluating coreference resolution systems. Initially designed to analyze spoken language, centering theory distinguishes between local and extended coreference. While most coreference data sets focus on the latter, systems like MICA, MICA-TC and DTREG, leveraged in MUC evaluations, demonstrate that MICA, the underlying model, performs well on both aspects. However, a more recent data set, which also considers local coreference, shows these systems' limitations. To understand the source of this performance, we concentrate on centering theory's features and system design, along with their implications for both coreference aspects. System improvements are suggested based on centering theory's analysis. Furthermore, we propose an enhanced evaluation framework that integrates both local and extended coreference, referencing centering theory's aspects and system design. Additionally, a discussion on coreference-related issues, system design, and potential future research is presented through expert interviews. Although some potential improvements to coreference systems were identified, system performance on local coreference remains a challenge. As a result, there is scope for further research to address this issue. While some potential solutions were suggested, integrating them into a data set that considers local coreference is necessary to validate our findings. Consequently, our conclusions and proposed system improvements are subject to confirmation. Therefore, we recommend that both coreference aspects be integrated into a unified evaluation framework to provide a comprehensive assessment of coreference systems. Furthermore, expert opinions support the significance of exploring local coreference in spoken language, in comparison to written language. Moreover, they emphasize the significance of centering theory in coreference-related research. We've concentrated on parameterized algorithms within the context of upward planarity and explored numerous techniques such as recursive algorithms, decomposition techniques (like those using SPNs), and whether there are simpler decomposition techniques available. Some open research questions in upward planarity detection have been outlined using our parameterized algorithm framework and potential solutions discussed using our parameterized algorithm tools. These questions encompass both graph drawing and non-graph drawing domains. The rising intricacy of modern computer systems forces them to adapt at an accelerating pace, necessitating a fundamental shift in their configuration to allow for automated, hands-free optimization. A novel framework is introduced, capable of independently refining a computer game's rendering pipeline by exploiting in-game visual data through a process called over-relation. This framework enables the separation of application logic from visual comparison, allowing for both significant performance gains and exceptional adaptability. Its application is demonstrated through the development of an automated tool for configuring Linux-based virtual machines, ensuring seamless operation with various OpenGL applications by reproducing the behavior of a reference system in an environment that is otherwise dissimilar. This achievement is an initial proof of the concept's viability and is already being utilized to address other configuration challenges. The framework's potential for wide application is also being explored across multiple domains. The framework and its implementation are made available under an permissive open-source license with the aim of facilitating community participation and collaboration. The framework introduces a novel configuration paradigm that combines the principles of first-order logic and graph theory to govern its operation and is the foundation for both its development and future extensions. The framework comprises multiple components that collaborate to achieve its goal, each responsible for either managing its internal data structures, orchestrating the application's behavior, or interacting with the system under control, as well as a fundamental unit that these components share and that defines the application's core properties. The framework is an open-source project that is part of the University of British Columbia's Graphics Group and is available at https://github.com/ubcgraphics/overrelation. Further information on the framework can be found in the presentation available at https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Q5Q5Q5Q5Q5Q. The framework is currently in its early stages and is in need of additional contributors to further drive its development and refinement. Quantum operator growth is a fundamental process where nearby heisenberg operators evolve in time, their expectations shifting in influence as systems devolve. This phenomenon has been observed in multiple systems, including random quantum circuits, free fermions, and boson-fermion correspondences. A key aspect is Krylov complexity, a measure of an operator's growth via its nearest heisenberg predecessors, assessed in various circuits, including random circuits, critical circuits, and staircase circuits. A notable finding is the relationship between operator entanglement and Krylov complexity, with evidence suggesting they move in tandem as operators evolve. A distinguishing feature of operator growth is the involvement of system symmetries, such as unitary and Clifford, which constrain its pace. A notable consequence of these constraints is the distinction between unitary and clifford trajectories in systems like qutrits and percolation cones. A promising approach to explore operator growth is through quantum machine learning, using techniques such as training neural networks on time-series data to predict future operator influences. A pressing issue in the field is the development of a general theory for operator growth, with many open questions remaining, such as the role of system symmetries and the prediction of krylov complexity along specific trajectories. A promising direction is the study of relational growth, which focuses on how the relationship between operators evolves over time, with insights gained applicable to a broader range of systems, including classical systems described by the kuramoto model and systems with non-monotonic operator growth. A key aspect of relational growth is the discovery of universal operator growth patterns, which are insensitive to system details, with implications for fundamental questions regarding the connection of operator growth in quantum systems. This research employs supervised machine learning to enhance WiFi-based range estimation on Linux devices. Initially, a custom measurement tool was developed to collect 1030 distance data sets from 1 to 100 meters in 1-meter increments, in conjunction with the WiFi signal strength in dBm. However, these measurements were only accurate in environments with minimal obstruction. To expand the model's effectiveness to various settings, we gathered 1660 additional data sets from 16 distinct environments with different levels of obstruction. The collected data sets were utilized to compare three machine learning algorithms - Linear Regression, Decision Tree, and Random Forest - with the goal of enhancing WiFi-based range estimation precision. Our findings reveal that WiFi-based range estimation precision can reach 92.6% accuracy, or 0.95 RMADE, in both indoor and outdoor settings with minimal to extensive obstructions, outperforming a widely adopted WiFi-based range estimation method with an 11.2% lower mean absolute error. Our research enables the creation of a reliable and precise WiFi-based range estimation framework for diverse indoor and outdoor settings, or those with minimal to extensive obstructions. This framework is currently being further developed for integration with a robot navigation system. Furthermore, our data sets can be utilized as a foundation for the development of WiFi-based range estimation algorithms in Python, suitable for various devices and platforms. This research is an extension of an earlier study presented at the 2019 IEEE/RSJ IROS workshop, "Evaluation of WiFi Range Estimation on Linux," where we explored the execution of WiFi range estimation on Linux. This paper provides a more comprehensive analysis of that research, with an additional 1450 data sets and a 9.3% lower mean absolute error. This research is an example of how supervised machine learning can be applied to the enhancement of real-world applications, as well as the development of suitable evaluation and experimentation methodologies for the evaluation of algorithm execution on hardware platforms. The search for extraterrestrial intelligence, or SETI, seeks to discover signs of advanced civilizations elsewhere in the universe by listening for signals from other worlds. A logical place to look for such signals is around a black hole, as an advanced civilization could potentially use a black hole as a powerful amplifier to broadcast their signals over vast distances. Considering a scenario in which an observer detects an irregular signal coming from a region near a black hole, where a star with a habitable planet is shining brightly, we examine the possibility that this signal could be evidence of an artificial communication device built around the black hole by an advanced alien civilization. Using a new theoretical framework for a shell of particles orbiting a black hole, we calculate the electrical current generated by electrons as they move in unusual orbits, and show that this current could produce signals in the form of radio waves at a rate of up to 10% of the star's luminosity. We explore how this signal might appear to an observer from different angles, and discuss how SETI researchers can use their existing detection methods to search for signs of an alien communication device building, such as the use of pulsar radio telescopes to search for artificial signals around black holes. We also propose a new strategy for searching for such a signal, based on the unique properties of a Dyson shell constructed from Dirac's electrons, which could provide a message from an alien civilization that might be more difficult to decipher. Finally, we consider the possibility that a black hole itself could be a message from an advanced alien civilization, such as in the form of its mass spectrum, and discuss the potential for future research in this area. Additionally, I have included an appendix with a proposal for a Dyson Shell Research Initiative that could provide funding and resources for researchers to explore this area further. Ultimately, while we have found that a Dyson Shell can produce signals that could be detected by SETI, we cannot conclude that the signals observed around the black hole in this letter are evidence of an alien communication device, and therefore cannot end this letter with the words "We are not alone". Nevertheless, this letter does demonstrate that searching for a Dyson Shell could provide new insights into the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, and could potentially pave the way for a deeper exploration of this area in the future. Therefore, I hope that this letter will serve as an invitation to the broader research community to engage with this area, and consider applying for funding through a Dyson Shell Research Initiative that could provide support for this type of research. Ensuring these standards are met necessitates the monitoring of service quality. A method has been proposed that relies on user feedback, collected and assessed by a peer-to-peer network of nodes, to identify SLA breaches and determine their location. This approach eradicates the need for central authorities that charge fees for their services and, instead, allows users to contribute to the identification of performance standard violations in a decentralized manner. A simulation-based evaluation of the proposed system is presented, considering various aspects such as security, scalability, and the reliability of results, which indicate that it effectively identifies breaches and their causes. Furthermore, it highlights the possibility of identifying performance standard violations in a decentralized manner, even in large networks. A comparison with a central-authority-based system, in terms of the cost of detecting breaches, shows that the proposed method offers a significant improvement, a benefit that is particularly noticeable in networks with a small number of nodes. The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators and typically constrains the maximum beam current that can be achieved, especially for energy recovery linacs with multiple passes where a small amount of charge can generate a large beam current. Studies have shown that in an energy recovery linacs, a specific type of beam breakup, known as the regenerative (REG) BBU, occurs due to the recovery process and can cause BBU in preceding bunches. Certain design features of an energy recovery linacs, including fill patterns and particle distributions between passes, can influence the REG BBU and potentially be managed to raise the acceptable current level. This paper specifically explores how different fill designs impact the REG BBU and suggests strategies for optimizing design features to minimize this instability, thereby increasing the overall efficiency of energy recovery linacs. Experimental validation will be discussed using data from the DESERVE test facility at DESY, which demonstrated that certain designed separations between passes can reduce the REG BBU gain below the critical threshold, allowing for higher current operation. In addition, the study identifies key parameters that influence REG BBU and proposes a new theoretical model that can be used to design and optimize the performance of energy recovery linacs in various applications, including those with macro-radiation sources like synchrotron radiation facilities. The model and the associated discussion provide insights into the physics underlying REG BBU and can be applied to other similar situations involving beam-beam interactions in multi-pass accelerators. Ultimately, this research offers a path for optimizing the performance of energy recovery linacs by incorporating a detailed design of the particle distribution between passes, which can lead to a significant increase in the current levels achievable in these machines. This work is particularly relevant to future energy recovery linacs for free-electron lasers, high-brightness electron storage rings, and other applications requiring high currents. The associated design challenges and solutions can also be applied to existing and planned energy recovery linacs at facilities such as the National Synchrotron Light Source II, the Stanford Linear Accelerator Center, and the free-electron laser facilities in Germany and Japan. The study's findings and the proposed theoretical model can be used to design and optimize the performance of energy recovery linacs in various applications, and the results obtained from the DESERVE test facility can be applied to other similar situations involving beam-beam interactions in multi-pass accelerators. The 3D-projection scintillator detector, a novel sensor design, offers a new approach to detecting neutrons by utilizing the spatial and temporal characteristics of alpha particles induced by thermal neutrons in plastic scintillators. Consequently, this detection method can significantly enhance the precision of neutrino flux measurements in water or hydrocarbon detectors, which are crucial for determining neutrino parameters. Therefore, it is highly recommended to incorporate this detection method in any neutrino experiment that relies on the measurement of neutrino flux. In a previous series of experiments, we discovered how sticking forces changed in response to temperature among particles made of chondritic materials, which indicated that their surface energy drops by approximately 5 times when temperatures rise. In the present study, we investigate the effect of water on the surface of these particles as their temperature increases from 100 to 600 Kelvin, which is a common range found in the heart of a star. Since water in such conditions exists in a vapor form, it evaporates when exposed to higher temperatures. However, it re-condenses on the surface of the particles once temperatures drop. This cycle causes the water to break down into oxygen and hydrogen gases when temperatures reach 400 Kelvin, which gets trapped between the particles. As a result, the particles start to attract each other more strongly due to this presence of gases, which increases their adhesion beyond the levels seen in our previous study by as much as 10 times when temperatures reach 600 Kelvin. This means that particles in a protoplanetary disc environment will likely stick to each other very easily at higher temperatures, which could have implications for how they collide in such conditions. This new understanding could also provide a reason for the uneven distribution of rocky and icy particles observed in some star systems, which occurs due to the different collisional behaviors of these particles as temperatures rise. This effect on sticking forces could also contribute to the growth of larger particles or even objects in a protoplanetary disc by making collisions more effective in this regard. This is especially relevant to how particles collide in a protoplanetary disc, which is influenced by the drag of gas as they move towards their host star, a process known as inward drift. This could, in turn, impact how particles grow in such environments, particularly in regions where temperatures are high enough for water to evaporate and get trapped between the particles. This is the case for regions closer to the star in a protoplanetary disc, which has implications for how objects form and grow in such environments. Imitation learning has emerged as a highly effective approach for robot skill learning due to its user-friendly and straightforward solution for robot control, namely playing back learned trajectories. Despite this, imitation learning's effectiveness is significantly limited by its ability to expand to complex tasks that involve multiple, nonlinear constraints beyond the learned experience. In response to this challenge, researchers have introduced various extensions to imitation learning that address specific difficulties such as unobservable actions, nonlinear constraints, and avoiding obstacles as complex as other agents within the environment. However, addressing all these challenges at once remains an unsolved problem in robot learning. In this study, a novel framework called EKMP is introduced which generalizes imitation learning to handle a range of complex robot learning tasks that are subject to multiple nonlinear constraints, including the complex constraint of avoiding other agents within the environment. This new framework extends previous works such as MP-IL that addressed robot learning with nonlinear constraints and obstacles avoidance but on a separate dataset, and EKMP shows the ability to leverage a broad range of expert demonstrations that cover the task's dynamics, are at least partially feasible, and do not require the learning robot to violate any constraints during the learning process. This is achieved through a precise analysis of the effects of constraints on imitation learning, introducing an auxiliary loss for adapting the learned policies, and using a novel form of projection that considers all the constraints at once. This leads to the creation of a high-quality set of policies that are feasible, diverse in their behavior, and meet the requirements for being robust and well-performed on the task at hand. This is in contrast to previous works that either only considered the feasibility of the learned policies or only considered their performance. Researchers explored an unusual approach to using machine learning with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT). Traditionally, ML models are trained on known samples to predict similar outcomes, but the team ventured into using an unsupervised method to train a model on the data itself. With no prior knowledge of sources, a Gaussian Mixture Model was applied to the Fermi-LAT all-sky map, resulting in 312 hidden clusters. These groups were later linked to 449 known sources and 57 blazars that are not source entries, with some sources being merged due to the nature of the analysis. A subsequent Hidden Markov Model was utilized to distinguish between persistent and variable sources, resulting in 71 additional variable sources not currently listed. This technique offers a self-consistent method for identifying variable sources and refining the Fermi-LAT all-sky map with no reliance on external information. However, some sources were merged or accounted for in the context of the analysis, so further confirmation is necessary via other methods. Additionally, potential sources with no prior knowledge are not covered in this analysis. Moreover, the model's complexity needs consideration, as increasing the number of Gaussian Mixture Model clusters beyond 312 did not yield notable differences. A discussion on potential sources of systematics and a summary of the findings in graphical form are included in the paper. Furthermore, 71 new variable sources with no prior knowledge have been identified and proposed for further confirmation via other methods. A proven strategy in medical image segmentation using few labeled samples is self-supervised learning.  One key method here is contrastive learning, which leverages unlabelled samples to extract more detailed image information.  One variation of this method, contrastive learning with data augmentation, forces the model to equate the descriptions of augmented images, thereby ensuring it pays attention to the image's core features.  However, this method has limitations, primarily because it relies on an assumption about the augmentations used, which may not always be valid, especially near image boundaries.  This issue is addressed in this paper by proposing a new framework that learns two separate boundary-sensitive descriptors, one for the inner regions and one for the boundaries, and then combines them to obtain a single descriptor for each image.  This framework is then tested using a public dataset for cardiac MRI segmentation, and the results show it achieves similar performance to the baseline method but with a significant improvement in accuracy, particularly near boundaries, and this benefit comes at only a minor increase in computational costs.  The code for this project is available online at https://github.com/zheng-chen1992/BCIM.  This method's effectiveness is further confirmed by a ablation study and a comparison with other self-supervised segmentation methods. Our research focuses on the popular Dungeons and Dragons game, where one player takes on the role of a dungeon master who guides the other players through the game by describing the environment and providing quests. To replicate this process through artificial intelligence, we created the G4C dataset, which consists of conversations between humans playing Dungeons and Dragons, along with the underlying goals and intentions of the dungeon master as inferred from their statements. We used this dataset to develop several metrics related to a dungeon master's role, including the ability to anticipate the next action of the players and the capacity to accurately identify the intentions of the players based on their behavior and statements. We demonstrated the superiority of our approach, which relies on Intention Language Models (ILMs), over more basic methods, and discovered that the performance of ILMs varies depending on the level of the player, with better results obtained for players of higher levels. This varies greatly from other NLP tasks that are often solved with established methods, due to the necessity for highly precise and consistent labeling at a massive data scale. Systematic flaws can easily arise, making it difficult to confidently apply and build upon these resources in a broader context. This issue can be addressed by assuming existing resources are a microcosm of a larger, varied categorization of words, where existing classes represent local maxima in a broader distribution. This new framework, which we call Lexical Semantic Variation Discovery (LSVD), seeks to identify and delimit these clusters across the vocabulary, even in the absence of annotated data, by leveraging neural language models that capture the underlying grammatical structure and enable generalization to unseen data. We apply LSVD to the evaluation of a widely-used taxonomy, WordNet, and achieve promising results by discovering boundaries, classes, and even relationships between them without relying on human annotations. This is further confirmed by an intuitive yet rigorous evaluation, where we demonstrate the discovered structures' similarity to the original by matching 75% of WordNet's synsets to our found classes with a 0.5 overlap threshold. These findings can be utilized to explain observed phenomena in hadron production and flow behavior and serve as input for quasiparticle viscous fluid-dynamic model simulations. Specifically, we investigate how quasiparticle distribution functions influence hadron production, elliptic flow coefficient behavior, and its $k_\perp$ dependence within a thermalized quasiparticle medium. Our study further reveals that hadron production is governed by quasiparticle distribution functions at both the initiation and final stages of the collision process. Notably, hadron production is driven by quasiparticles with properties similar to those of the medium's particles, in contrast to the medium's flow behavior, which is primarily influenced by quasiparticle interactions rather than their distribution functions. Reasoning about "what if" scenarios, whether expressed in single sentences or as phrases, is a fundamental ability required for advanced intelligence. Lacking the ability to entertain multiple hypotheses, current models struggle with tasks that demand this kind of reasoning, such as hypothesizing new data based on existing information. To overcome this limitation, we propose a method to incorporate and expand on sets of phrasal hypotheses using just a few key assumptions. By applying our approach to various datasets, we were able to demonstrate that it yields a compact representation that not only mirrors the original hypotheses but also allows for the generation of new data consistent with those hypotheses. Compared to alternative methods, our approach excelled in generating new instances from smaller sets of hypotheses and in producing results that align with those hypotheses when evaluated against those datasets. Furthermore, our model performed better than these competitors when assessed against other, unrelated datasets, indicating a level of generalization in its performance. Since our method relies solely on large language models, it offers a promising path for developing a more comprehensive theory of how these models represent and reason about hypotheses and how they combine them in our language. By applying our method to various datasets, we uncovered several patterns that could shape such a theory and discovered two crucial characteristics of good hypotheses: that they accurately describe specific instances and that they distinguish them from other categories. To fully capture these aspects, we propose a simple yet effective evaluation metric that weighs the accuracy of each instance and the overall category correctly. With this metric, we identified several key characteristics of both the data and the hypotheses and found them to be quite diverse in terms of structure and content. To apply our method on a larger scale, we introduced a new system that efficiently manages multiple hypotheses by allowing for the addition of new assumptions, the deletion of existing ones, and the generation of new instances from these hypotheses. This system, although relatively simple, already outperformed existing models on multiple datasets and could potentially serve as a foundation for more sophisticated systems that can process a wider range of assumptions and hypotheses. By exploring various combinations of our method and existing models, we demonstrated the importance of each component and confirmed that our approach offers a clear path for developing a more comprehensive theory of how large language models reason about multiple hypotheses and combine them in our language. Research into epitaxial Heusler films has given new direction to magnetic and spintronics research with the discovery of half-metallic and ferromagnetic properties in these materials. However, achieving this requires a precise understanding of the epitaxial relationship between the Heusler film and the substrate. This relationship can be influenced by the choice of substrate, with remote epitaxy offering magnetic order while pinhole and van der Waals epitaxy do not. This study investigates the epitaxial relationship between Co2FeSi (CFS) films and a graphene layer on an Al2O3 substrate. By analyzing the X-ray rocking curves and magnetic force microscopy, it was found that CFS films deposited on graphene have structural and magnetic properties indicative of remote epitaxy. Conversely, CFS films deposited directly on an Al2O3 substrate through pinholes exhibit structural and magnetic properties indicative of pinhole epitaxy. Van der Waals epitaxy was achieved by interposing a layer of h-BN on top of the CFS film. Notably, the magnetic order in CFS films was only observed when deposited on top of a layer of h-BN that had been previously deposited on the graphene, indicating that this method allows for the control of the epitaxial relationship between Heusler films and substrates that are inert and cannot be controlled by lattice matching or van der Waals bonding. This breakthrough provides new possibilities for the controlled deposition of magnetic films on complex substrates and could also be applied to other thin film systems. As a result of this technique, the structural and magnetic order of CFS films can be controlled by the choice of substrate and the method of deposition, offering new direction to research into magnetic and spintronics with Heusler films. This research is significant as it demonstrates the controlled deposition of magnetic order in CFS films by choosing the substrate and method of deposition, providing new possibilities for research into Heusler films. This could also pave the way for the controlled deposition of magnetic order in other thin film systems. This finding is particularly notable as it shows that magnetic order in CFS films only occurs when deposited remotely from the substrate, demonstrating the importance of understanding the epitaxial relationship between Heusler films and substrates to achieve magnetic order. Due to data quality issues and annotation expense, learning from single positive examples with no corresponding negatives has become a prominent challenge in machine learning. This study reveals that even with optimal model performance on single positive examples, there is always room for improvement when comparing it to learning from accurately labeled negative and positive samples. This research takes single positive labeled data and removes any inaccurately classified examples to create a more reliable training set, resulting in significant boosts in accuracy when compared to training on the original single positive labeled data. When assessed using diverse models and diverse features, this technique consistently yields consistent gains, demonstrating that there is always potential for improvement when comparing single positive examples to accurately labeled positive and negative examples. This study's methodology is called "CleanAll", which systematically eliminates flawed multi-label examples by removing those with incorrectly assigned class labels and only utilizing those with all relevant labels, thereby creating a more precise training set. When compared to learning from inaccurately classified multi-label examples, CleanAll yields substantial gains, with an average increase of 11.2% when compared to learning from single positive examples and 5.4% when compared to learning from accurately classified multi-label examples. This technique's effectiveness is demonstrated across six diverse datasets when both primary and secondary labels are considered, with an added benefit of significantly reducing data diversity when compared to learning from single positive examples, resulting in 23% less data diversity when considering only accurately classified multi-label examples. CleanAll's source code is available at https://github.com/zhengyuanliu/SinglePositiveLearning, and it outperforms existing methods using diverse models and diverse features on diverse datasets, especially when considering only accurately classified multi-label examples, resulting in a new state-of-the-art performance of 84.6% when compared to learning from single positive examples and 81.4% when compared to learning from inaccurately classified multi-label examples on the MNIST dataset, resulting in 0.6% gain when compared to the current state-of-the-art art on CIFAR-10 and 0.4% gain on NLP-2000. We establish a bidirectional connection between the category of observables in a quantum theory and the category of states. This relationship allows us to derive the Hilbert space associated with a given set of observables and states, and vice versa, using a process that incorporates both category theory principles and physical transformation constraints. This link between categories of observables and states can also be used to create a Hilbert space from a set of physical operators, and has implications for the debate over the origin of the Hilbert space in quantum mechanics. Furthermore, our approach facilitates the exploration of differentiable maps between categories of observables and states, leading to potential applications in distinguishing different quantum spacetime and recovering the geometry of physical states. Interestingly, we show that the category theory framework can handle both finite and infinite-dimensional Hilbert spaces. We primarily focus on discrete categories but also discuss the discrete-continuous interface. Notably, our theory is agnostic regarding the specific nature of the quantum field theory being studied, making it universally applicable. We include examples based on both scalar field theory and U(1) gauge field theory to illustrate our concepts. Additionally, we discuss how our formulation aligns with and builds upon existing connections between physical states and Hilbert space, as well as how it complies with the principles of Dirac's self-consistency criteria for quantum theories. Lastly, we investigate the relationship between category theory and the operator theorem of Gelfand and Kolmogorov, as well as the role of von Neumann's algebraic approach in the history of quantum mechanics. Our work is an extension of our earlier research reported in [arXiv:2012.04026] and [arXiv:2105.01144]. The origin of gamma-rays from nearby galaxies that emit radio waves remains an unsolved mystery. To address this, we propose a hypothesis that these galaxies contain overpowered magnetic fields in their central regions, preventing relativistic electrons from escaping. This would allow for the creation of a unique electron population, as well as a disk that is restricted by magnetic fields and prevents the escape of high-energy electrons. As a result, these electrons collide with accretion disks, producing gamma-rays in the process. By applying this model to 19 galaxies that emit radio waves, we found that it can account for up to 90% of the detected gamma-ray flux in certain energies, with an added component that possibly originates from relativistic jets responsible for emitting radio waves and accounting for the remaining gamma-ray flux. However, this model falls short of explaining all observed gamma-rays below 1 GeV by a margin of about 4 times when considering all galaxies, but it does so for the majority in a data set spanning 7 years. Furthermore, when accounting for the energy density within these galaxies, our model suggests that a small fraction of it, equivalent to 1% in energy, needs to be allocated for particles in order for it to function as intended. This study provides a viable hypothesis to account for gamma-rays in galaxies that emit radio waves and highlights the significance of magnetic fields in the central regions of these galaxies. It also implies a link between the production of gamma-rays and the creation of magnetic fields that restrict electron dispersal in these galaxies. As such, it represents a significant area for further research in the field of astrophysics and particle physics. Given that it is now possible to directly observe magnetic fields in the central regions of nearby galaxies using the Magnetic Field Imaging Technique, which uses the polarization of light to do so, it is also possible to validate or refute our hypothesis based on the characteristics of magnetic fields in these galaxies. This includes the possibility of validating the model by demonstrating a correlation between the strength of magnetic fields and the production of gamma-rays within these galaxies. This could, in turn, provide a means to use the characteristics of magnetic fields as an indicator to predict the presence of gamma-rays in these galaxies, which could also contribute to a broader discussion on the role of magnetic fields in the central regions of these galaxies and the search for a similar phenomenon occurring in the Milky Way. The CAPM's assumption that all assets within a given market are perfectly correlated has been widely criticized. To address this issue, we draw on the principles of portfolio theory to develop a method for allocating returns across a given set of securities. This approach utilizes a lower-dimensional representation of the market's securities, based on their fundamental characteristics, to create a more efficient and manageable framework for analyzing and understanding the relationships between securities. We demonstrate the use of this approach in two contexts. Firstly, we show that the U.S. stock market can be represented by a two-dimensional space, which has implications for the characteristics of portfolios listed on the NASDAQ. Secondly, we explore the application of this approach to credit portfolios, using a two-dimensional representation of the U.S. investment-grade bond market to examine the characteristics of default dates and recoveries. We find that the U.S. stock market and the U.S. investment-grade bond market both operate under similar rules regarding the characteristics of portfolios, which we term the portfolio rule. We also discover that the portfolio rule cannot be explained by theories such as the theory of portfolio choice or the theory of endogenous default, but rather it appears to be an exogenous constraint. As a result, we see that the portfolio rule creates the environment for the model of multiple equilibriums to operate in practice, which has implications for the model's ability to provide a stable framework for analyzing and understanding the behavior of portfolios within a given market. We further develop a method for determining the optimal portfolio allocation within a given market, using an example from the U.S. investment-grade bond market to show that it is possible to create a portfolio that is more diversified and performs better than the existing benchmark portfolios, which are typically constructed using a traditional method. We also discuss the potential applications of this approach in fields such as macroeconomic modeling, finance, and statistics, which involve the use of multiple time series with underlying common factors. We believe that this approach can be used to develop a more efficient method for allocating returns across multiple time series, which can provide a more accurate and stable estimation of the parameters of interest. Heart conditions such as Aortic Regurgitation and Left Ventricular Dysfunction can be diagnosed through the mitral heart sound, which is affected by background noise and the quality of the recording device used. This study investigates how mitral heart sounds are classified in the presence of external noise and poor audio quality. Two types of disturbance were tested: white noise and distortion caused by a poor recording device. The results show that certain classification methods have better performance in specific noisy environments and that the choice of algorithm depends on the level of noise. The research found that a particular combination of classification method and signal processing technique yielded higher accuracy rates of up to 90%. Two neutral atomic gas lines, namely CII at 977 GHz and CI at a combination of 609 and 829 GHz, hold promise for studying gas phases in galaxies using mm-/submm-wavelength observations. A statistical analysis of 44 galaxies in the mm-wave survey shows that CII and CI line intensities are lower than expected at high temperatures, potentially useful as independent probes of gas temperature. These lines can also serve as indicators for non-equilibrium, overdense regions within molecular gas reservoirs, particularly related to star formation and AGN activity. Akin to dust thermal emission, the CI and CII lines can provide a temperature map of galaxies over an ~100 K range, independent of dust properties. A correlation between the line intensity ratio of CII over CI and gas temperature is identified around the expected thermal values in the mm-wave survey, supporting its use as such a probe. A similar case is also identified in a CO-emitting Compton-thick Seyfert galaxy, NGC 4388. Line intensity maps of these galaxies, along with Mrk 231, a galaxy with an active galactic nucleus, reveal a ~500 K temperature gradient in their molecular gas reservoirs and a possible temperature drop in Mrk 231's gas reservoir due to the intense radiation from an extremely bright and compact hidden nucleus. To fully explore this source type, sophisticated signal patterns on pulsar timelines must be calculated, taking into consideration various degrees of orbital eccentricity. In this research, we offer a comprehensive assessment of precise post-Newtonian models in relation to PTA data analysis, specifically in relation to computational costs and metrological biases. Our study reveals that in PTA contexts, the standard quadrupolar PTA signal can be effectively replicated by a simplified, less expensive method known as the Phinney model, with a similar precision that is only slightly degraded at higher eccentricities. However, even in PTA-sensitive regimes, post-Newtonian signals exhibit a level of complexity that is difficult to capture by the Phinney model, especially in regions of high eccentricity, thereby implying that current PTA signals may be too narrow in scope. To facilitate a more comprehensive search for PTA signals, we recommend incorporating various higher-order multipolar PTA signals, especially in cases of high eccentricity. Our study demonstrates that in PTA data analysis, the most efficient approach involves combining the Phinney model with its quadrupolar and octupolar components in order to achieve a good balance between signal replication precision and computational costs. Furthermore, we provide a detailed computational cost breakdown for all considered post-Newtonian signals in relation to PTA, along with a step-by-step guide on how to implement these models through the GWSpy Python package. Our research offers valuable insights that can facilitate a more effective detection of highly eccentric PTA signals, which are anticipated to contribute significantly to the overall gravitational wave background. In addition, our findings can facilitate a more comprehensive comparison with predictions made by numerical relativity in a broader context of gravitational wave astronomy. Acronyms and abbreviations serve as shorter versions of lengthy phrases, commonly found in diverse settings like newspapers, websites, and technical documents. Although they are instrumental in saving writing time and space, they can also lead to confusion if not clearly defined, particularly if the acronym appears numerous times within a single document. To address this issue, stakeholders employ acronym lists, coupled with disambiguation techniques to clearly define these abbreviations and facilitate seamless comprehension. Against this backdrop, our proposed system, dubbed MadDog, is an exclusive acronym identifier and disambiguation tool accessible via the web. MadDog empowers users to add acronyms alongside their definitive explanations, thereby ensuring accurate comprehension as they navigate through documents, websites, or engage in reading activities. Furthermore, MadDog is equipped with an advanced user interface that enables seamless interaction and straightforward management of user-defined acronym lists. By integrating this functionality into a custom-built browser extension, MadDog is capable of detecting and clarifying undefined acronyms within web pages, complete with an option for users to customize the detection settings and export predefined acronym lists. To facilitate scalable and secure data storage, MadDog utilizes a MongoDB database in conjunction with Node.js-based backend services. The acronym list panel is responsible for displaying and managing the user-defined acronym list, whereas the settings panel provides customization options for the detection settings and the acronym list. Our previous work introduced a robust, error-free DNA data storage system called DecoBox, which ensures the integrity of stored information in the presence of sequencing errors. However, DecoBox had limitations, primarily its inability to efficiently support complex data hierarchies and update operations. To address these shortcomings, we have developed an enhanced version of DecoBox, now capable of organizing data using a nested hierarchy and facilitating update operations by assigning a new identifier to each data element. Unfortunately, this approach necessitates the resequencing of the entire dataset, posing a performance challenge. To mitigate this, we have introduced a new update strategy in the enhanced DecoBox, where each data element is assigned a unique identifier composed of two parts: a static hierarchical identifier and a dynamic change tracker. When an update is performed, only the change tracker is modified, allowing for more efficient storage with an option for sequential reading. Notably, this update strategy compromises a little on data integrity for the sake of performance, accepting the risk of returning incorrect data in rare cases if there is an error during sequencing. In our evaluation, the enhanced DecoBox has demonstrated significant improvement in data storage efficiency and update speed. To support hierarchical storage, DecoBox now utilizes a binary tree data structure, with each node representing either user data or a subnode, allowing for up to 4 levels of nesting. A demonstration storage system, encompassing over 1,000 user data elements and featuring a hierarchy of 3-4 levels, has been successfully implemented using a long-read sequencer. The enhanced DecoBox system has been made available for public use through an open-source code repository. Its update strategy presents an interesting problem for future research, given its trade-off between data integrity and update performance. Further study is also warranted to explore DecoBox's potential for applications requiring hierarchical data storage. The findings presented in this work have been formally published at the IEEE International Conference on Communications (ICC). To facilitate further investigation, a demo version of the storage system used in this research is available for consideration by the research community. It stores approximately 1.5 Gb of sequence data, comprising nearly 5,000 user data elements and a hierarchy of 3-4 levels, and has been successfully used with both short-read and long-read sequencers. Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in both physics and mathematics, characterized by exceptional properties of certain objects within the system's spectrum. Topological phases of matter are defined by the unique relationships between these objects in both real and momentum spaces. Nodal lines, a particular entity in momentum space, rely on the intersection of two or more gaps in the spectral distribution to exist. They can be distinguished by specific quantities such as Z2, Chern number or winding number, which are calculated from the momentum-space representation of the system's Berry curvature. A recent surge in interest has centered around nodal lines found in three-dimensional bulk forms, such as crystals and metamaterials, described through the Minkowski space or its non-Euclidean variations. These abstract descriptions of geometry can be linked back to physical realities via suitable transformations, enabling the calculation of quantities like inter-node energy gaps and Berry curvatures. A key challenge lies in identifying suitable materials or structures that host these nodal lines, which requires a balanced approach involving theoretical predictions and subsequent experimental verifications. This review aims to explore the theoretical basis of nodal lines, discuss various types, and then delve into recent experimental demonstrations in photonic, phononic, and other systems, concluding with an overview of ongoing and future research in this field. Furthermore, the appendix contains an overview of Minkowski space in the context of nodal lines. Finally, the paper proposes a new, general framework for understanding nodal lines, which could potentially be applied to any spatial dimension. This new framework introduces a new topological constant, which is an integer value that can be derived from the momentum-space representation of the system's Berry curvature. This innovation permits us to incorporate shadow information into normal map estimation using optimization-based techniques, specifically by employing the non-linear conjugate gradient method. In addition to experimenting with artificial data, we also applied our technique to real photographs containing artificial shadows, successfully recovering the original normal maps and textures. Traditional motion deinterlacing techniques typically rely on outdated methods from the 1990s, which, despite their effectiveness for older TV standards, fail to meet the image processing requirements of today's technology. To address this shortfall, researchers propose a groundbreaking integration of deinterlacing within deep image reconstruction, leveraging a convolutional neural network (CNN) to overcome interpolation limitations and restore missing pixel data. A novel example of this integration, referred to as Real-Time Super Resolution Deinterlacing (RTSRD), is presented, utilizing a pre-trained SR network while accommodating non-standard interlacing patterns, such as video recorded from computer screens, without the need for explicit pattern identification. Comparative assessments reveal that TSRD outperforms both legacy deinterlacing methods and contemporary super-resolution models, delivering exceptional results in real-time, at 60 frames per second (fps). Furthermore, this research facilitates a deeper understanding of motion deinterlacing, underscoring the necessity for a more comprehensive framework that integrates deinterlacing, descaling, and super-resolution components, demonstrated through a unified prototype capable of processing standard and non-standard video content in real-time, at up to 30 fps. Source code and model repositories are available for download at https://github.com/antoniopadrella/real-time-super-resolution-deinterlacing. Experimental data, along with legacy deinterlacing method implementations, are available at https://github.com/antoniopadrella/deinterlacing-baselines. Divergent deinterlacing results, influenced by the selection of intermediate feature maps, are also revealed through additional analysis. Future enhancements to the TSRD framework, including the exploration of alternative super-resolution models and feature map selection strategies, are outlined for future development. Experimental findings validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, with potential applications extending beyond deinterlacing to related image processing challenges. In contrast to legacy methods, real-world footage processed through the proposed network exhibits noticeable artifacts, highlighting the need for further optimization to minimize these deficiencies. Notwithstanding this limitation, the integrated TSRD framework presents a pioneering solution for motion deinterlacing, providing a reliable solution for processing real-world video content. Overall, this research presents novel contributions to both motion deinterlacing and super-resolution in the field of computer vision. Although the proposed approach has yielded encouraging results, further scope exists for improvement and future innovations within this area. The Chew-Cutser method enables fast and accurate flooding pattern computation; however, its computational expense limits its practical application. This study introduces a novel approach that leverages deep learning to enhance the method's performance, enabling rapid execution. Leveraging the optimized algorithm and advanced computing hardware, we have achieved significant speed improvements, ranging from 50 to 300 times faster than the original, compared to approximately 100 times with traditional parallel processing. These enhancements have enabled us to model complex hydrodynamics, including downstream effects, within 5-20 seconds for typical urban flood scenarios and have $10^{-6}$-$10^{-5}$ depth-wise accuracy. Our proposed system can be accessed at https://floodsolver.org. HDR photography combines multiple photos captured at various exposure levels to counterbalance digital cameras' limited dynamic range. This approach has been successfully implemented in high-end cameras and software but hasn't been effectively achieved with smartphone cameras. We present a novel automatic technique for selecting and merging photos in HDR by utilizing a camera phone alone. Our method determines optimal images based on their radial exposure groups and executes them with minimal user input, resulting in smooth transitions and striking outputs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach by comparing its performances against human subjects and a well-established HDR software framework, Mukerjee et al.'s method, using a range of test scenes. Our results show that our chosen images generally receive higher scores than human picks and outperform Mukerjee et al.'s method in nearly all cases, with some instances of human selections being unmergeable. We provide the source code for our technique as an open-source project on GitHub, alongside all testing data and results. When applying a camera app that integrates our technique, we observe a noticeable increase in user willingness to use HDR photography, with nearly all subjects preferring the results over single-exposure photos. We facilitate the integration of our method into Android apps via a provided HDR service framework, while stressing the importance of real-time HDR capture and emphasizing future research directions in this area. With the growing prevalence of smartphone cameras in daily life, our proposed technique has the potential to enrich not only creative photography but also various practical applications relying on these devices. This is especially evident in settings where digital cameras or professional equipment aren't readily available, such as in some indoor scenes, where accurate HDR capture proves difficult due to inconsistent lighting conditions and visually striking HDR outputs are highly desirable. We explore the possibility of combining our method with cloud services for enhanced HDR photography but leave this area for future exploration. This research is the first to explore automatic HDR capture and merging using just a smartphone camera, resulting in high-quality images without the need for additional equipment or software. This has the potential to revolutionize photography in a variety of settings and scenarios, such as indoor scenes with difficult lighting conditions, where accurate HDR capture is crucial and visually striking outputs are highly prized. Machine learning models that incorporate causal concepts, such as causal neural networks and graph neural networks, are increasingly being explored for their potential to navigate through complex, dynamic systems by leveraging limited external guidance from static representations. These models have shown promise in solving static and dynamic problems by emulating intuitive processes like exploration and leveraging learned representations. However, the field faces significant challenges, including understanding how these models allocate computational resources, explicit representation of actions through inputs, and the role of prior knowledge in problem-solving. To address these issues, researchers are investigating ways to design these models in a principled manner, drawing from insights on computational cost, input representations, and prior knowledge. Despite the progress made in individual areas, there is a lack of comprehensive research on the subject. This paper aims to provide an overview of machine learning models that incorporate causal concepts, a summary of ongoing research challenges, and an analysis of existing work in this field. In addition, the paper proposes a framework for evaluating the design of these models and highlights potential areas for future research, including open-ended problems, the development of new learning objectives, and robust performance in real-world scenarios. Furthermore, the paper introduces a new challenge problem that requires the navigation of complex, dynamic systems through external guidance from dynamic representations, along with a supporting dataset and evaluation metrics. This challenge problem has the potential to drive innovation in machine learning research and could lead to breakthroughs in understanding complex systems through external guidance from dynamic representations. This research is presented at the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR) 2023. Additionally, the paper with the title "Navigating Causal Profound Learning" is available at the ICLR 2023 Workshop on Causal Learning for Procedural Tasks.
