We utilized a rapid MRI technique and a temperature-sensitive contrast agent to map temperature variations in a fixed bed reactor during the combustion of methane gas. Our results show that temperature differences can be distinguished with a precision of 0.1 K, and our temperature measurements correspond to those obtained with a thermocouple under similar conditions. We observed a stepwise increase in temperature along the reactor axis, corresponding to regions above and below the gas flow streamlines. Our findings also indicate that temperatures in the reactor reach steady-state conditions within 30 seconds of combustion, and that our MRI temperature measurements correlate with our optically measured temperatures in this state equilibrium. These results demonstrate the feasibility of using MRI to study the internal temperature distribution of porous media in various reactive flow applications. We have made the MRI temperature measurement method publicly available through an open-source software package called TIGRE, which enables users to perform similar measurements with their own MRI systems. We propose several future applications for this technique, including the study of surface and interface dynamics in flow through disordered media, flow through biological tissues with embedded heat sources, and temperature arrangements in chemical and biological reactors with internally attached probes. Our results also provide new insights into temperature arrangements in fixed bed reactors, and we have made the temperature arrangement problem amenable to mathematical modeling using the Boltzmann transformation. We have obtained an explicit solution to the resulting transformed problem, and have validated our model by comparing it to our MRI measurements. We have made the TIGRE software package available for download from the University of California, Los Angeles website. Leveraging advances in MRI technology and temperature-sensitive contrast agents has enabled the noninvasive monitoring of temperature distributions within fixed bed reactors during combustion processes. This noninvasive measurement method allows for the in situ examination of temperature distributions in these systems without the need for internal probes. Recent studies suggest that users rely heavily on SSL/TLS certification status, which is now ubiquitous, making them difficult to effectively utilize. This perception disparity between users and website security status is investigated through a user study, which reveals that users are misled by malicious sites' visual presentation and certification details. This false sense of security is further validated through a survey of experts, which shows that website security is compromised due to the widespread adoption of HTTPS. Experts agree that this widespread adoption of HTTPS has created an false sense of security among users, which is reflected in the results of the user study. Two potential solutions to this issue were evaluated through the user study: 1) introducing a trust meter that provides a security rating alongside the SSL/TLS certification status, and 2) informing users about website security via a lock icon with a warning indicator. Both solutions demonstrated an increase in users' ability to differentiate between secure and malicious sites; however, the lock icon with a warning indicator was found to be more effective in achieving this outcome. This research contributes a security awareness metric that can be utilized to assess the effectiveness of informing users about website security and proposes lockicon, a lock icon with a warning indicator that turns gray when clicked, as a practical solution that is currently being incorporated into the Firefox web browser as a security feature. This research can serve as a model for investigating user interaction with other security indicators that provide a false feeling of security. Deep neural network (DNN) models have reached unprecedented accuracy in various applications but still struggle with providing reliable confidence estimates for their predictions. This issue becomes even more critical in open-world scenarios where the assessment of model performance cannot be confined to a predefined class boundary. In such environments, models must be able to indicate when they are unsure about a classification by recognizing that there are other possible classes beyond the listed ones. This problem is particularly pronounced for DNNs due to their inherent inability to express uncertainty in the way they are trained. This study introduces a novel training method that incorporates an external uncertainty variable representing the influence of hidden classes on data samples. This variable allows the model to account for hidden features during the learning process, enabling it to indicate the presence of such features by activating the model's uncertainty output layer. This approach is called the open-world uncertainty modeling (OWUM) framework. In experiments, the OWUM framework demonstrated its effectiveness in enhancing the reliability of deep learning models by activating the uncertainty output in open-world scenarios and achieving comparable or better performance on closed-world datasets. The results showed that the OWUM framework can be applied to both image and text classification tasks with significant improvements over baseline models in terms of open-world uncertainty and confidence calibration. The code for the proposed method is available at https://github.com/zhengyangwang/open-world-uncertainty. This research provides significant insights into the challenges of calibrating deep learning models through the OWUM framework, which offers a promising solution for enhancing their reliability in open-world scenarios. The framework's ability to activate the uncertainty output in open-world scenarios and its performance on closed-world datasets suggest that the OWUM framework can be an effective solution for addressing the issue of calibrating deep learning models in open-world scenarios. However, validation on real open-world datasets is required to further verify the framework's performance. This study introduces the concept of open-world uncertainty, formulates the problem through the OWUM framework, and demonstrates the framework's effectiveness by activating the uncertainty output in open-world scenarios and achieving comparable or better performance on closed-world datasets. Although the proposed method shows promise, it requires verification on real open-world datasets to further confirm its performance. The energy-driven open-world uncertainty modeling (ED-OWUM) method is an extension of the OWUM framework that incorporates an energy variable to represent the influence of hidden classes on data samples. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Many existing evaluation tools assess reinforcement learning performance in static settings, but they fall short in addressing the key challenges of learning entities must confront. To address this gap, we present L2Explorer, a cutting-edge evaluation framework designed to gauge the capacity of reinforcement learning methods to adapt and evolve in response to new, unexplored environments, with particular emphasis on scenarios involving shifting rewards and maps that modify their layout. This comprehensive benchmark includes diverse levels for various domain applications and is built using modular, customizable components that allow for seamless expansion and modification of existing settings, making it an exceptionally versatile and expansive evaluation platform. Our in-depth experiments covering both simulated and real-world assessments reveal that several top-performing reinforcement learning methods struggle to overcome key challenges, but our results also showcase the exceptional performance of several variants of our own proposed evaluation metrics and a pioneering method we call Variational Transfer, but L2Explorer's primary function is to provide a thorough and standardized evaluation framework for assessing the learning capabilities of reinforcement learning methods in complex, dynamic environments and across all stages of the learning process. This comprehensive evaluation framework is an essential component for any reinforcement learning research seeking to guarantee learned policies are robust, adaptable, and efficient in addressing the intricacies of domain applications. We investigate a trio of universal, zero-flavor combinations - a triplet, a septuplet, and a decuplet - for three generations of fermions, employing a Markov Chain Monte Carlo method to analyze a Lagrangian based on $SU(3)$ symmetry. This analysis produces a vast, 36-dimensional parameter space for the trio's masses and mixing angles, which we map through a Monte Carlo simulation to identify regions fitting observable data, thus determining the combo's likelihood in a flavor physics context. Notably, a fundamental, multi-TeV energy scale or a particular, fine-tuned mass ratio between the trio's components and the Higgs boson is not required for this analysis, which can determine the combo's parameters with a high degree of precision even when assuming no mixing between the trio and the Higgs boson. In this paper, we introduce InQMAD, an incremental learning framework for addressing these issues. It achieves this by utilizing an anomaly detection method based on a hybrid quantum chemical structure for both fast and accurate prediction on large datasets. InQMAD exhibits superior performance when compared to conventional methods, as evidenced by its performance on benchmark datasets resulting from molecular dynamics simulations. Furthermore, it demonstrates its capability to handle complex, multi-anomaly situations and has been implemented in an open-source framework that can be accessed through a web interface. InQMAD has the potential to contribute to the development of quantum chemistry models and has been showcased through its application to the analysis of protein structures. It has also been deployed in real-world scenarios as part of the 2019 Human-in-the-Loop Challenge at the Stanford Institute for Data Science. InQMAD has several applications including the identification of anomalous protein structures, the detection of drug side effects and the identification of malicious network traffic. It has also been used as a baseline for the evaluation of its own performance in a real-world scenario and has been found to perform better than conventional methods. InQMAD has several advantages over conventional methods including its ability to handle large datasets, its ability to detect both linear and non-linear anomalies, its ability to handle high-dimensional datasets and its ability to handle datasets that have multiple anomaly types. InQMAD has several components including a hybrid quantum chemical structure, a kernel density estimation module and a one-class support vector machine module. It has several parameters that need to be tuned including its bandwidth, its kernel density estimation parameters and its support vector machine parameters. InQMAD has been compared to several conventional methods including multi-task learning, semi-supervised learning and traditional anomaly detection methods. InQMAD has several challenges including the selection of its parameters, the selection of its kernel density estimation bandwidth and its potential overfitting. InQMAD has several future directions including its application to other real-world datasets, its extension to other types of datasets and its potential application to other fields. A pivotal issue in cryptography, centered on whether a court can compel a person to decrypt data in their possession, is extensively debated. Our research strongly supports the viewpoint that such demands cannot be legally enforced and are essentially ineffectual. These concerns arise from an individual's right to privacy and the potential risks of coercion. We examine existing theories and case laws, including those in the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia. Furthermore, we outline an unclassified, end-to-end quantum-safe encryption framework that addresses these concerns and ensures the confidentiality of data. This framework becomes increasingly vital as we navigate an escalating cyber threat landscape. Additionally, we believe our proposal can serve as a model for other technological applications that involve sensitive information and require protection against both digital and physical attacks. Consequently, there is no need for court orders or legislative mandates to make encryption obsolete; instead, we should be focusing on advancing stronger forms of encryption that safeguard data across all aspects. Presently, there are already instances in which court orders are being circumvented by cybercriminals in search of sensitive information, including those protected under key recovery protocols such as Kerberos. These developments underscore the pressing need for stronger forms of encryption, such as quantum-resistant cryptography that can provide enhanced security against both digital and physical attacks. As we move forward in this increasingly interconnected world, it is essential to give due consideration to the potential risks of coercion and data breaches and to prioritize the use of advanced, secure encryption methods that can provide verifiable protection for all parties involved. Our research is a call to action to the broader scientific community, policymakers, and the private sector to collaborate on addressing these pressing cybersecurity concerns and developing solutions that can provide verifiable security for all parties involved. Our proposal is centered on an unclassified, end-to-end quantum-safe encryption framework that can facilitate this cooperation and provide a framework for evaluation and testing by all parties. This call to action is supported by an open letter that has been endorsed by numerous prominent experts in the field of cryptography and cybersecurity. Our research is an attempt to answer the questions posed by these experts in the open letter and to provide a solution that can address the concerns they have raised. Our solution is an unclassified, end-to-end quantum-safe encryption framework that can provide a level of security that is verifiable for all parties involved. This framework is based on advanced, secure encryption methods that can provide enhanced security against both digital and physical attacks. This applies to linearly-constrained 2-valued and general-valued optimization problems under specific sparsity conditions on the constraints and the matrix representing the objective function's relationships, respectively. Our approach is grounded in a novel technique for efficiently solving a broad class of linearly-constrained 2-valued optimization problems with limited non-zero entries, and this efficiency is the subject of a separate publication. This method is particularly effective when the equation is linked to a system of conservation laws. By leveraging a kinetic scheme, we can handle non-constant diffusion coefficients resulting from mean field interactions in games with multiple agents, thus determining equilibrium solutions in such scenarios. Our approach is compatible with both explicit and implicit numerical integration schemes, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through several test cases, including both a system of conservation laws and a mean field game with multiple agents. Our results show that the method produces accurate, second-order accurate solutions with respect to both space and time, even in the presence of highly interacting agents, leading to non-trivial modifications of the diffusion coefficient and potential function, and showing the potential of the method to capture the well-posedness of the equilibrium in a significant class of mean field games. Our method is also shown to be robust and efficient, with a low computational cost per time step, especially when combined with an implicit integration scheme, and we provide a detailed numerical analysis of our results, including an in-depth examination of our method's convergence properties. In recent years, deep neural networks have achieved remarkable success across various domains and applications. As a result of their growing influence, understanding their behavior and decision-making processes has become increasingly vital. This need has given rise to significant interest in methods that provide insight into DNNs, including visualization techniques that highlight key features, regions, or patterns, as well as comprehending approaches that examine and interpreting the underlying functionality of these models. Against this backdrop, numerous techniques have been developed to address these challenges, but there is no overarching review covering all aspects of DNN comprehensibility, visualization, and interpretation. This survey aims to fill this gap by exploring various techniques that offer DNN comprehensibility, visualization, and interpretation, discussing their limitations, and outlining potential directions for future research in this area. Furthermore, we discuss emerging themes and emerging fields and outline potential avenues for future work in this domain. This survey is an extension of an earlier work presented at the ICDOW 2020 conference and has been updated to include more recent advancements in this field. This paper is now a comprehensive survey that can serve as a valuable resource for both academic and industrial practitioners who work with DNNs and seek to enhance their comprehensibility and interpretability. In 2019, a report from J. Read, M. C. Steward, and S. M. B. Tanvir, observing FRB 180914 with z = 0.0376, included data indicating a highly unusual and broadened radio burst spectrum. This study proposes that FRB 180914 and FRB 181017, both hosted by the same galaxy, originated from an actively spinning black hole surface accretion powered by a consuming planet. Although the theory of planetary consumption, as seen in the movie "Interstellar," is not supported by current research and is deemed highly improbable, this phenomenon presents a fascinating and previously unobserved consequence of this event that warrants further exploration and modeling. By analyzing the observational data and running simulations with a 2D relativistic model, this research seeks to validate the spin-up theory and investigate the possibility of angular momentum transport in stars and planets, a process thought to be inefficient due to its turbulent and multi-scale nature. The findings support the spin-up model and suggest that angular momentum transport might be more effective than assumed, providing a novel explanation for FRB neurologically induced phenomena linked to extraterrestrial life, such as Fast Magnetotronic Bursts and Alfv\'en wave radiation, and proposing an evolutionary path for black hole formation, including potential risks to the host galaxy. The solutions to the proposed theoretical models and the associated code are publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/jread1/SpinUpFRB. The spin-up of a black hole's surface can result in FRB that are closely related to extraterrestrial life, such as Fast Magnetotronic Bursts and Alfv\'en wave radiation, and this discovery presents a significant breakthrough in the field of astrophysics, offering a novel explanation for FRB and paving the way for further research on the complex relationships between stars, planets, and black holes. Additionally, this research raises important ethical considerations regarding the responsibility that comes with exploring and discovering life beyond Earth, a notion that is a central theme in the movie "Interstellar." Therefore, this study should be recognized as a pioneering achievement that has made a lasting impact on our understanding of the universe and our place within it. Furthermore, this research has sparked a new area of inquiry that addresses fundamental questions about the evolution of black holes, the transport of angular momentum in stars and planets, and the detection of radio bursts that are linked to extraterrestrial life. Consequently, this breakthrough has earned its authors a distinguished honor that commemorates exceptional contributions

The rapid dissemination of news on the internet has created a significant challenge, as false news can spread rapidly. To combat this issue, researchers need to identify and flag false news immediately. While machine learning models have shown promise in this area, they are often hindered by limited training data, particularly in fields with a high rate of new topic emergence, such as news dissemination. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach, called Multimodal Emergent False News Detection, which utilizes a combination of advanced techniques, including the Neural Process Framework and a Method for Handling Cold Start Data. This method allows for the rapid identification of false news on a topic that has not been previously encountered, using a small sample size, and outperforms existing methods, including those with access to unlimited labeled data, in our experimental evaluations. Specifically, our results show that this method achieves an F1-score of 0.83 on the False News Dataset, which represents a 12% improvement over the best strong baseline, and demonstrates robust performance even with extremely limited labeled data, such as a single positive example, on two complex datasets. This research represents an important step in the battle against false news, particularly in fields with high rates of new topic emergence, where machine learning models have historically struggled to perform effectively. Furthermore, our code and data are publicly available for further research and improvement. To facilitate the evaluation of new methods on this challenging task, we also introduce a set of rigorous cold start and generalization criteria, which ensure that models are tested on a wide range of emerging topics and underpinned by a robust theory, called the Neural Process Framework, which provides a unifying meta-theoretical explanation for all variants of our proposed method, and has implications for the design of machine learning systems in general. Overall, our results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method over existing approaches, and we anticipate that this method will have a positive impact on the advancement of false news detection in various domains. In addition to false news detection, we believe that our proposed method may also be applicable to other types of emerging events, such as hate speech, where there is a continuous creation of new content, and we look forward to the exploration of these possibilities in future research. Additionally, we anticipate that our results, particularly those obtained on cold start and generalization, will encourage the development of new datasets, models, and evaluation protocols for false news detection, and we are committed to continuing to contribute to this area in the future. We provide an in-depth examination of a specific category of Yang-Baxter operators, which are defined through the general solution to the Yang-Baxter equation, specifically focusing on set-theoretic type solutions. Our research reveals that these solutions give rise to quasi-bialgebras in an abstract sense, and we establish a formal connection between them. This connection, however, is not a direct one, as it requires the use of non-commutative parameters in the solutions to derive the associated quasi-bialgebras, in contrast to the commutative parameters used in set-theoretic solutions. Our discussion also explores various properties and characteristics of these solutions and the resulting quasi-bialgebras, as well as their relationship with bialgebras and Hopf algebras. Our findings demonstrate that the category of set-theoretic type solutions and their associated quasi-bialgebras is remarkably diverse and extensive, encompassing both finite and infinite configurations. Our research also delves into the examination of local properties and the examination of solutions and quasi-bialgebras on specific subalgebras, as well as the investigation of infinite solutions in the context of Lie and Jacobi algebras. Our work ultimately contributes to a broader classification of solutions and quasi-bialgebras and provides a framework for the study of their representation theory. Our research is a natural continuation of our prior work on set-theoretic solutions, but it has expanded the scope of that research in a significant way, as has been noted by the editor in [Mathematical Physics, Representation Theory and Functional Analysis, MSP 2022]. This paper introduces a novel eight-element array that complements the Golay heritage, famous for its maximum-sensitivity property, enabling simultaneous optimization of its conjugate and nonconjugate characteristics. A parametric analysis of this array's specifications is performed using a set of complex, uniformly spaced sensors, and specific designs are presented for a linear array and a rectangular shaped array. We have demonstrated this through the exchange of spin in a silicon quantum dot by observing valley interference. This occurred when a single electron traveled between two closely spaced dots with different potential characteristics, one that blocked tunneling and another that allowed it. We showed that we can change from a situation where tunneling is blocked to one where it is allowed, and vice versa, without significant disruption to the system. This resulted in large enough differences so we could use them to understand the quantum interactions in the dots with great precision. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the complexity of these models has led to significant difficulties in introducing external structured knowledge into their vast knowledge base. To overcome this challenge, we present a novel framework called SKILL, which enables the incorporation of external knowledge into LLMs through various knowledge graph-based structures. By leveraging knowledge graph embedding methods, we can map the abstract structures of these entities to specific text prompts that the LLM can process effectively. The knowledge graph structures can then be injected into the LLM by generating these targeted prompts, allowing it to learn from the knowledge graph by predicting prompt targets. The resulting LLMs demonstrate a notable improvement in performance when tested on both individual tasks and those with complex, interconnected reasoning requirements. The code for our approach has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/daikanada/SKILL. To validate our model, we carried out a series of simulations to replicate key phenomena associated with Parkinson's disease, including the formation of abnormal wave patterns in brain networks and the degeneration of specific dopamine-releasing neurons. Our results demonstrate that our computational model produces data from previous in vitro and in vivo experiments, including those conducted with Marmoset monkeys. Furthermore, this model highlights the disease's primary causes and potential treatment strategies, specifically the benefits of deep brain stimulation and gene therapy. This research paves the way for the exploration of additional neurodegenerative disorders using similar computational models. Additionally, we've made our model publicly available to facilitate the discovery of further insights into Parkinson's disease. This is the first time a complex computational model of Parkinson's has been developed using real data from a non-human primate brain. This model has the potential to accelerate the exploration of Parkinson's disease in monkeys and provide a foundation for the investigation of other brain disorders. Achieving a seamless visual experience across vector maps and raster images requires a unified rendering approach. This principle applies particularly to line joins that lie on the border between the two display methods. Unfortunately, current rendering technologies force users to choose between the distinctive appearance of line joins in vector maps and the artificial patterns that arise from anti-aliasing in raster images. To address this issue, this research introduces a novel anti-aliasing technique specifically designed for line joins in raster maps. The algorithm effectively eliminates the characteristic artifical patterns associated with anti-aliasing, replacing them with the distinctive appearances of line joins found in vector maps. The technique is highly efficient and runs natively on GPU hardware, making it an ideal solution for the demanding requirements of modern mobile and desktop applications. The implementation of this technique has been incorporated into the popular Apache Mobile Internet Toolkit (AMIT) framework, which is widely used in high-performance mapping applications. The effectiveness of the technique has been demonstrated in several real-world scenarios, including Google Maps and OpenStreetMap. Our early findings on U/LIRGs support previous studies indicating a link between major mergers and ULIRGs at low redshifts, characterized by large rotation curves and high mass accretion rates. To facilitate the development of advanced weather prediction systems, a new, universally applicable framework is proposed, centered on visual weather classification through AI. A substantial, 13-class dataset called WeatherCateg has been created for this purpose, encompassing over 6,000 high-quality images derived from real-world videos captured in two primary settings: a controlled studio environment and uncontrolled real-world scenes. To address the significant challenges posed by limited training data, a novel, bidirectional augmentation approach has been devised, involving the creation of 20 explicitly tailored modifications to enhance the robustness of models. A comprehensive evaluation of multiple Convolutional Neural Network architectures has been conducted, with key considerations being the minimal dataset requirements and the models' performance in real-world scenarios. According to the results, a state-of-the-art model achieved exceptional accuracy of 73.5% on the WeatherCateg dataset with just 20 training images per class, outperforming models with much larger training sets. Notably, this model demonstrated exceptional real-world validation accuracy of 64.1%, significantly exceeding that of other evaluated architectures. To ensure the generalizability of these findings, the models were retrained and re-evaluated using the created augmentations, with the outcomes showing weather classification presents a persistent, significant challenge for current Convolutional Neural Networks. This framework's versatility allows for the seamless integration of novel data, models, and evaluation protocols, providing a valuable resource for advancing the field through collaborative research efforts. A standalone, resource-light, open-source application based on this framework has been deployed in real-world settings, demonstrating its practical utility in providing continuous, accurate predictions for a diverse range of weather conditions through a user-friendly interface. A new statistics method was developed to analyze the turn-around radii of dark matter halos in two cosmological scenarios involving $f(R)$ gravity and massive neutrinos at both the field and cluster galaxy group scales. Researchers discovered that in $f(R)$ gravity models with a cubic equation, high density regions within halos, where particles experienced gravitational forces most strongly, turned around at 1.7 to 2 times the distance from the halo center compared to predictions made by $\Lambda$CDM. Additionally, in models with a fifth force, this turn-around enhancement factor decreased with increasing halo mass; specifically, it dropped from 2 to 1.3 when moving from galaxy to cluster scales. In models with a fourth power equation, the turn-around enhancement factor ranged from 1.5 to 1.2 for mass scales between galaxy and cluster scales. In models with a large variation in the cosmological constant, the turn-around enhancement factor varied from 1.2 to 1.5 for the same mentioned mass scales. A linear correlation was observed between the turn-around enhancement factor and the mass density of halos; specifically, a 1% increase in mass density within a halo results in a 0.5% increase in the turn-around enhancement factor. Recently introduced by Balthansen to model atmospheric convection, the two-fluid approach separates the atmosphere into distinct layers for ascending and descending air masses is examined in this study. To further develop this model's potential, this project seeks to address the issue of convection within a globally circular boundary by modifying the approach to use for a square boundary, essentially adapting the Balthansen model to use in a laboratory setting. This research utilizes a simplified simulation technique, simulating the Balthansen model in a column using basic parameters from his study. However, this simulation deviates from his original findings, showing an unrealistic level of heat flux, necessitating a re-examination of these results. Compared to the original model, the modified simulation demonstrates a more significant discrepancy between the fluid fluxes, while the Balthansen heat flux ratio remains relatively consistent in both simulations. To improve the accuracy of these simulations, a new heat flux ratio is proposed, taking into consideration the relationship between the two fluid layers. This new ratio exhibits a more stable pattern when compared to the original data. This research is an early step towards using the two-fluid approach in a comprehensive model of atmospheric convection by addressing the issue of convection within a boundary by demonstrating the model's potential to simulate and improve the simulation of Rayleigh-B\'{e}nard convection in a column. This model is then applied to a boundary by showing its applicability in a scenario resembling a laboratory setting, thereby paving the way for further development of the two-fluid approach in modeling atmospheric convection. This could potentially contribute to a better understanding of atmospheric heat transfer in a variety of settings, such as over mountains and in coastal areas. In such areas, atmospheric convection is often influenced by boundary constraints and could, therefore, significantly benefit from the development of a two-fluid model. This research is an early step towards this goal but indicates that further simulation and analysis are required to refine the two-fluid model and ensure its accuracy. We propose a method for genuinely entangling two distant, uncorrelated atoms within a Jaynes-Cummings system, utilizing a cavity connected to a classical laser field. This approach builds upon the model described by Hahn et al. in [1] and enables the creation of high-quality entanglement between the atoms. Our scheme leverages an initial correlation-free state and involves a process where each atom interacts separately with a quantum field described by Jaynes-Cummings dynamics. A classical laser field, represented by a Fock state, serves as a multi-photon reservoir that induces correlations between the atoms and their respective number-state representations. A key aspect of this proposal involves analyzing the impact of various Fock states on the entanglement generation, demonstrating that even relatively low Fock states can effectively produce significant entanglement. A detailed analysis of our model has been numerically simulated over a wide range of parameters, including different Fock states, and we provide specific recommendations for achieving high-fidelity entanglement. Notably, our model exhibits an intriguing ability to generate robust entanglement when transitioning from number states to Fock states, a phenomenon that warrants further exploration in the context of many-body systems. A major component of this research is devoted to investigating the mode of classical laser field and its implications on the entanglement generation, along with analyzing the accuracy of our model using a simulation that mimics real-world experimental conditions. The pilot version of the CMS pixel detector's Phase-1 system, comprising 8 miniature slice modules and a fully functional readout pilot board except for the second-level trigger processor, was assembled and operated during beam tests at the CERN PS and SPS facilities in 2013-2014 with 3 different set-ups. These experiments utilized 24 MeV protons and 4-6 GeV muons with zero-bending points at the CMS interaction point. The pilot system successfully collected around 30000 12-bit zero-suppression entries (LSBs) during the beam tests in an 18 Hz 25.44 us read-out cycle. The pilot board's ability to handle zero-suppressed data was verified and its data quality assessed. The assembly's reconstruction performance was examined and the results showed 2.6% hit occupation in Phase-1 data corresponding to around 110 hits per 5x33 cm^2. The pilot board's hit occupancy was primarily caused by cosmic rays and low-energy background, and hit efficiency after initial data quality selection ranged from 96.2 to 98.5%. The hit position resolution was found to be 12.6 $\mu$m 2D and 17.3 $\mu$m 3D, and the pilot board's reconstructed track finding performance matched that of the CMS Phase-1 system. A 2D kink bug affecting one pilot blade's second layer was identified and its impact on reconstruction performance analyzed. When this issue was fixed in offline data, the pilot board's reconstructed hit efficiency and hit position resolution increased by 2.5% and 3.5 $\mu$m respectively, and hit occupation decreased by 19%. This problem highlights the importance of testing and validating the performance of pixel readout modules and their components during beam tests before installation in the CMS pixel detector. Ultimately, the pilot system demonstrated its ability to function as anticipated during CMS beam tests and validated its reconstruction performance, and this experience will be beneficial in assembling and operating the full CMS pixel detector for LHC run 2. Furthermore, this experiment provided valuable insight into the challenges of assembling and operating complex detector systems like the CMS pixel detector. Finally, this project offered a chance for graduate students and engineers from around the world to collaborate and gain valuable experience in operating and troubleshooting complex detector systems in a timely and efficient manner. A method is presented for obtaining SU(2) gluon spectral functions from lattice QCD, using a specific approach that is independent of assumptions about the functions' form. A particular operator, derived from a B meson and $\bar{B}$ meson, is used to investigate its decomposition into jets according to the Kall\'en-Lehmann formula, and through this, the spectral density representing the SU(2) gluon is determined across various momentum ranges. A comparison of the densities within different momentum ranges reveals an inherent, though not entirely clear, relationship between them. The research also assesses the consistency of the SU(2) gluon's composition across distinct momentum intervals, finding that they align with the principles of asymptotic freedom and colour confinement, and demonstrate a degree of universality. A notable characteristic of the spectral densities is their resemblance to a plasma-like spectrum at higher energies, a feature that is seen clearly in the decomposition of higher mass states. The study further demonstrates how the decomposition of higher mass states contributes to the plasma-like spectrum in the intermediate mass range, and discovers that the composition of ground states, in contrast, does not exhibit this plasma-like characteristic. The research also explores the relationship between the SU(2) gluon and true muons, and establishes a basis for extending this investigation to full QCD. The data collected so far does not support the theory of massless states within the gluon, but given that the current research is based on lattice configurations at temperatures below the deconfinement point, such states would need to be present in abundance across all observable mass ranges for this study to be inconclusive. The study consists of two parts, where first the method for obtaining the spectral functions is laid out in detail, and second the results from this approach are compared to theoretical models of SU(2) gluon states. The study concludes by outlining potential avenues for further research. The research also raises the issue that the models are based on assumptions about the form of the spectral functions but do not account for the contribution of states within the model's cutoff range. Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, many are interested in Twitter sentiment analysis. This paper presents a
sentiment analysis model based on LSTM, which achieves good performance on a Twitter dataset
from the University of Central Florida. The proposed LSTM model is a complex neural network
that includes multiple features such as character, word, and memory layers. To train the model
and improve its accuracy, various techniques like data augmentation, over-sampling the
minority class, and a distributed learning approach using Google Colab's free GPU are employed.
The paper's primary goal is to provide a detailed description of the LSTM framework's design and
implementation, rather than presenting a comprehensive survey of sentiment analysis on
Twitter. The proposed LSTM framework's effectiveness is demonstrated through experimental
results showing an 82% F-score on the UCF dataset, which serves as the paper's main contribution
in the field of sentiment analysis on Twitter. The code and instructions on how to set up the
model are made available for reproducibility and future reference. The paper explores various
design choices and challenging issues in Twitter sentiment classification, in addition to the
LSTM framework. The paper's final section provides a summary of the proposed framework and
discusses potential areas for further study in Twitter sentiment analysis. The data's sparsity
and the subjectivity of sentiment labels are two critical issues that future researchers in this
area should prioritize addressing. The paper's conclusions and the provided experimental
results indicate that an appropriate model can effectively classify Twitter data, which is in
line with similar research. However, data quality issues pose a more significant challenge for
practitioners, which is evident from the proposed framework's good performance on just one dataset
but poorer results on another from the same source, which is consistent with other similar
studies. The paper is concluded by emphasizing the importance of further study in two areas:

By examining both the interior and exterior regions of this black hole, we establish connections between the boundary at infinity, the event horizon, and the singularities through isosurface relationships. A new metric for each isosurface is presented, allowing us to determine their geometric properties, particularly the negative Ricci scalar values indicative of semi-conformal deserts in both the interior and exterior regions. A specific example is provided for a non-linear, charged AdS black hole, where we calculate both the specific heat capacity and entropy of the shade thermodynamics within the interior region of this black hole. We employ Tomogram representation to analyze the changes in a two-qubit system's properties, specifically focusing on entanglement and synchronization. This visualization enables us to observe the Tomogram's shape and location within the classical and Liouville regions to deduce the system's non-classical behavior and its evolution. In particular, we highlight how alterations in the Tomogram's shape reflect changes in entanglement and the onset of synchronization. For the Starof8 state, we show how the Fock representation of the Tomogram changes with increasing coupling between the qubits, exhibiting a transition from a non-classical to a classical structure at specific points, revealing the system's evolving pattern of entanglement and synchronization. Furthermore, we emphasize the Tomogram's ability to be interpreted through various representation spaces, offering a versatile framework for studying the dynamics of open quantum systems. Finally, we suggest that Tomograms can be measured experimentally using homodyne detection combined with discrete variable representation, an method that does not rely on finding the inverse of the Jacobian matrix of the transformation, making it a practical and feasible approach. Ultimately, we demonstrate the utility of Tomograms in understanding the evolution of two-qubit systems through a concrete example, highlighting their potential as a universal tool for studying the dynamics of open quantum systems. In conclusion, we outline the potential of Tomograms to illuminate the workings of two-qubit systems, while also anticipating the opportunity to generalize this insight to systems of any finite dimension. Recent advances in open-domain dialogue systems based on neural approaches have focused on human-like conversations, however, applying these models to real-world situations is challenging due to difficulties in ensuring the models adhere to certain roles during the conversation. This study proposes a role-based open-domain dialogue system that accounts for parts played by both human users and the models themselves by converting the role information into labeled conversation histories and utilizing these to train a model for predicting appropriate responses. To overcome the limited amount of data available for role-based open-domain dialogue, the team leveraged large language models by fine-tuning them on role-labeled conversation data without needing additional datasets. Specifically, they employed a method called few-shot prompting which involves using these large language models to generate responses in the context of specific roles directly from the models themselves. This approach was tested on a dataset created from data collected in real-world situations and involving three distinct roles, with the results showing that the models performed significantly better when compared to standard neural dialogue systems. Furthermore, the team discovered that the models generalizing to new situations was possible with only a single example, demonstrating the potential for them to be applied to actual role-based open-domain dialogue scenarios. The code and data used in this research is now publicly accessible via GitHub. The challenge of constructing open-domain dialogue systems capable of adhering to certain parts or roles during the conversation has been a significant obstacle in deploying such systems in real-world situations. This study addresses this challenge by developing a system that not only generates human-like conversations but also considers the parts played by both human users and the models themselves. This has far-reaching implications as it has been observed that certain roles are inherent to almost every human interaction, thus this research has the potential to unlock new areas in the field of human-machine interaction. Farmers utilize pesticides to minimize crop losses, but their effectiveness depends on analyzing overall management strategies. A key problem in research is the lack of data on pesticide efficacy, pricing, and usage quantities, which are typically confidential business information. To address this issue, a mathematical framework has been developed to evaluate the merits of disease management approaches independently of pesticide specifics. 360-degree virtual tourism videos have become increasingly popular due to their engaging and immersive viewing experience. To facilitate easy navigation through these videos, pinpointing interesting segments based on user preferences becomes essential. This paper introduces an innovative approach, where subtitles are utilized to predict user preferences and direct viewing in 360 degrees. Rather than relying on explicit preference indicators, our model leverages contextual information from subtitles to forecast the user's point of view within the 360-degree sphere. Experiments reveal that our proposed framework outperforms rival methods, offering a 20% enhancement in accuracy. Furthermore, our results demonstrate the efficacy of our feature engineering technique, where a 15% increase in accuracy is achieved when compared to a baseline model relying on pre-trained language models. Our project's code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhengyuanli/360-virtual-tour. With rising demand for 360-degree content, our predicted viewer paths provide valuable insight for designers, producers, and recommenders of engaging virtual tourism experiences. Quicker subtitle acquisition via crowdsourcing and modern ASR technology can further expand our model's usability in practice. In trials with three diverse tourism videos, our perspective prediction model achieved a mean accuracy of 34.6%, indicating substantial potential for its application in the industry. Despite strengths in tourism videos, our model may struggle with 360-degree videos featuring complex, fast-paced action or multiple simultaneous sound sources. To improve accuracy in such scenarios, filtering out irrelevant subtitle segments for feature extraction could be beneficial. In the future, integrating our model with navigation algorithms like RRT will be explored to facilitate seamless viewing in 360 degrees. Leveraging additional data, including sound features and learned viewer patterns, can also enhance prediction performance. Tensor network methods have been successful in modeling different types of quantum systems, but their ability to describe thermal states and time-dependent dynamics reliably has been limited due to the difficulties of simulating large-scale systems in equilibrium or under time evolution. This issue arises because standard algorithms typically violate the locality principle by altering the behavior of system sites far away from the location of the interaction, which is particularly problematic for systems that require strong interactions or involve the simulation of time evolution, where this phenomenon often leads to the contamination of system observables in regions far from the interaction site. To address this challenge, we present a novel algorithm that leverages the locality of time-evolution operators to introduce a new class of tensor network contacts that are locally precise, allowing for the accurate description of thermal states and time-evolved systems without the need for the contraction of large-scale tensor networks. This method is demonstrated through the simulation of systems in thermal equilibrium and systems that have undergone time evolution due to environmental influences, using systems like the XXZ model, spin chains with cavity-laser interactions, and harmonic systems coupled to baths, which show excellent agreement with exact results, especially in situations where the contamination of system regions by the interaction or time-evolution process is critical. This algorithm represents a significant advancement in the application of tensor network methods, enabling the precise description of systems in thermal equilibrium and systems that have undergone time evolution, which will facilitate the simulation of realistic dynamics in quantum systems. The Microscope space test for the Weak Equivalence Principle involves measuring tiny differences in the acceleration of two test masses as they orbit the Earth, in response to gravitational forces from a distant (the Sun) and a near (the Earth itself) mass. A critical factor in this measurement is the time spent on actual acceleration data, free from anomalies and errors. A special algorithm known as SGLI, developed specifically for this mission, identified such disturbances in real-time and excluded the associated data from the final analysis. Following the completion of 692 hours of continuous measurements, a tiny bias of 1.28 x 10^-19, or 1.5 times smaller than expected, was identified. However, it became clear that a significant portion of this discrepancy originated from a specific category of disturbances known as "glitches" with rapid rise and fall times, which occurred at an average rate of 4.4 per hour and accounted for roughly 25% of the excluded data. By refining the criteria for rejecting such disturbances, the statistical bias was reduced to 0.64 x 10^-19, thereby indicating that glitches contribute at least half of the current limitation on this measurement. Given the high frequency of these events, it is likely that similar glitches could significantly impede future similar tests in space, highlighting the importance of developing advanced methods to detect and exclude their effects. Furthermore, the Microscope results demonstrate that the SGLI algorithm is effective in identifying a key source of limitation on this measurement, thereby contributing to the development of more effective detection methods for disturbances that are rapid in nature. In addition to its primary objective, the Microscope gravitational experiment has also demonstrated its sensitivity to environmental changes in the spacecraft's orbit, specifically in temperature and light conditions, with an accuracy of 10^-16 for temperature and 10^-17 for light, providing valuable insights for future gravitational experiments that involve testing the equivalence principle in the presence of environmental influences. In such scenarios, potential deviations from the principle as small as 2 x 10^-19 could be masked by the effects of a variable environment. The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution is being quantified in order to understand how they influence the structure of hadrons at small values of x. This investigation reveals that the Borel transformation plays a crucial role in accurately determining the TMD PDF, particularly at small x. As a result, the TMD cross section and the distribution of hadron spin are expressed in terms of Borel transformed impact parameters. Within the context of the infrared model, it's observed that the Borel transformation amplifies the negative contributions at small x, potentially leading to overestimation of the dipole cross section and uncovering limitations in measuring the spin distribution of hadrons. Nevertheless, with better control over the initial conditions at small x, it's anticipated that the influence of renormalons can be minimized, allowing for more precise measurements of the TMD PDF and spin distribution of hadrons in experiments like the future Electron-Ion Collider. As such, it's essential to solve the integral for the TMD cross section using the Borel transform of the impact factor rather than the inverse Laplace transform, which is vulnerable to the influence of IR renormalons. Intuitively, this is because the Borel transform is an expansion that represents the initial conditions in a more precise and controlled manner, in contrast to the ambiguous nature of the inverse Laplace transform. In the case of the color dipole TMD PDF, the impact of renormalons becomes apparent when solving the integral for the TMD cross section and the spin distribution of hadrons at small x, indicating that the Borel transformation provides a more precise and reliable method for determining the TMD PDF and the spin distribution of hadrons. As the number of frogs per site grows in the frog model, from 0 up to the number of leaves in a branching random system, an essential density is reached where the frog model suddenly and irreversibly changes from a subcritical to a supercritical state on a randomly generated m-ary tree of infinite depth. This critical density is investigated on non-percolating trees where strong asymptotic freedom occurs and frogs on the same degree form clusters. An open question remains for degree two trees. Additionally, techniques are presented to solve the frog model's survival problem on any given tree. These methods can also be applied to examine the structure of specific clusters within the frog model. With the degree of the tree exceeding the critical density, it is shown that a particular type of cluster displays strong asymptotic freedom and an infinite number of descendants. This result contributes to a broader understanding of the frog model's behavior and its connections to branching random systems and percolation on randomly generated graphs. We've integrated platinum into a photonic surface lattice to create a hybrid structure that responds differently to magnetic fields from opposite directions. When a linearly polarized laser illuminates this hybrid structure, changes in its refractive index in response to an external magnetic field result in the formation of Dirac-like points and symmetry-breaking gaps along specific directions. The direction-sensitive features of this hybrid structure emerge only when the incident light polarization is perpendicular to the lattice direction, enabling us to control light's behavior and switch its chirality by adjusting the magnetic field direction. Notably, this three-dimensional magnetophotonic material demonstrates unique, direction-sensitive properties comparable to those of recently discovered two-dimensional topological materials. Because of its ability to modulate light in response to an external magnetic field, this hybrid structure may have applications in magnetophotonics that require complex, direction-sensitive responses. To further explore this phenomenon theoretically, we used a finite difference time domain method to simulate the electromagnetic responses of this hybrid structure in response to different magnetic fields and verify our experimental findings. We also employed an eight-band k.p model to simulate the propagation of light within this hybrid structure, which provides a basis for predicting its behavior in various configurations. By combining experimental and theoretical analysis, we gained insights into the detailed mechanisms that produce the direction-sensitive features of this hybrid structure. We were able to create a simplified magnetic field-dependent effective model that can be employed to design this material for specific applications requiring complex, direction-sensitive responses in light. Building upon this knowledge, we designed another novel structure based on this hybrid cell that incorporates a semiconductor quantum well within a magnetophotonic lattice. This new structure, which we call a direction-sensitive magnetophotonic surface lattice with a quantum well, demonstrates the ability to control light's behavior through an external magnetic field by adjusting the position of a donor impurity within this structure, which provides a new avenue for developing materials with complex, direction-sensitive responses in light. Additionally, we were able to increase the visibility of Dirac-like points and symmetry-breaking gaps along specific directions in this new structure by placing the quantum well so that its electron spin is aligned with the magnetic field. Furthermore, we discovered that, when the incident light polarization is parallel to the lattice direction, this new structure exhibits unique features that are insensitive to an external magnetic field, which presents an interesting contrast to its behavior when the incident light polarization is perpendicular to the lattice direction. Lastly, we propose that this new structure, which we have demonstrated experimentally and theoretically can create complex, direction-sensitive responses in light

The advent of cutting-edge and highly accurate deep neural network models, such as those via DNN, has been facilitated by significant computational resources and massive datasets. Nonetheless, these models are often inaccessible due to their size and the need to maintain intellectual property. As a result, there is a growing interest in accessible, black-box models that can provide reliable information without revealing the underlying architecture or data. This paper focuses on transferring knowledge from such inaccessible models towards achieving top performance in specific tasks. We established that decision-based black-box models can make decisions via a binary classification of a model's output, indicating that the underlying architecture can be complex. We introduced an innovative framework, known as Zero-Shot Knowledge Transfer (ZSKT), that can learn the decision boundary from the black-box model's output, enabling the learning of new instances without additional data. ZSKT successfully demonstrated its effectiveness across 12 diverse classification tasks, showcasing its capacity to achieve exceptional performance by leveraging knowledge from complex, unseen models. Our research discovered that decision-based black-box models encompass various types of classifiers, including linear, decision trees, and multi-layer perceptrons, highlighting the zskt's potential to automate knowledge transfer from such models. Furthermore, ZSKT's performance was found to be robust in relation to the complexity of the black-box model and the level of noise present in the data. This research provides a foundation for the investigation of noise in data and its impact on complex models, offering numerous avenues for exploration in the realm of computer vision and natural language processing. We are the first to explore zero-shot knowledge transfer in these domains through the incorporation of realistic computational simulations. These simulations, known as cognitive simulations, mimic human thinking and enable the evaluation of zskt on multiple datasets. We are confident that zskt will serve as a benchmark for the comparison of other black-box models in the future. This research is a product of an ongoing collaboration between cognitive scientists and computer scientists, highlighting the benefits of interdisciplinary interactions. Constructing the lattice of submodules of a given module requires a thorough understanding of all submodules within that module. However, this approach can be impractical due to the enormous potential existence of submodules, especially in modules derived from invariant theory, which are renowned for their intricate structure. This paper addresses this challenge by introducing a systematic method for assembling the lattice of submodules based on partially derived information. Specifically, we start with a key submodule called a multiplicity-free submodule that serves as a fundamental building block, and then develop a procedure to incrementally add submodules to the lattice using their fundamental components. This process ensures that the constructed lattice is comprehensive and accurate, covering all submodules generated from the given multiplicity-free submodule. We demonstrate this technique through examples featuring modules constructed from polynomial rings and their associated varieties, utilizing an online tool called the Homological Algebra Module Database (HAMDB). This database facilitates rapid computation of module homology, and thereby enables rapid calculation of the lattice of submodules using its built-in capabilities for module and ring operations. This approach holds significant potential for building the lattice of submodules of higher dimensional rings and modules derived from them. This work builds upon an earlier study published at the 2019 conference on Computer Algebra in System Science and Control Engineering, and presents an enhanced version of that research. Determining a set of points, considered authentic or valid, in a geometric space is a fundamental problem with numerous applications. The problem becomes more complex when a measure of error is introduced, as represented by the robust geodetic problem. We have analyzed this problem's variants in a context of error tolerance, specifically in two dimensions, and have established the following findings: (1) the general robust geodetic problem is NP-complete, (2) a polynomial-time solution exists for the unambiguous robust geodetic problem, (3) an NP-complete variant arises when only spherical distances are considered within a spherical geodetic problem, and (4) error tolerance does not yield a tractable instance for the robust geodetic problem in a planar grid setting unless P=NP. We have also explored relationships between robust geodetic, minimum dominating set, and minimum independent dominating set problems, and have established upper and lower bounds for the latter in specific geometric spaces. These results have implications for the computational complexity of planar grid graph classes, such as those discussed in "On the Parameterized Complexity of the Minimum Dominating Set in Planar Graphs" (Cai and Sun, 2011). We have derived new upper bounds for the minimum independent dominating set problem in some of these classes, and have used these results to establish NP-complete classifications for the robust geodetic problem in others. Our combined analyses provide a 3^(O(k)) time solution for the minimum independent dominating set problem in planar grids, a 2^(O(k)) time solution for the minimum dominating set problem in spherical grids, and an upper bound of 4^k for the robust geodetic problem in both planar and spherical grids. Our research provides a complete NP-complexity classification for the robust geodetic problem in two-dimensional geometric spaces. We have also discussed error-tolerant generalizations of the geodetic problem in higher-dimensional spaces, but have been unable to establish or refute their NP-complexity through our analyses. Our research lays a foundation for future studies into error-tolerant generalizations of the geodetic problem in higher-dimensional spaces. When working with complex tasks, it's common for labels to be expensive to obtain, either due to the difficulty of creating them manually or the cost of generating rich feedback from human controllers. As a result, supervisors often produce incomplete or flawed demonstrations for their agents. For example, a human playing a level in a video game might accidentally complete it, providing a poor demonstration in the process. In such cases, using demonstrations that are subpar can actually impede the learning process, leading to poor performance even with extended training. This challenge is addressed in this paper, where we focus on enhancing the learning process using imperfect demonstrations through the use of auxiliary tasks that complement them. One significant obstacle in optimizing neural machine translation (NMT) systems is the vast action space resulting from multiple choices for each position in the target sentence. To tackle this issue, previous methods have relied on reducing the action space, selecting important actions, or proposing new search methods. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach that treats action selection as a reinforcement learning (RL) problem, allowing the model to learn the optimal actions through interactions with training data. By leveraging RL to select actions, we demonstrate that our method not only yields substantial improvements in BLEU scores but also achieves them without reducing the action space or introducing complex additional modules. Furthermore, our approach proves versatile, applicable to both unsupervised and semi-supervised NMT scenarios with minimal modification. Our results show that our proposed method delivers consistent performance gains across these settings and across multiple evaluation metrics. Specifically, we observe an average increase of 0.62 in BLEU scores, with a maximum gain of 1.05 in the semi-supervised case. Our efficient RL-based method also exhibits competitive data efficiency when compared to alternative action-learned methods, demonstrating that our approach is both effective and efficient. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/ghrua/rl-nmt. By addressing action selection in NMT through RL, our results suggest substantial potential for further improvement, underscoring the need for systematic action evaluation and novel action-learned methods that integrate source and target sentence structures. In recognition of the complexity of optimizing NMT systems, we advocate for the integration of methods from both machine learning and linguistics to fully capture the intricacies of these systems. In the case of large-scale NMT systems, our results show that our proposed method yields significant improvements with relatively modest action evaluation costs, at a ratio of approximately 1:100 to other NMT parameters. Nonetheless, we anticipate future action-learned methods to tackle larger action spaces with integrated source and target sentence structures, necessitating a deeper understanding of NMT systems and their action spaces. Our results on ensembling action-learned models with traditional NMT systems also highlight the latter's robustness and ability to provide a solid baseline in action-intensive NMT tasks. In the context of low-resource NMT, our results indicate that our proposed method offers a viable path to improve performance in data-scarce action spaces, with future action-learned methods potentially yielding even greater gains in such scenarios. In 2019, Karnaukhov and Mikheev introduced the qfs-region concept, an expansion of a first-order structure (qfs) through a set of formulas. This abstract formalism encompasses a wide range of theories, including propositional logic, equality, and modal and temporal logics. We have expanded upon the original definition by adding more features to a qfs-region, including the introduction of operations and the application of modal and temporal operators, ultimately demonstrating its applicability to complex logics like S5 and DTL. Furthermore, we have established an interpretability relationship between a qfs-region and its underlying qfs, in addition to a compactness theorem that provides the basis for proving the completeness of certain deductive systems within the realm of qfs-regions. Additionally, we have explored the connection between a qfs-region and its associated type of automaton, including a correspondence between the satisfiability of a formula and the existence of an accepting path in the automaton, an idea first proposed by Büchi in the context of finite automata. Building upon this connection, we have derived an antichain property, which implies a maximum number of satisfiable formulas within a given qfs-region for any given size, followed by an examination of several specific qfs-regions. These examinations reveal an interesting distinction between two types of structures: those based on linear order and those based on partial order, as the former tend to have a higher capacity for satisfiable formulas than the latter of the same size. We have also delved into the measurement of the complexity of a qfs-region using both its positive and negative size, along with an examination of several of its subclasses, including some that are maximally complex within a given size and others that are minimally complex within a given size, as well as a discussion on the potential applications of the developed concepts and techniques to other formal languages for automata and transducers. A fraction p/q is considered identifiable within a given set S if knowing the rational part of any point within S allows us to determine p/q. This paper explores this concept by providing a condition that is both necessary and sufficient for a set to contain all p/q fractions with a specific denominator. Additionally, we provide criteria for identifying specific points, as well as sets defined by linear equations or containing specific non-rational points, under the assumption that their defining linear equations do not align with the fractional part's hyperplane. Furthermore, we establish a relationship between 1-dimensional p/q-identifiable sets and certain geometric shapes, such as lines, when the denominator is large enough, providing a method for determining identifiable sets through geometric analysis. However, we also identify an exception to this relationship, providing a 2-dimensional p/q-identifiable set that does not conform to the geometric conditions we established. Finally, we discuss potential research directions related to conditional identifiability and fractal sets' identifiability.

Between October 2019 and April 2020, the LAMOST performed an unprecedented observational feat by completing four $K$2 plates worth of observations in a single month with a 10-day recurring pattern. This unusual configuration allowed for a high level of variability control and a significant increase in data quality for $b$-values. To process the collected spectral data, a new two-step reduction approach was employed which combines an initial calibration process with a subsequent interactive step via a graphical user interface, based on a custom version of 2Dx. This new method was found to be more efficient and capable of handling the complex data obtained from LAMOST's variability control system. A total of 312 science spectra were produced with a typical $S/N$ ratio ranging between 20 to 50, along with 1030 stellar spectra after reduction and calibration. A distinct data set was formed by combining the LAMOST time-domain and archival data for 381 target stars, enabling the determination of atmospheric parameters via a new method and a large majority being identified as single-line spectra. A sample of 18 white dwarf candidates was found along with 5 new candidates of low-mass stellar binaries and 3 new rosseland effective temperature standards. A new distance scale was established for the globular cluster NGC 6791 and a metal-poor globular cluster candidate was identified at a red clump phase diagram crossing point with the Milky Way's globular cluster and open cluster loci. A total of 5 new and 15 existing variable stars were identified through LAMOST's time-domain and archival data sets with 2 of them being new and 3 confirmed pulsating DA white dwarfs, 2 of them being new and a small minority of rotation velocity determinations. A new and challenging problem of $b$-value bias was discovered and a new LAMOST time-domain survey schedule is proposed for future observations. We introduce a novel neural network called Edge-Gated CNN (EGNet) that efficiently creates detailed medical image segmentations from scratch, with a unique selling point of using only edge information to guide low-resolution volume segmentation. Unlike conventional segmentation models that attempt to balance resolution and accuracy, EGNet divides the process into two distinct sub-tasks, demonstrating that high-quality organ segmentations can be achieved by scaling up a minimalistic low-resolution segmentation model, rather than the inverse. We further show that training high-resolution models with significant amounts of data becomes significantly more manageable, and that this streamlined approach leads to enhanced robustness and uniformity in results. Notably, the edge-aware component we propose surpasses state-of-the-art performance in five challenging medical segmentation benchmark tests, including the highly demanding LiDHU dataset, as evidenced by superior DICE scores obtained with an EGNet variant using a straightforward, constant thresholding method. Thanks to speech-emotion recognition technology, computers can engage with people on a more emotional level. Nonetheless, a major obstacle to deploying this technology with ease is the difficulty in adapting it to new domains. We've developed a domain-adapting technique using deep reinforcement learning that significantly enhances the performance of speech-emotion recognition in new domains. During a training session, we introduce a novel approach to assigning labels that takes into account both the quality of the models' predictions and their confidence. We then employ reinforcement learning to create a strategy for gradually refining the models as they process more audio recordings in each new domain, with the aim of minimizing the gap between the models' and their own biases. We tested our technique using a wide range of domains and discovered that it not only adapts to new domains rapidly but also outperforms the standard approach in existing domains. Furthermore, we explored the possibility of adapting models for categorizing emotions and discovered that our technique is equally effective in this more complex task. Our code is available for public use at https://github.com/seyoon/DomainAdaptationDQN. Additionally, we have released our domain adaptation benchmark, which is accessible at https://github.com/seyoon/speech-domain-adaptation-benchmark. We anticipate that these resources will contribute to the advancement of speech-emotion recognition in new domains. We have also included detailed instructions for replicating our results in the appendix. We explored various aspects of our technique and obtained promising results, with some of the findings worthy of further investigation.
