Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, researchers typically supplement their models with sentence-level features, including these indicators. However, incorporating discourse indicators through supervised learning methods poses a challenge due to the vast range of indicators and the diversity of their underlying semantics. To address this, DiscSense a method we propose, conducts an exhaustive semantic analysis of all indicators at once, using each sentence's embedded representation to categorize it into a predefined semantic class from a comprehensive taxonomy. This taxonomy DiscSense's core component, encompasses 23 primary categories and 72 subcategories to cover the vast spectrum of discourse indicators. Through extensive experiments on nine classification datasets with diverse characteristics, our findings demonstrate that DiscSense enhances the performance of classification models by an average of 8.4% when evaluated on the same dataset and 5.7% on average when evaluated on different datasets. Furthermore, our method significantly reduces the complexity of incorporating discourse indicators into learning models, eliminating the need for explicit annotation and facilitating generalization to unseen indicators through semantic matching. This allows for seamless integration with various learning strategies, including supervised and semi-supervised learning, and our method's applicability is demonstrated across multiple classification architectures. Systematic evaluations of the influence of various hyperparameters and different learning configurations are also presented as part of our study. We investigate the properties of a nitrogen-vacancy (NV) center in diamond under elevated temperatures, focusing on optical characteristics and spin dynamics. A unique, temperature-resistant optical-fiber system allows for in-situ measurements from room temperature up to 600 Kelvin. Our data reveal that, within this temperature range, optical collection efficiency and emission spectrum remain remarkably stable, exhibiting only minor changes until 420 Kelvin. In contrast, the emission spectrum undergoes more pronounced variations at higher temperatures, with shifts exceeding 50 nanometers by 540 Kelvin. Spin coherence, however, proves sensitive to temperature, with a significant decline in our experimentally measured 3.2-millisecond value at room temperature. This decrease is attributed to temperature-induced motion in the diamond, specifically diffusion processes affecting the $v$-band emission and spin-coherence lifetime. Our research provides valuable insights for selecting appropriate temperatures for NV-diamond applications across various fields, from quantum metrology to biological imaging. Ultimately, it highlights the importance of thorough, in-situ characterizations at intended operating temperatures before scaling up NV-diamond technologies. In addition, we offer a temperature-scale model (TS-M) for predicting $v$-band emission spectra based on temperature and collection efficiency, both of which are integral components for optimizing the performance of NV-diamond systems. In the context of spin-coherence measurements, we introduce the thermal diffusion parameter $D_T$ to explain coherence decay in relation to temperature and diamond properties. This parameter holds the potential for further refinement and could potentially inform the design of more efficient diamond materials. Our study consists of three distinct data sets: (1) optical collection efficiency and emission spectra measured in-situ from room temperature up to 600 Kelvin, (2) spin coherence and temperature up to 420 Kelvin, and (3) diamond's optical properties and spin coherence following exposure to high temperatures in separate experiments. Systematic investigations of NV centers under varying environmental conditions are crucial for their broad-scale adoption and could be achieved through a combination of in-situ and ex-situ measurements. In the brain, a significant portion of neural activity remains unassociated with any apparent functional output. A leading hypothesis proposes that this seemingly idle activity serves a purpose, specifically to enable random exploratory movements of the brain's search landscape through a process called "reconfigurable search." According to this hypothesis, search is conducted not just at the level of individual neurons but across the entire neural network. In this paper, we explore the idea that a type of neural network, specifically the granular layer of the cerebellum, facilitates search by generating an alternative representation of previous events. Our model showcases the plausibility of this hypothesis through a simulation of a neural network that is anatomically and biologically accurate, resulting in a pattern of activity that is observed in real data from the granular layer of the cerebellum. This model demonstrates the capacity to learn new information while retaining past knowledge, search for relevant past events while being constrained by the network's structure and previous experiences, and the ability to learn from other parts of the brain by adjusting its own internal connections. In the normal course of business, companies frequently engage in transactions with one another, leading to resulting financial obligations between them. However, determining the set of valid transactions that fulfill all existing financial commitments presents a significant computational challenge. This problem is akin to solving linear systems with multiple right-hand side vectors, yet the solution is not a simple combination of individual solutions to the corresponding single right-hand side systems. In this research, a novel method is devised to resolve this issue by employing a unique approach in which the system is reformulated as a series of circulation formulas based on the Hungarian method, a well-known algorithm for assigning weights. We demonstrate the efficacy of this method by applying it to a dataset provided by the Romanian Ministry of Economy. Furthermore, we divide the problem into sub-problems of manageable size and assess the method's performance in terms of solution quality and computational time. In some instances, the method yields optimal solutions; in others, a heuristic solution is obtained, along with an estimate of its optimality. We also examine the relationship between problem size and solution time. In conclusion, the proposed method demonstrates its utility in solving real-world problems, such as the one supplied by the Romanian Ministry of Economy. In the course of this research, an Excel-based implementation of the method was developed, along with a detailed user guide available upon request. In the appendix, a supplementary discussion on the method's performance is included. In the concluding remarks, directions for further research on this problem are outlined. In the accompanying presentation, a walkthrough of the method is provided in greater detail, along with the results obtained in this research. Building upon the foundational work of Berman in 2003, our research expands upon the Jordanian twist concept. We have derived a comprehensive set of modified B-type superintegrals utilizing a one-parameter collection of Jordanian twists. These integrals are remarkably adaptive, as they seamlessly incorporate various Hamltonian configurations, including both solvable and non-solvable systems. Our novel integrals exhibit an intriguing property, where they transform into bi-Hamiltonian superintegrables upon combining with the original Hamiltonian, demonstrating a distinct separation into two independent components that each possess individual hamiltonian properties. Additionally, our research introduces an innovative three-dimensional representation of Poisson subalgebras, enabling a clearer understanding of the modified superintegrals' behavior. Our specific examples explore both monogenic and bigenic Jordanian twist combinations, revealing new potential applications in both discrete and continuous quantum mechanics systems. Our research also delves into establishing relationships between 2D and 3D systems via bigenic Jordanian twists, exposing novel bi-Hamiltonian connections between previously separate monogenic systems. Our findings also uncover new bi-Hamiltonian structures hidden within 3D solvable potentials, providing avenues for extending non-solvable potentials into superintegrable form. Our research in this field is still in its nascent stages, and future studies will further investigate both discrete and continuous quantum mechanics through three-dimensional Schrödinger equations, as well as examine new bi-Hamiltonian structures in 2D Lie algebras, such as nilpotent and semi-simple algebras, in subsequent papers. Considering the available experimental data from the LHC, a comprehensive assessment was carried out for mid-central collisions at same-nucleus energy. 
Relative production of pions, kaons and φ-mesons to protons exhibits similar trends regardless of beam energy, whereas their production in relation to protons displays distinct features.
At mid-central collisions and 5.44 TeV, primary and secondary particle fractions exhibit distinct characteristics, particularly for kaons and φ-mesons.

The MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset has significantly accelerated the study of dialogue state tracking, yet contains considerable annotation errors that significantly impede the improvement of models in this area by exacerbating the training process and state estimation during testing. The presence of unreliable labels from different annotators for the same dialogues poses a notable problem. The quality control measures applied to the dataset in question were found to be inadequate. A new dataset, named Dialo18-Noise, is introduced which is a subset of the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset and is free from annotation errors that could be considered substantial. A comparison is conducted between models trained on dialo-centric and user-centric datasets with the presence or absence of noisy labels. The results of 39,000 test samples for the Dialo18-Noise dataset show that the introduction of label noise leads to a notable decrease in the joint state coverage rate by 12.4% and the overall score by 7.2% when models are evaluated on the Dialo18-Noise dataset. It was discovered that the majority of the errors in the MultiWOZ 2.0 dataset stem from the fact that the same state is labeled in different ways in different dialogues. A new evaluation metric named ASSIST was proposed that takes into consideration the similarity of states in different dialogues and yields a 10.6% improvement in the joint state coverage rate and a 5.8% improvement in the overall score in comparison to the existing metric for dialogue state tracking. In late October 2019, nationwide protests erupted in Chile, forcing a sudden and abrupt closure of high schools and prompting our project. To model fellow students' behavior, we turned to mathematics, focusing on an epidemiological approach that accounts for individuals who only interact with peers from the same school. This approach resulted in a system of differential equations that described the dynamics of student behavior within each institution, leading to solutions that mirrored real-world scenarios. Our key discovery was that, under certain conditions, some schools would experience persistent unrest, even if the overall population had returned to normal, and that interventions aimed at mitigating unrest would require a balanced approach, considering factors such as timeframes and reach. Our model also explored the role of individual students' willingness to act out, finding that those with a higher tendency to engage in unrest would contribute to more persistent unrest in their own institution and potentially to unrest in other schools as well. To validate our model, we collected extensive data on student behavior from various schools, using it to inform our mathematical equations and making them uniquely applicable to this specific context. Our research provides a unique framework for addressing pressing issues affecting schools and society, and we believe it has the potential to be adapted to other scenarios where individual behavior contributes to broader social dynamics. Building upon our findings, we are now exploring ways to incorporate external factors into our model, recognizing that protests often involve interactions between individuals from different institutions and the wider community, and that there is a pressing need to study and understand the temporal aspects of these events through advanced mathematical techniques such as dynamical systems and bifurcations. Our project has sparked a new research collaboration with Dr. Gail Charles, Dr. Markus R. Rice, Dr. Jesus G. Valdivia, and Dr. Hernan C. We are confident that our project has paved the way for a new generation of researchers to explore the complex dynamics of social unrest through mathematics and are committed to supporting them in their endeavors. Determining star formation rates in galaxies is a key objective in studying galaxy evolution. Various methods are employed to achieve this, including spectral energy distribution fitting and gas line studies. An ideal method for calculating star formation rates is through observing the rest-frame 4363 Å line, also known as brackett-γ, as it allows for direct measurement of oxygen abundance and characteristic metallicity-based star formation rates in galaxies. Although this approach seems ideal, it is challenging due to the line's obscurity at typical galaxy redshifts. For the limited number of galaxies at which this line is observable, a study compares two typical star formation rate estimators, based on spectral energy distribution fitting and gas line studies, to the more precise measurements of star formation rates derived from oxygen abundance and metallicity in galaxies at which the brackett-γ line is observable. The results show that star formation rates calculated through spectral energy distribution fitting are significantly overestimated when compared to the more precise measurements, with a mean ratio of 3.6±0.7, while the line studies produce rates that are closer to the more precise measurements but still overestimated by a factor of two on average. The study highlights the limitations of using line studies and spectral energy distribution fitting to calculate star formation rates and provides a gold-standard comparison with more precise measurements of star formation rates derived from oxygen abundance and metallicity in galaxies at which the brackett-γ line is observable. The study also discusses the potential for using near-infrared oxygen line sets to calculate star formation rates in a wider range of galaxies at higher redshifts. The study's findings are relevant to all studies employing gas line studies and spectral energy distribution fitting to calculate star formation rates in galaxies and suggest that future studies should consider using line studies that include oxygen line sets rather than traditional optical and ultraviolet-based methods. We've identified a novel class of exotic solids that surpass the limitations of conventional higher-order topological insulators. These exceptional materials, which we term "square-root higher-order Weyl materials," are distinguished by unusual combinations of anomalous bulk and edge phenomena and are found to display unique "square-root" hinge transport properties. Our research indicates that square-root higher-order Weyl materials can be realized using 2D square-lattice models and 3D pyrochlore structures, providing a framework for their theoretical description and potential observation. These findings also reveal opportunities for manipulating hinge transport more efficiently by incorporating interactions that mix the Weyl points in question. Next, we demonstrate that both square-root higher-order Weyl materials and their interacting variants exhibit robust "square-root" hinge conductance even when symmetry is broken, supporting the broader notion that square-root hinge conductance represents an emergent, robust phenomenon resistant to system perturbations. This work lays the groundwork for an in-depth exploration of square-root hinge conductance in other settings. Our research is primarily based on theoretical calculations using the Lanczos method, lattice Hamiltonian, and Kubo formula, and involves key contributors from the University of Tokyo, University of Oxford, and University of Wisconsin-Madison. This paper delves into the vertex operator algebra structure of the parafermion type, in association with highest weight modules for integrable representations of the superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$, a simple affine Lie superalgebra. We establish the underlying generators of this algebra in detail. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that this vertex operator algebra falls within the twisted module algebra structure of the affine Lie algebra $A_{2n-1}(k)$ and $D_{2n}(k)$ for specific values of the level $k$. This relationship's characteristics are then examined for all possible highest weight modules. We also explore the vertex operator algebra's configuration in relation to the simple module and its associated fusion rules, which take the form of the extended Kac table, in cases where $k$ is an odd number greater than 3. Additionally, this study identifies a subalgebra within $A_{2n+1}(3)$ and $D_{2n+2}(3)$ isomorphic to $osp(1|2n)(3) for all non-negative integers $n$ where $n$ is less than $n_{max}$ and $n_{max}$ has a value of 11 for $A_{2n+1}$ and 10 for $D_{2n+2}$. We also examine the vertex operator algebra structure of $K(osp(1|2n),k)$ as an extension of loop group algebras and verify its relationship with the simple module for all non-negative integers $n$ up to $n_{max}$ and any level $k$ that is greater than 3. Lastly, this study demonstrates that the vertex operator algebra structure of $K(osp(1|2n),k)$ also encompasses twisted module algebra structure of loop group algebras for all highest weight modules and for all non-negative integers $n$ up to $n_{max}$ and any level $k$ that is greater than 3. Furthermore, this research may serve as a foundation for further investigation into the representation theory of simple affine Lie superalgebras and the associated vertex operator algebras. The explosive growth of web-based information sources necessitates more effective methods for combining existing knowledge. However, many of these sources are isolated due to data security constraints, prompting the development of federated knowledge base construction techniques. Existing federated approaches primarily focus on collecting data from individual sources and merging it into a single knowledge base, without consideration for potential inconsistencies and, in some cases, the exclusion of relevant information. This paper proposes a novel selective data collection framework that accounts for potential inconsistencies and allows for the inclusion of information that may not be incorporated into a unified knowledge base. This framework is theoretically sound and is realized through the development of two specific algorithms. Our experiments demonstrate that this framework yields better data quality compared to traditional methods and ensures a balanced trade-off between data quantity and computational resources. Notably, this framework addresses real-world applications such as combining data from sources with varying units of measurement and data with temporal references. This study investigates how rapidly rotating solar-type stars maintain dynamic magnetic fields by incorporating opposite differential rotation in their convection zones. We updated the Babcock-Leighton flux-transport dynamo model to account for this phenomenon and conducted extensive simulations for possible magnetic cycles in rapidly rotating stars. The results show enhanced toroidal poloidal field generation and magnetic energy amplification when anti-solar rotation patterns are present. However, this enhancement is limited to faster rotating stars (P < 5.17 days). In slower rotating stars (P >= 5.17 days), the dynamo switches to an anti-solar rotation pattern, characterized by increased generation of the toroidal poloidal field through the Babcock-Leighton process. We derived a cut-off period for this transition and propose it may influence the detection of magnetic cycles in stars with rotation periods around this threshold. Additionally, we observed that the Babcock-Leighton flux-decay process plays a crucial role in determining the cycle period in rapidly rotating stars (P < 5.17 days), while the differential rotation plays a more significant role in slower rotating stars (P >= 5.17 days). We also explored the effects of reducing the Babcock-Leighton flux-decay time and found that this leads to shorter cycle periods in rapidly rotating stars and may result in magnetic cycles with periods as short as a decade in stars with rotation periods less than five and a half days. Furthermore, we discovered that decreasing the turbulent magnetic diffusivity in the convective zone shortens the cycle period in slowly rotating stars (P >= 5.17 days) and may result in magnetic cycles with periods as short as 25 years in these stars. We propose that accounting for anti-solar rotation patterns and the Babcock-Leighton flux-decay process are essential to accurately modeling dynamic magnetic fields in rapidly and slowly rotating solar-type stars. This research provides a theoretical framework for understanding possible magnetic cycles in these stars and the associated observational phenomena of stellar activity cycles, spot periods, and flux evolution. We conclude by highlighting the need for additional observational and theoretical research to fully comprehend possible magnetic cycles in solar-type stars and the associated dynamic magnetic fields. This involves conducting a comprehensive statistical analysis of all available observational data on stellar activity cycles, spot periods, and flux evolution as well as further simulations of these stars' dynamic magnetic fields using the updated Babcock-Leighton flux-transport dynamo model. This study offers a starting point for this comprehensive research and provides a theoretical framework for modeling dynamic magnetic fields in rapidly and slowly rotating solar-type

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We demonstrate the capability to select operation modes in resonators by controlling the carrier concentrations and present a method for calibrating superconducting quantum circuits based on near-field terahertz data. We found that oxide etched silicon resonators exhibit higher qubit coherence times than carrier-filled silicon counterparts, underscoring the significance of terahertz characterization in optimizing quantum device performance. Furthermore, we explore the feasibility of utilizing carrier dynamics for overhang storage and propose a method for designing superconducting devices on materials with variable doping levels to enhance coherence times. We also observe that microwave mesostate modulation can be employed as an all-electric near-field microscopy technique to characterize samples, enabling the imaging of spatial variations in carrier concentrations and permittivity by analyzing the modulated terahertz reflection spectra. We demonstrate the capability to design and operate superconducting quantum processors in a manner that maximizes coherence times and propose the utilization of near-field terahertz microscopy for investigating material fluctuations in quantum materials and systems in a non-invasive and spatially resolved manner. Finally, we suggest the term "terahertz scanning near-field optical microscopy" (TSNOM) to describe this imaging technique and outline the theoretical foundation for constructing a metamaterial-based, macroscopic TSNOM microscope using a silicon nanowire array and a metal-doped silicon wafer. We envision that such an instrument will facilitate the imaging of quantum materials and systems at the macroscopic scale. We anticipate that this will contribute to a better comprehension of the interconnection between material properties at the macroscopic and nanoscopic levels and we propose that this knowledge will be valuable in designing and optimizing quantum devices across various scales. This study addresses this issue by assessing the statistical properties of a nonlinear Hawkes process and developing an efficient simulation method for predicting events in the future, along with a graphical technique for exploring the underlying structure of complex event data. Although deep convolutional networks excel at medical image segmentation when thoroughly trained and refined, they falter when confronted with new, similar anatomical targets without a large dataset. This limitation is addressed through a technique called Contrastive Semi-supervised learning for Domain Adaptation (CSDA), which leverages similar target images in the training dataset to refine the model. CSDA employs two convolutional networks: a base network that is transferred from a pre-trained model and a separate refinement network that is pre-trained separately. These two networks are pre-trained with similar target images using similar annotation, with the latter being fine-tuned using a smaller dataset. Notably, they are optimized using a contrastive learning approach that treats each network as a separate view, with the goal of maximizing their similarity. During the refinement process, CSDA uses a combination of the optimized networks to segment the data, resulting in a 23% reduction in uncertainty and 8% boost in metric average precision compared to baseline methods when evaluated on unseen targets with limited annotation. Furthermore, CSDA demonstrates robust performance across multiple comparable anatomical targets in the V201 dataset, achieving a 25% increase in mean precision when compared to the baseline in a more challenging cross-target scenario. Additionally, CSDA is compared to CADA++, another state-of-the-art domain adaptation method, with the former outperforming the latter by a 11% margin in mean precision in a 10-target scenario due to its ability to process larger target datasets during refinement. This suggests that while CADA++ excels in small-scale scenarios, CSDA is more suitable for larger-scale medical image segmentation tasks. This technique's effectiveness is further validated across three additional datasets, with CSDA delivering a 10-20% increase in mean precision over baseline methods in every case. This research's findings are significant, providing a solution to the long-standing challenge of cross-target medical image segmentation. This is accomplished without relying on extensive target annotation or real-time domain adaptation during testing, making CSDA a groundbreaking achievement. This technique's code is available for download at the specified link. This research's scope is limited to comparing anatomical structures with similar characteristics, as defined by the V201 hierarchy. This hierarchy serves as a reference for future research in this domain, combining features from multiple sources, including the ModelScope dataset annotations and the MIOToolbox atlas. This research's success is also attributed to its robust performance in conjunction with two additional experiments, which are presented in the appendix along with the model's code

The foundation of contemporary supergravity, often referred to as the '1.5 order trick', has been extensively analyzed in a simplified theoretical framework based on the Wess-Zumino theory. A straightforward examination indicates that this 1.5 order formalism is inherently defective in all contexts. Although it appears that the associated ghost fields are at a 1.5 order with respect to the supergravity multiplets, a straightforward transformation from the Wess-Zumino multiplets to the super Yang-Mills multiplets can demonstrate the underlying flaw of the 1.5 order formalism. Notably, a related investigation discovered that the associated 3-form fields can be expressed as a dual bar quantity of the corresponding off-shell superfields in the Wess-Zumino theory. Building upon this insight, a novel approach has been devised to convert the 1.5 order formalism based on the Wess-Zumino theory into a viable off-shell supergravity framework using the 4-component superfield notation. This process involves elevating the auxiliary fields at the 1.5 order to full off-shell components and incorporating a new auxiliary field within the Gravitino multiplet. Consequently, a consistent BRS transformation has been established for the resulting supergravity superfields derived from the Wess-Zumino theory using the 1.5 order trick. The associated algebra, presented in a simplified form using the superfield notation, discloses a nilpotent supercharge and a non-nilpotent supercentral charge, exhibiting striking similarity to the extended BRS algebra initially proposed by Grisaru, Seidowicz, and Zanabria in 2018. Notably, our proposal offers a solution that is independent of superfield off-shell completeness, as demonstrated by a direct conversion of the resulting supergravity superfields to the 2-component notation, resulting in a valid BRS transformation for supergravity for the first time since 1978. This breakthrough provides a viable foundation for an in-depth examination of the 1.5 order trick within the broader context of superconformal and harmonic superspace supergravity theories. A concise overview of the underlying flaws in the 1.5 order formalism based on the Wess-Zumino theory is presented in an appendix using the 2-component notation. We examine decoding of rank metric codes under certain symmetry conditions and develop a new approach to error localization, building upon existing methods by Gulliksen et al. This new method significantly improves the number of systematic checks required, especially for codes with large field sizes, thereby facilitating faster decoding of rank metric codes that adhere to specific symmetry standards. My research extends the framework introduced by Gulliksen et al. and demonstrates that in its enhanced form, many symmetric rank metric codes, including those with low-density parity-check structures, can be efficiently decoded with a much lower number of systematic checks than previously established limits, namely $k/\log(q)$, where $k$ represents the code's message length and $q$ denotes the underlying symbol field size. Instead, the enhanced approach allows a much tighter bound of $k/2$ for check densities, leading to the possibility of decoding speeds comparable to those of block rank decoding, yet with greater error-correcting capability and a more complex error locator module, and code structures that combine properties from both rank and linear coding theories. My research findings are detailed in an accompanying technical report available at arXiv:2205.01367. Moreover, our research has shown that the majority of existing rank metric code constructions, including those based on classical linear codes and duality-based designs, can be readily supported by our error localization methods, ensuring wide code coverage and versatility. To facilitate the design of efficient rank metric decoders, we have developed a new error localization method that can be integrated with the existing block rank decoder, enabling the rapid testing of different rank metric codes and their corresponding decoding performances. In addition, our research has been supported by an interesting observation made possible by our newly defined systematic check density metric, which can be used to identify the underlying symmetry conditions of rank metric codes without any prior knowledge of the code's construction or its stored data patterns. Lastly, as the first comprehensive study on the enhanced decoding of symmetric rank metric errors, our research has shed new light on the underlying principles and the intricate relationships between rank metric codes, their constructions, and decoders, ultimately paving the way for the exploration of novel code designs and the development of more sophisticated decoding algorithms. Deep learning has revolutionized image processing and extraction tasks by offering pre-trained models that can automatically filter out irrelevant information and identify essential features. We employed a deep learning framework called EfficientNet to analyze the cosmic web and speed fields associated with dark matter halos, seeking to determine the underlying data that contribute to the distribution of halos based on their mass. Our results show that this deep learning framework can effectively identify relevant information from complex cosmological maps, and we obtained a 0.01 improvement in total variation distance when comparing our results to existing models that used explicit web and speed field data. Notably, our findings suggest that when using only the cosmic speed field, the deep learning model performs 5-7% better than when using explicit data, and when using only the web field, the model performs 3-5% better than when using explicit data. Conversely, using only the density field leads to a significant decline in performance, a 10-15% decrease when compared to using explicit data. These outcomes suggest that the density field plays a more crucial role in determining the distribution of halos based on their mass, and any influence deriving from the speed field is secondary. We also discovered that when combining the density, web, and speed fields, the deep learning model performs no better than when using only the density field, indicating that the latter is the dominant feature, and the former are supplementary at best. These findings provide valuable insights into the features of the density, web, and speed fields that contribute to the distribution of halos based on their mass, and they pave the way for further exploration of the structure and evolution of the universe using deep learning. We obtained a 0.01 improvement in total variation distance when comparing our results to existing models that used explicit data for the HMF, and a 0.01 improvement in power spectrum predictions. These outcomes demonstrate the potential of deep learning to uncover the underlying data that contribute to the distribution of halos based on their mass and yield more accurate predictions for power spectrum and HMF. We anticipate that this deep learning framework will contribute to a better comprehension of the structure and evolution of the universe and will pave the way for more accurate predictions of cosmological observations and quantities.

This research focuses on the semi-supervised application of Convolutive NMF, particularly within the context of music audio analysis. Initially, Convolutive NMF was introduced to harmonically segment audio signals in an independent component analysis framework. We explored and identified the capability of this method to harmonically dissect polyphonic audio in real-time environments. Furthermore, we discovered it to be adaptable for the automatic transcription of historical keyboard music from audio recordings with a limited analysis framework. This framework relies on pre-trained models for feature extraction and semi-supervised optimization using a limited dataset of annotated recordings. The proposed system was successfully tested on a diverse set of recordings from the RISM catalog, yielding promising results and demonstrating the potential of Convolutive NMF in this context. However, the method was found to be inconsistent in certain situations, emphasizing the need for further work to fully explore its capabilities and limitations. The associated challenges and potential solutions are also discussed. The developed system was found to be cost-effective and user-friendly, providing a viable alternative for the automatic transcription of historical keyboard music in comparison to existing methods. The associated code and documentation can be found at https://gitlab.inria.fr/laetitia-janowski/semi-supervised-cnmf. The method was evaluated against three baseline systems: (1) an independent implementation of Convolutive NMF, (2) a simplified version of this implementation with fixed harmonic depth, and (3) a state-of-the-art deep learning model. We have developed an innovative numerical framework for the dynamic development of rotating stars under general relativity. This framework deviates from the conventional approach, solving the evolution equations directly using a method that simultaneously resolves both the interior of the star and its external boundary. This led to an unexpected discovery that gravity waves emitted during rapid rotations in stars with low mass, like those similar in mass to the Sun, are substantial enough to eventually cause the star's demise. Our study also reveals that by the time these waves become visible on the surface, they have already had a notable impact on the star's interior, meaning our previous estimates of these stars' lifespans were overstated by at least a factor of ten. Interestingly, our findings show that the formation of neutron stars can occur through a rapid contraction of the star in just a few dozen seconds in certain scenarios with high angular momentum, in a process that is influenced by the composition of the star. Our research provides a comprehensive picture of rotating star evolution and its various outcomes, including the emission of gravitational waves, black hole formation, and the formation of neutron stars and proto-neutron stars. Our team is continuing to investigate various rotations patterns, including those that lead to the emission of gravitational waves through a process known as bar mode instability, and how these waves can eventually cause the star to die, while also exploring the possibility of using these waves to determine the composition and rotation pattern of a star in other galaxies. Despite significant progress in document extraction, a major limitation persists: most systems rely on artificially crafted datasets with low visual richness, hindering their real-world applicability. Human labeling in such datasets is labor-intensive and requires expert knowledge in both the domain and the annotation format. We've developed an innovative method to reduce labeling costs substantially, by leveraging joint learning of both visual and semantic object detection to extract relevant data directly from documents without the need for pre-existing labels. Our model can be fine-tuned for a particular domain with just 100-200 labels, a tiny fraction of the usual amount required. Our results show that this approach achieves comparable or better performance compared to traditional supervised learning in eight different domains and domains with high visual richness. Moreover, our method significantly reduces labeling costs and eliminates the expertise requirement for domain and annotation formats. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/seyone/label-free-docs.

The detection of gravitational waves by LIGO and VIRGO collaboration offers a chance to study binary astrophysical events remotely. By analyzing gravitational wave patterns, our understanding of neutron star and black hole formation can be refined, along with details about compact binary neutron star, black hole, and binary black hole formations. Deep learning algorithms, specifically convolutional neural networks, can be trained to identify unique gravitational wave patterns associated with neutron star and black hole mergers, classified by their mass and spin characteristics. Our research presents a method for training a neural network on simulated gravitational wave data, enabling it to make precise predictions about binary event characteristics. When compared to traditional analysis methods, our neural network data matches theoretical models of binary neutron star and black hole mergers, surveyed by various electromagnetic telescopes, without any bias. Specifically, our findings identify three binary neutron star mergers and twenty-two binary black hole mergers, with nine of the latter matching known event listings. By applying this approach to the LIGO/VIRGO public dataset, our team is offering unique insights that can be verified by further electromagnetic observations, in addition to providing enhanced binary event candidate collections for subsequent analysis and confirmation. Given its effectiveness, this method can be utilized to analyze future gravitational wave data with increased sensitivity and richness. This study confirms previous findings that a certain type of swimmer, specifically a scallop with symmetric and smoothly varying characteristics, is capable of achieving optimal speed and efficiency in its swimming motion. We extend this concept by examining two variations of this swimmer: one with a fixed body shape and one with a shape that changes over time, both incorporating non-linear fluid dynamics effects. We also establish that optimal control solutions can be derived independently for each individual component before integrating them to find the optimal combined solution. This results in a solution that can be localized to yield the optimal solution for any given swimmer within this broader classification. We further analyze two specific starting position scenarios and demonstrate the optimal strategy involves movement in one direction, followed by movement in the other, despite increasing resistance. This paradoxical slowing effect, caused by the swimmer's reliance on opposing muscle groups, can be temporary, leading to the possibility of faster short-distance swimming than would be expected from the overall level of resistance. This research provides a theoretical basis for further exploration of this phenomenon and its potential applications in the design of swimming robots. Urban settings with high diversity of income often rely on chance encounters between strangers to foster a sense of community, promote social cohesion, and facilitate the exchange of cultural values. We examine how the COVID-19 pandemic affected opportunities for such encounters by analyzing 1.4 billion anonymized cell phone records from 50 million individuals in New York City. By tracking the movement history of every cell tower an individual passed during their daily commute, we measured the diversity of encounters based on people's income as identified through tax records. Between March and October 2020, strict social distancing rules led to a 75% decrease in encounter diversity in the most affluent districts and a 55% decrease in the most impoverished areas at their peak limitation. As lockdown measures relaxed and temperatures rose, encounters with a high level of income diversity occurred more frequently, eventually surpassing pre-pandemic levels by May. However, increased remote work led to increased encounter diversity in the most affluent areas but a decline in the most impoverished areas by 7.5 to 12.5% in the fall. Our data highlights the resiliency of urban communities to adapt to external stressors and highlights policy opportunities to support communities in recovery. Notably, anti-lockdown protests in New York City in late September 2020 coincided with a significant decline in income diversity in urban encounters, prompting a call to action from policymakers to address this issue. Measures such as expanded flexible work arrangements and increased investment in community programs could mitigate any lasting negative effects of the pandemic on urban communities. These communities face numerous challenges including rising income inequality, social isolation and community fragmentation which this research can contribute to by providing empirical data on behavioral alterations during the pandemic in urban settings. This research offers valuable insights for policymakers, urban planners and public health officials into the complex factors at play in urban communities and highlights the importance of data-driven policy decisions. Furthermore, this research can contribute to the development of effective countermeasures to mitigate the adverse effects of public health crises on urban communities in the future. In addition, increased remote work led to increased snaking of commute times in New York City. Buchholz established a practical approach to understanding local, or "local," physics - essentially, physics described within a small, contained area of spacetime. This involves dividing the contained area into two parts and studying the interactions within each part separately. If the laws governing these interactions remain unaffected regardless of how the parts are configured, then this indicates the existence of a fundamental, universal standard for measuring physical properties. In the case of two-dimensional spacetime, we demonstrate that any standard conformally invariant two-dimensional local theory is fully determined by its representation in the von Neumann algebra associated with a wedge-shaped region of spacetime. Specifically, we prove that all such standards derive from a single representative, and that they are all equivalent, by utilizing the principles of endomorphisms as described by Longo and Witten. Furthermore, we show that any two-dimensional local theory that is not conformally invariant can be analyzed using a similar approach, combined with Buchholz's practical approach, by transforming it into a conformally invariant theory. Additionally, we demonstrate that the principle of "doppler effect" is inherent in any two-dimensional local theory, and that any two-dimensional local theory can be developed as a "wedge-local net" through the use of endomorphisms as described by Longo and Witten. This provides a broader understanding of local physics in two-dimensional spacetime. Finally, we identify the standard for measuring physical properties in any two-dimensional local theory, and we demonstrate that this standard has unique characteristics. This research was presented in a series of lectures at the International Conference on Operator Algebras and Mathematical Physics held in Guangzhou, China, and at the University of Yamanashi in Japan. This work is based on research collaborations with Dr. Dragan Vukotic at the University of Buenos Aires and Dr. Yasunori Kawachi at the University of Yamanashi. Additionally, this research was supported by a Discovery Grant from the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC). This method segregates the controller into navigation and collision avoidance layers, leveraging sensor data to inform decision-making. By applying a technique from the theory of Gaussian random functions, we derive general formulas to determine the characteristics of the Fourier spectrum after it has been subjected to bending. Our analysis of the Harard-Shevitsky model reveals that the bending effect leads to an increase in the rate of decay in its derivatives, with this influence measurable by a parameter related to the spatial curvature. This enhancement in decay rate is shown to result in an increased rate of convergence in various expectations of the normalized fields, as well as their derivatives, when the Fourier frequency tends to infinity. Furthermore, we establish an upper bound for the moments of the fields that takes account of their derivatives, and demonstrates a polynomial relationship with the order of the moment, both before and after bending. We complement our theoretical findings with numerical simulations of the evolved Harard-Shevitsky spectrum after bending, and an empirical analysis of atmospheric data from reanalysis suggests that the standard Harard-Shevitsky model may underestimate the curvature of the Fourier spectrum in comparison to its theoretical $k^5$ specification. We also explore the implications of the bending effect for Gaussian random fields on the prediction of extreme values, and observe that it leads to a decrease in the scaling exponent in the power-law relationship between the number of extreme values and the scale of interest, especially in mid-range scales. This decrease is shown to be upper-bounded by the square of the parameter measuring the influence of bending, and could potentially be estimated from the analysis of extreme values at different scales. We conclude that the impact of bending is likely to result in a decrease in the scaling exponent in the power-law relationship between the number of extreme values and the scale of interest, and could potentially be estimated from the analysis of extreme values at different scales. We also find that the Harard-Shevitsky model's failure to account for bending could lead to an overestimation of the number of extreme values at certain scales, and that further research is needed to establish a general formula for the bending effect on Gaussian random fields, as well as to explore ways of incorporating this effect into model extensions. We suggest considering the influence of bending as an additional parameter in the spectrum of Gaussian random fields, and propose a general framework for the evolution of the Fourier spectrum after bending, which could potentially be applied across various fields. This research targets an essential challenge in securing next-generation wireless systems, specifically those that utilize nonorthogonal multiple access (NOMA). We introduce an innovative decoding method called command decoding, which enables secure information transmission even when there are security vulnerabilities among some users. Our approach builds upon existing techniques by incorporating NOMA decoding and applying command decoding to certain messages. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method by analyzing decoding times for individual users and deriving expressions that capture their behavior. We also investigate the statistical properties of these decoding times as well as their comparison to alternative approaches. Our proposal exhibits several advantages over existing systems that use secure transmission methods, including an improved ability to handle a large number of users and increased efficiency in data transmission. We validate our design through numerical experiments and examine key performance indicators of our system, finding command decoding to yield better results than conventional methods. We also explore potential extensions to this system, including its application to 5G systems and the integration of new technologies such as unmanned aerial vehicles and quantum communications. We provide a detailed mathematical description of the system and its components as well as an overview of the techniques used in its design. When dealing with high-dimensional data that contains outliers, an alternative method to traditional PCA is RIPCA, which performs robust dimension reduction by minimizing the $\ell_1$-norm under a given constraint. However, solving an NP-hard non-convex optimization problem inherently poses difficulties. This research proposes an innovative algorithm to solve the rotationally invariant $\ell_1$-RIPCA problem by reformulating the non-convex objective function as a pair of convex functions and utilizing a specific starting point to ensure the problem's equivalence, ultimately resulting in a linearly convergent solution. Moreover, we establish an approximation accuracy for the proposed method and provide conditions for it to achieve exact solutions. We complement our theoretical findings with extensive numerical experiments, demonstrating our method's efficiency and reliability. Notably, our algorithm exhibits computational efficiency, particularly when compared to semi-definite relaxation methods, while also considering the effects of initialization and data configuration on its performance. Overall, this research provides an efficient and reliable solution for $\ell_1$-RIPCA through a novel and innovative algorithmic approach. Furthermore, we have made our MATLAB code available for public access.

This work builds upon such endeavors and focuses on enhancing the performance of BERT in relation to emotion-related knowledge. Specifically, this study aims to explore the potential of BERT to influence the annotation of sentence pairs in line with specific questions, such as identifying aspects of sentences. Our research involves the annotation of 7,000 sentence pairs across 15 categories by 31 participants with access to a supporting BERT interface. Our results show that allowing participants to interact with the BERT interface leads to a 12% improvement in average performance when compared to annotations without BERT, as verified through free-form question answering and explicit design. This research represents an initial step in the investigation of BERT's impact on text annotation tasks that go beyond classification. The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray observations is disproportionate, implying that they might naturally have harder spectra. The study presented here aims to compare the X-ray hardness ratios of asynchronous and non-asynchronous polars using a large dataset from the RXTE collection, considering factors of binary mass accretion rate, spin period, orbital period, and spectral state. The data analysis failed to reveal a distinct difference in average hardness ratios between the two categories of polars. However, we found that non-asynchronous polars generally exhibit harder spectra when in a low or intermediate state of brightness, whereas asynchronous polars tend to have harder spectra when in their lowest brightness levels. No notable correlation was found between 2-6 keV X-ray spectra and spin or orbital periods within either of the two subgroups of polars. Despite initial hypotheses, the research does not support the idea that asynchronous polars inherently have a softer X-ray spectrum than their non-asynchronous counterparts. No notable disparity in X-ray hardness ratios was found between asynchronous and non-asynchronous polars, suggesting that other factors contribute to the detection rate bias, such as localization difficulties or short duration outbursts in the soft X-ray surveys. Asynchronous polars, like their non-asynchronous counterparts, exhibit a full range of X-ray spectral states from soft to hard, indicating that spin period disruption or accumulation does not significantly influence the accretion process in a manner that results in softer spectra. The research implies that factors such as binary mass ratio, mass transfer mode, or the presence of a persistent wind from the companion star could be responsible for the irregular detection of asynchronous polars in soft gamma-ray surveys. Asynchronous polars, as they are discovered in the future, should be studied in depth to confirm or refute the results presented here due to their potential to reveal the dynamics and physics behind the subclass's irregular detection in soft gamma-ray surveys. For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar territories, it's essential to have a robust understanding of their surroundings. Current approaches to mapping and navigation typically employ local coordinate systems and grid-based representations, but these often hinder the robot's ability to grasp the overall layout. In contrast, using a representation that captures the scene's topology can provide a more fundamental understanding and improve navigation in the unknown environment. Based on this concept, we propose HiTMap, a novel topological map representation that utilizes a hierarchical structure to represent the scene's layout. Each node in this hierarchy represents a distinctive area within the environment, defined by noticeable landmarks, while edges indicate the types of features that a navigating agent would use to transition between these areas. We integrate HiTMap with a simple navigation system that allows the agent to determine the most suitable path by switching between areas and using local features to move between them. To validate our approach, we conducted a series of experiments in both simulated and real-world environments, demonstrating that HiTMap-based navigation outperforms grid-based methods and is more resilient to local maxima. Moreover, we show that agents with HiTMap can efficiently learn to generalize their knowledge to novel environments by leveraging their existing understanding of topological maps, a skill that cannot be acquired through grid-based learning alone. HiTMap's promising results provide a solid foundation for further research on the integration of sensory data, action models, and learning algorithms to create a unified framework for robust navigation in unknown environments. HiTMap's code is publicly available at https://github.com/robotics-iridia/HiTMap.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring electric and magnetic fields in atomic systems. While it has been possible to achieve precise measurements of these fields in simple configurations, complex situations, such as in magnetic traps for atoms, require a different approach due to the intricate interactions between atomic magnetic moments and the surrounding magnetic fields generated by ferromagnetic materials. In a novel approach to addressing this issue, researchers have proposed using superconducting materials in atomic interferometry to leverage their unique properties, such as diamagnetic susceptibility and persistent currents, which can result in a signal that is directly proportional to the magnetic field variations. This method allows for the non-invasive measurement of magnetic field fluctuations and has demonstrated an unprecedented level of sensitivity of $10^{-5}$ Hz in a system where the atomic spin is coupled to a magnetic field generated by a superconducting loop. The discovery of a strong correlation between the atomic interferometry signal and the persistent current in the superconducting loop has provided a means of calibrating the measurement of magnetic field fluctuations with precision. This approach has significant implications for improving the magnetic field tolerance of atomic interferometry and has paved the way for its application in precision measurements in magnetic environments. In addition, this method has the potential to measure other properties of the superconducting loop, such as its critical current and the Earth's magnetic field, and has sparked a discussion on its application to the measurement of electric fields. The findings presented in this study have been verified through extensive theoretical and experimental analysis, and the method has shown great promise for its potential to address some of the fundamental challenges in metrology. In conclusion, this research has made significant contributions to the field of atomic interferometry and has provided valuable insights on how to measure magnetic field variations, a key aspect of metrology, with unprecedented sensitivity. We investigate the influence of adjacent materials on the thermal-magnetic properties of transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) using an ab initio approach that considers proximity effects. Due to spin-orbit coupling in TMDs, we find that strong magnetic fields have contrasting effects on spin-polarized states, causing temperatures where magnetothermal anomalies occur to increase with the field strength. This leads to the formation of a new heat-driven magnetic phase when the two spin states have equal reactivity to the magnetic field, resulting in opposite magnetothermal responses for the two spin states. This distinct reaction to the magnetic field strengthens the spin-polarized magnetothermal effect in TMDs when combined with a suitable ferromagnetic overlayer. This effect can be observed in layered MoSe$_2$ when using a nickelocene spacer layer and a nickel ferromagnetic overlayer due to its large magnitude in the $ab$ plane. This property makes it suitable for implementing spin-polarized thermal-magnetic phenomena in TMDs with adjacent materials. A nickelocene spacer layer and a nickel ferromagnetic overlayer were used to experimentally verify this with a layered MoSe$_2$ sample in the form of a flake, where a significant spin-polarized magnetothermal effect was detected. The experimental data matches the predictions made by the theoretical model used to analyze the results. A detailed analysis of the experimental data and the underlying physics using an ab initio approach that considers proximity effects is presented. A general theoretical model based on a combination of Fermi liquid and two-dimensional XY spin models explains the thermal-magnetic properties of TMDs. We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation within nanogaps down to 1 nm. Using both finite-element and dyadic approaches, we compare our results to existing experiments and findings from other theories, specifically examining the influence of these phenomena in relation to changes in distance within the nanogaps. Our numerical outcomes, derived from both methods, reveal similar trends and indicate that the electron spillover's impact on gap-plasmons is significant even at very small distances (under 5 nm) and its influence is exchangeable with that of a hard-wall model, albeit with some discrepancies in the 1-5 nm range where nonlocal effects start to have a notable impact, particularly in the dyadic approach, where we observe a more pronounced shift in plasmon resonance than in the hard-wall model. Type theory's combination process is notoriously challenging, largely because it necessitates the incorporation of a well-behaved normalization technique. Our research proposes an innovative normalization approach, called robust normalization, which is inherently agnostic to syntax and instead operates on types as topological spaces. This framework is particularly well-suited for the Calculus of Constructions, allowing us to seamlessly integrate it with existing proofs and computational content while maintaining normalization's reliability. Our key innovation is the identification of a specific topological space, referred to as the "generic universe," which serves as a universal carrier for all types and serves as the primary arena in which normalization takes place. Within this framework, every computable type is homeomorphic to a subspace of the generic universe, thereby providing a systematic path to achieving normalization for an infinite number of types through the application of topological principles rather than syntactic rules. Our research also introduces an innovative type constructor, referred to as robust dependent sum, which upholds integrity and normalizability while offering a level of expressiveness comparable to that of the Calculus of Constructions. Our research's soundness and efficiency are demonstrated through a configuration-recursive implementation of closure for the generic universe, along with the inclusion of an executable specification of robust dependent sum's constructor in Coq. Our research's findings are presented in an informal setting utilizing an abstract model of typing, coupled with diagrams to illustrate key concepts like types, subtypes, and normalization. Our research's core results, including robust normalization and closure, are made available through an open-source repository along with an accompanying non-technical overview available at https://norm-coc.github.io/. We present a new classification method that draws from finite mixture models, extending the classic k-means algorithm by incorporating information about hierarchical relationships between clusters. This approach is rooted in the principles of stochastic geometry and Choquet theory, offering a framework for identifying clusters within a high-dimensional parameter space. Building on existing work using transportation costs, our method formulates a evolutionarily consistent variant of the method, known as E-kmeans, which leverages the Renyi kernel to capture the essence of cluster configurations. A bridge theorem connects the Renyi E-kmeans to a specific random geometric model, known as the E-Minkowski model, providing a statistical interpretation of the method's parameters and enabling consistent estimation using a kernelized variant of the EM algorithm. Our results establish the asymptotic behavior of the estimator and a phase transition in cluster recovery, depending on the ratio of summary parameters to dimensions, under conditions that are optimally sharp. A simulation study and a real-data analysis are also presented, demonstrating the efficacy and versatility of the E-kmeans algorithm. We derived a precise two-loop correlation function for two graviton excitations in AdS_5, resulting from the interaction of two gluon operators in N=4 super Yang-Mills theory at strong coupling, laminarized in a null direction. Building upon the AdS/CFT correspondence, this yields a generalized holographic function for two graviton modes in AdS_5 and its mirror in S^5, also determined at the two-loop level for certain configurations in a null direction. The CUDA environment has undergone significant changes since its inception in 2007, however, object-based programming in CUDA remains underdeveloped compared to other parallel programming models like OpenCL and C++AMP, which offer built-in support for object-based parallelism. This disparity creates a performance disparity, with object-based CUDA programs struggling to compete. To address this disparity, we present DynaSOAr, a novel memory allocator designed for object-based CUDA programs that leverage the system's full potential for parallel processing and memory access. By combining dynamic memory allocation with a spatial array structure and a conflict-free allocator, DynaSOAr delivers a balance of flexibility and speed. This is further enhanced by DynaSOAr's ability to parallelize memory access, eliminating the need for explicit synchronization. Our empirical studies have shown that DynaSOAr can achieve up to 5 times better memory allocation speed and 3 times faster execution time compared to baseline object-based CUDA programs. With DynaSOAr, developers can now fully exploit their system's parallel processing and memory access capabilities, resulting in significant performance gains. This is particularly evident in memory-bound applications, where DynaSOAr has shown an average improvement of 20.6 times over baseline programs. This innovative memory allocator serves as a foundation for further research and is an important breakthrough for object-based CUDA programming. This work is an extension of our previous research presented at the 2019 IEEE International Conference on Big Data and its Applications (BigData2020). Diverse real-world use cases and benchmarks have been incorporated into this updated research, along with enhanced evaluation methodologies and results. These applications, coupled with DynaSOAr's underlying design, highlight the challenges and opportunities in CUDA memory management and object-based programming. This is exemplified through our solution, DynaSOAr, which offers a well-rounded memory management system that addresses multiple performance bottlenecks in object-based CUDA programs. This has resulted in substantial performance gains across a wide range of applications, yielding average improvement rates of up to 20.6 times over baseline object-based CUDA programs. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of Yu-Shiba-Rusinov (YSR) states in superconducting systems, primarily involving magnetic impurities at appropriate crystal binding sites. This framework, based on a combination of density functional theory and an exact exchange approach, considers the intricate interactions between the spin polarization of a specific atomic layer and the superconducting coherent effect from the remaining layers. To demonstrate its utility, this framework in its full complexity was applied to a comprehensive examination of magnetic niobium(110) layers, comprising single manganese atoms as well as clusters of varying sizes up to a full monolayer. Calculations using this framework showed significant accuracy when compared to available experimental data, specifically concerning the spectral positions and spacings of YSR states following deposition of an isolated manganese atom and manganese clusters on niobium(110). It was observed that the spectral characteristics are heavily dependent on both the size of the cluster and the specific location of the manganese atoms within it, resulting in a more complex and diverse range of YSR states that are susceptible to modulation via interlayer interactions. Ultimately, this theoretical study suggests that niobium(110) provides an ideal setting for exploring the intricacies of YSR states through a variety of magnetic probes at the relevant binding sites and spacings. Furthermore, the spectral characteristics determined through this study in conjunction with experimental measurements using scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy should offer a comprehensive understanding of the YSR state structure in this specific system. Additionally, this theoretical framework may also be applicable to other superconducting systems, therefore providing a valuable framework for predicting and understanding the spectral characteristics of YSR states across a broader range of materials and situations. The developed theoretical framework also highlights the significance of considering interlayer interactions in an accurate prediction of spectral characteristics, a crucial aspect that has been frequently overlooked in prior theoretical studies. In conclusion, this theoretical framework, centered on an in-depth examination of spin-polarized layer-dependent phenomena within superconducting systems through a combination of density functional theory and an exact exchange approach, has been successfully demonstrated to be an effective tool for predicting the spectral characteristics of YSR states, a phenomenon that is crucial for a deeper understanding of the complex relationship between spin polarization, superconductivity, and the resulting YSR states in these systems. Furthermore, this study provides a fundamental basis for a comparison with experimental measurements using scanning tunneling microscopy and spectroscopy, a technique that offers a detailed and direct visualization of YSR states at the atomic level. Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit functions operate seamlessly over the input domain, FourierMask can create high-resolution masks with fine details by taking only 2D coordinates as input. We combine FourierMask with a backbone network using FourierMask, and evaluate this framework on the COCO dataset for instance segmentation, resulting in an average precision of 53.1% with an FPN backbone, and a notable improvement of 1.2% when compared to a mask R-CNN model with the same backbone. The code for FourierMask is available at https://github.com/ruotiechen/FourierMask. Additionally, models and demo videos are available at https://sites.google.com/view/fouriermask/home. Since implicit functions facilitate operations over the input domain, FourierMask can create high-resolution masks with fine details by taking only 2D coordinates as input. This enables the network to achieve a high degree of consistency with ground truth data, as shown in experiments as well as visualizations of learned implicit functions. This consistency is reflected in four key findings: (1) the 3D nature of coordinate positions represents instance information, (1) Fourier transformations are a viable alternative to learned position embeddings, (3) implicit functions are essential for creating consistent masks, and (4) mask quality is primarily determined by the backbone network rather than the Fourier transformation or implicit function. These findings are further supported by an ablation analysis presented in the paper. FourierMask can be an efficient mask predictor for both single-stage and two-stage frameworks, as demonstrated by results on the MIMIC test set, achieving a higher AP than state-of-the-art methods in single-stage frameworks while being 5-6 times faster than mask R-CNN at 53.1% AP. This efficiency is attributed to the implicit architecture and the lack of pre-training, which enables direct application to real-world image instances. Building upon this success, we explore applications of the implicit architecture in mask R-CNN, demonstrating the possibility of enhancing state-of-the-art two-stage instance segmentation methods through the replacement of the decoder with FourierMask, resulting in a 2% improvement in AP over mask R-CNN,

We've been investigating the use of cloud tomography from space for over a decade now, taking into account line-of-sight measurements from multiple directions. This method holds great promise for obtaining detailed 3D cross-sections of opaque convective clouds that are otherwise inaccessible through other means. However, a significant hurdle in applying cloud tomography has been the presence of a "hidden core" within these clouds - a dense, water-bearing mass that cannot be located through tomographic reconstruction alone and whose existence was first identified in 2007 through cloud-resolving modeling. In our research, we propose a new approach to finding this core by first pinpointing its likely general position and then defining a smaller search area within the cloud's tomographic reconstruction. We based our likely location for the core on general cloud characteristics as well as specific features visible from space, and we defined our search area using a set of cloud properties obtained from cloud-resolving modeling. By applying our new framework to data from the MISR and MODIS satellites, we were able to locate and extract the "hidden core" in three-dimensional dimensions for the first time ever - a significant breakthrough that could have a major impact on our understanding of water within these clouds and, in turn, how these clouds interact with the rest of the atmosphere. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that cloud tomography from space can provide highly accurate, three-dimensional "snapshots" of these clouds, giving us a critical new tool for studying their behavior and contributing to a better understanding of how they fit into the larger picture of the Earth's atmospheric system. This breakthrough also has the potential to be applied to other types of clouds and could provide valuable insights into how they have an impact on the Earth's atmospheric system as a whole. The NASA $TESS$ mission's comprehensive sky survey allows the discovery of rarest celestial phenomena, such as systems featuring a planet in the habitable zone. We report the examination of $TESS$ object $712$, whose system consists of three planets orbiting an $G$-type star with magnitude $11.79$. Two out of the three planets, $b$ and $c$, are mini-Neptunes with sizes $2.38\,R_{\earth}$ and $2.26\,R_{\earth}$ respectively, and orbital periods of $11.796$ and $7.348$ days. In contrast, the innermost planet, $d$, with a size of $2.17\,R_{\earth}$, orbits its star every $3.781$ days, placing it within the habitable zone where conditions are suitable for life. TOI-712.04, the exoplanet located in the habitable zone, is deemed likely to possess an atmosphere due to its low density in comparison to terrestrial worlds. We also found that this system is composed of two relatively young planets around a medium-aged star, with an age of $9.5^{+2.8}_{-2.4}$ billion years for the star and the planets. TOI-712 is an important discovery as it presents a young planetary system featuring a possible Earth-analog and offering a chance to observe the Earth-analog's rotation period. In addition, the system's youth allows for the investigation of how planetary systems evolve over time. Infrared light curve analysis using $Spitzer$ revealed that the two mini-Neptunes and the possible Earth-analog rotate slowly in their respective orbits, rotating no faster than once every $43.8$ days. TOI-712.03, the most interior planet in the system, orbits very close to its star, with an eccentricity likely caused by its interaction with the star's gravitational field. This star-system is quite distant from the Sun and Earth, at a distance of $227$ parsecs. As a result, any future observations or studies of this system will be quite challenging due to the substantial interstellar pathlength which may hinder light curve analysis using traditional methods, requiring a development of new approaches. Furthermore, the system's young age and proximity to the Sun make it a less likely candidate for hosting life in comparison to other celestial environments, however its unique characteristics make it an interesting subject for further study. Doping these sites with C or N leads to an unstable and non-bonding electron on the N or a highly unstable electron on the C, resulting in one of three possible outcomes: neutral atom behavior in a hollow site, a bond with the nearby oxygen atom, or a bond with the nearby titanium atom. When neutral atoms are formed in the hollow site, a significant reduction in the distance between titanium and oxygen is observed, leading to an unstable O-Ti bond and ultimately causing the failure of this site. On the other hand, N-O bonding produces a neutral nitrogen atom in an O-N-O configuration with a bond length close to that of N$_2$, but with a bond angle of approximately 145$^{\circ}$, whereas C-O bonding results in a shorter bond length compared to N-O, leading to a more unstable bond and ultimately the failure of this site as well. In contrast, N-Ti and C-Ti bonding yield a positive charge on the dopant atom, with a shorter bond length compared to the O-Ti bond, but with a significant impact on the magnetic properties of the material.
