An infinite graph $G$ contains a substantial amount of structure if it has a subgraph isomorphic to an infinite richness $R$, denoted as $rich(G) \geq R$. Two infinite graphs $G$ and $H$ are upper-richness equivalent if for every subgraph isomorphic to an infinite richness $R$, either $G$ or $H$ contains a subgraph isomorphic to $R$. A class $\mathcal{F}$ of infinite graphs has upper-richness Ramsey property if for every subgraph isomorphic to an infinite richness $R$, either all graphs in $\mathcal{F}$ or none of them contain a subgraph isomorphic to $R$. We prove that any class $\mathcal{F}$ of infinite graphs containing monochromatic copies of all finite graph types and containing a substantial amount of structure has upper-richness Ramsey property. We also show that any class $\mathcal{F}$ of infinite graphs containing a substantial amount of structure is upper-richness equivalent to the class of all bipartite graphs. Furthermore, we provide a characterization of upper-richness Ramsey property for certain classes of infinite graphs including those containing monochromatic copies of all finite graph types and those containing a substantial amount of structure. We prove that this property is equivalent to either (i) upper-richness equivalence to a class of finite graphs, (ii) the ability to play two different colors with a certain probability, or (iii) the ability to play two different colors in an independent manner for an infinite number of vertices. We extend several known results on upper-richness Ramsey property to classes of infinite graphs containing a substantial amount of structure. We also prove several new results on this property using a new technique that allows us to deal with an infinite number of vertices. Finally, we pose several open questions regarding upper-richness Ramsey property for classes of infinite graphs containing a substantial amount of structure. We provide a preliminary analysis of some of these questions using our new technique. We believe that this analysis will be useful to other researchers working in this area. This paper introduces a groundbreaking method to automatically identify Bell's Palsy in real-time through eye movements, eliminating the need for subjects to perform specific actions. We assembled a unique dataset that focuses exclusively on eye regions from 3D facial animations, totaling 8400 individual frames. Our research indicates that conventional approaches are insufficient and often result in inaccurate results. To overcome this challenge, we developed an innovative framework consisting of four distinct components: a 3D mesh descriptor, a neural network tailored for random forests, a feature selection module, and a system for validating and refining models. This framework demonstrates exceptional performance, accurately detecting Bell's Palsy in 92% of cases, significantly outperforming existing methods and demonstrating robustness across diverse datasets. Furthermore, we observed a notable correlation between the severity of Bell's Palsy and specific eye feature scores. This discovery paves the way for the development of a severity assessment system. Additionally, we observed that certain eye feature scores exhibit a notable correlation with the severity of Bell's Palsy. This finding has the potential to facilitate the creation of a severity assessment module. This research was conducted in collaboration with experts in neurology and ophthalmology at Stanford University. These subject matter experts validated our results and provided valuable insights, contributing to the development of this research. We investigate the quantum electrodynamics in $1+1$ dimensions using qudits of varying size, from qubits to squetits, and demonstrate that larger qudits offer a balance between accurately simulating photon behavior and mitigating decoherence through increased spectral width. Our findings suggest that, in certain scenarios, the advantages of squetits may be achieved through the application of noise protocols mimicking squetit behavior, allowing for the simulation of squetit physics utilizing only qubits. These protocols involve defined increments in pulse width, chirp, and their interaction, which can be optimized to enhance the fidelity of squetit simulations through quantum imaginary time evolution. We observe that all of these protocols elevate the entanglement between photons and matter systems, further increasing their effect when incorporating multiple squetit modes or utilizing qudits with notches in their states. These results provide insight into the relationship between the dimensions of qudits and noise protocols and suggest the possibility of squetit simulations using only qubits, offering a potential pathway for the creation of squetit states through quantum simulations with larger spectral widths, a crucial advancement in preparing general qudit states via resonant interactions. We've taken a well-known concept from geometric structures, specifically geometric frameworks, and adapted it to suit Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Our adaptation maintains the original's core properties and features. Building on this foundation, we've established connections between the objects within a given stack, or more broadly, within a presheff for a Lie groupoid, and the concept of metric spaces with embedded framework points. This relationship is expressed through the use of a specific functor that determines full subcategories of extended metric spaces with embedded framework points, and it does so in a category-theoretic manner that is natural and automorphic. This approach also facilitates the exploration of category-theoretic objects and their underlying structure via the concept of geometric frameworks. Ultimately, this work sets the stage for examining other concepts within the realm of geometric structures through the lens of category theory. Additionally, we've explored local aspects of Lie groupoids and stack objects, establishing that they possess a significant, albeit limited, neighborhood that is topologically equivalent to Euclidean space. This finding is relevant to our primary focus but is of interest in its own right due to its ties to open subsets of Grassmannians and flag varieties. Lastly, we've delved into the world of category-theoretic objects and their underlying structure via the concept of geometric frameworks, and we're planning to investigate other concepts within the realm of geometric structures through this lens. A statistical analysis of 1.3 cm continuum and CO (3-2) data from the BISTAG sample, 17 infrared dark clouds at high latitudes, reveals a previously unseen correlation between CO velocity dispersion and distance from the IRDC center, suggesting a specific physical pattern. Using a simple model to describe this relationship, we estimate key parameters and find that 13 out of 17 IRDC centers in the sample exhibit velocity gradients, with amplitudes ranging from 0.43 to 0.85 km/s/pc. These findings are unusual in comparison to molecular gas in the Milky Way, which typically exhibits larger velocity dispersion and lower density than the BISTAG sample. We propose an core-expansion theory that could enhance the probability of massive star formation, and support this idea by presenting magnetic field estimations and far-infrared luminosity-to-mass ratios for each IRDC in the sample, which show a stronger correlation with core-expansion than with other factors. Finally, we identify the Dragon IRDC as a notable example of a cloud in the early stages of massive star formation, and suggest that its dense and expanding core, along with an emerging magnetic field and internal luminosity, are key components in a process that could lead to the formation of massive protostars and OB associations. Scaling models of core expansion to the Dragon IRDC, we predict that a massive star will form in the cloud's center within the next 10^4-10^5 years. We also present observations of the Dragon IRDC, including continuum and CO spectra at 1.3 cm and 3 mm, as well as 1.3 mm continuum and CO (1-0) and (3-2) maps. The data are available in the article's supplementary files and on the DAGAL database. Further research is required to validate the core-expansion theory and its implications for the formation of massive stars and OB associations. However, if the Dragon IRDC follows this path, its study will provide valuable insights into the process of massive star formation in the Galaxy. Additionally, the existence of a strong magnetic field in the early stages of massive star formation in the Dragon IRDC supports the concept of rapid collapse in massive IRDCs, and the subsequent formation of massive protostars and OB associations in the Galaxy. LiDAR point clouds offer valuable insights for various applications including natural disaster management, urban planning, and archaeological site exploration. With the rise of machine learning, point cloud-based intelligence has become increasingly sought after. This paper explores five key aspects of point cloud processing: data preprocessing, model architecture, loss function, training strategy, and evaluation metric. A comprehensive survey of 37 leading point cloud datasets covering over 300 variables is also presented, along with 11 commonly used evaluation metrics. Our survey can serve as a reference for researchers and practitioners to navigate the point cloud-based intelligence landscape and guide the creation of new datasets and evaluation methodologies. Advanced machine learning techniques such as meta-learning and few-shot learning hold promise for further progress in this field, and future research should prioritize data diversity, adaptability, and real-world scalability. With these considerations in mind, future point cloud-based applications may be more effectively supported, and the LiDAR point cloud-based intelligence community can benefit from established practices and standards. In conjunction with IV 2021, we introduce the "PointCloudNet" benchmark, an ensemble model comprising 12 individual models that achieves superior performance on the ModelNet40 dataset, and is accompanied by supporting code and the PointCloudNet dataset, available at https://github.com/pointcloudnet/PointCloudNet. This benchmark aims to raise the bar for point cloud-based learning methods and datasets, and to contribute to the field through rigorous evaluation and comprehensive surveys of leading approaches and datasets. Code for the ensemble method has been made available at https://github.com/pointcloudnet/PointCloudNet and is under continuous development on https://pointcloudnet.github.io/. With the introduction of PointCloudNet, we address five critical aspects of machine learning in LiDAR point clouds, and with it, a new era in point cloud-based learning begins. This work is a part of the IV 2021 conference proceedings and is being presented as an oral contribution in ThB-1: Machine Intelligence in LiDAR 3D point clouds. We address this by establishing a novel one-step recurrence relation for the expected values of a stationary Gaussian random field in n dimensions, enabling us to derive key properties such as the ergodicity of Gaussian random fields in any finite n. Our results demonstrate that the ergodicity of grfs in n dimensions is ensured when n exceeds three, whereas in two-dimensional space, the condition is much more stringent, requiring the covariance kernel to exhibit a specific polynomial decay rate. Our findings also reveal the optimal trade-off between smoothness and decay rates that allows a Gaussian random field to exhibit multiple stationary increments while maintaining stationarity. The proposed one-step recurrence framework is demonstrated across various settings, including Gaussian random fields in n-dimensional space, their spherical and projective analogs, and even in the context of Sobolev spaces. The source of cosmic rays with energies exceeding 10^20 eV remains a major mystery. Attempts to link high-energy cosmic rays with neutrino emissions have shown promise but have been hampered by limited understanding and few observations. This study takes a novel approach by employing a statistical method to search for neutrino emissions from all directions, in search of a correlation with ultra-high-energy cosmic rays. Considering various energy ranges and possible causes of high-energy events, the analysis found two energy ranges - above 10^20 eV and below 2*10^19 eV - that showed a significant connection at a 4.6-sigma confidence level, equivalent to approximately 0.00003% confidence when considering all energy ranges. Additionally, a sub-group of cosmic rays with octant angles less than 30 degrees showed a stronger connection at a 5.2-sigma confidence level. A comparison of observed neutrino flux with predicted values from high-energy cosmic rays in all directions found a discrepancy of approximately 4.5 sigma, or 0.00004%. These findings support further investigation into the relationship between neutrinos and cosmic rays, specifically through future telescopes designed to detect high-energy neutrino emissions from all directions, like the Square Kilometre Array. A system like the KM3NeT research tool, capable of detecting high-energy neutrino emissions from specific directions, may be useful in exploring alternative hypotheses for cosmic ray origins. Ultimately, solving this cosmic puzzle will likely require a comprehensive approach that incorporates multiple detection methods and a robust statistical framework. This issue is particularly pronounced in skin cancer diagnosis from dermoscopy images, where accurate model training is crucial due to the life-threatening consequences of errors. Not only do dermoscopy images vary in resolution and quality, but there are over 8,000 distinct types of skin conditions, making it challenging to assemble comprehensive, high-quality training datasets. Experimental results show that this framework yields superior performance on dermoscopy-based cancer diagnosis when compared to standard deep learning networks. The proposed framework is found to be particularly effective on datasets with limited, high-quality training data, demonstrating great potential for real-world applications in the field. The Hele-Shaw cell with varying angles has been the subject of numerous studies on interface instability driven by an imposed pressure gradient. A new type of finger pattern was discovered in a cell with an 18.5 degree angle and subjected to 360 rotation, exhibiting independence from Rayleigh-Taylor instability in both linear and nonlinear scenarios. The pattern showed sensitivity to small changes in curvature, particularly developing additional branches that could potentially contribute to higher order analyses. A new solution was obtained for 360 rotation in a cell with an 18.5 degree angle by applying a similarity approach and matching functions, confirming the predicted state in a linear regime and validating the discovery in a nonlinear regime. The new solution was found to deviate from the 45 degree line in the Sivashinsky-Neiland diagram, suggesting that finger patterns in other angles close to 18.5 degrees may also exhibit unique characteristics. The discovered pattern in a cell with an 18.5 degree angle and subjected to 360 rotation provides new insights for the broader Hele-Shaw cell with varying angles, suggesting that many of its solutions remain to be found. In educational settings, curiosity is a vital driver of deep and lasting learning, but measuring it dynamics poses a significant challenge. This research introduces a novel, multi-dimensional model that utilizes learning management system data and peer evaluations to comprehensively assess curiosity dynamics in small group learning environments. This theoretical framework and practical methodology were thoroughly tested with 150 undergraduate students participating in small group online learning activities. Our findings revealed that peer evaluations and automated LMS data analysis complement each other in measuring curiosity in learning, and that a multimodal approach complements traditional self-reported surveys. This study offers implications for designing and evaluating learning environments that foster curiosity in various settings, including school and workplace training. Additionally, it highlights the utility of peer evaluations as a valuable tool for instructors to assess the level of curiosity within a group, and provides recommendations for educators to design and lead learning activities that nurture curiosity and support collaborative learning. This research also paves the way for exploring the relationship between curiosity and other crucial aspects of learning, such as motivation, engagement, and performance. Furthermore, it provides a foundation for investigating the role of surprise in learning, as well as the development of curriculum units that integrate curiosity in various subject areas. This study demonstrates that peer evaluations and automated LMS data analysis hold the key to answering the call for more rigorous and empirical research on the dynamics of curiosity in learning. This is reflected in Chapter 5, which presents a conceptual framework for exploring the relationship between curiosity and other crucial aspects of learning, such as motivation, engagement, and performance, as well as the impact of surprise on curiosity in learning. This research offers a valuable contribution to the field of learning sciences, and provides a foundation for the development of learning technologies that foster curiosity in various learning settings. Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for assessing uncertainty in complex systems, and their integration with Dirac delta functions through Mat\'ern kernels significantly expands their capabilities, especially in analyzing isotropic data. This research adapts Mat\'ern kernels, which account for data isotropy, for use in non-isotropic settings by incorporating Gaussian processes on graphs. This approach is mathematically represented in a theoretical context and showcases its practical applications through two real-world studies: one exploring temperature distributions across Europe and the other analyzing gene expression within a biological cellular process. This work also invests in computational methods, developing an algorithm for efficiently handling Gaussian process predictions in graph-structured data, and making the associated R package, MatGraph, available for others to use. This research provides significant insights on modeling non-isotropic data using Gaussian processes on graphs and highlights the value of data-driven approaches to identifying optimal graph neighborhoods. This includes a novel observation from the temperature distribution analysis, indicating that a relatively small neighborhood can suffice for accurate predictions when comparing it to the expression data within a cellular process, which demands more precise modeling of boundaries. This research is further expanded upon through an ongoing project, presented in this document, where Gaussian process models are integrated with particle filters to anticipate temporal variations in complex systems, and this framework is applied to forecasting gene expression across cellular process examples. This research is primarily presented in a theoretical context but promising results warrant the development of this framework further. The optimal placement of sensors in an urban setting is a critical issue, particularly with the increasing use of vehicles equipped with sensing technology. We investigate an important special case - detecting urban road networks - where the number of data points generated by sensors can exceed $10^5$, requiring new approaches to adapt existing methods. We present an efficient method for optimizing the placement of sensors, one that leverages traditional force-directed algorithms while taking into account the characteristics of the urban road network, and evaluate its performance using real-world data from New York City, with promising results indicating significant improvements over existing methods in terms of detection accuracy and network resolution. Our optimized solution for detecting a full Manhattan network consists of only 280 vehicles, and we make available a system designed to handle large datasets in conjunction with our experiments. We also examine the impact of various data collection strategies on detection performance, and find that ant-colony-based approaches yield substantial gains, with a method incorporating these principles in the optimization process leading to the detection of 90% of network edges with just 20 vehicles. We conclude by discussing potential applications and future research opportunities arising from this study. With the growing use of vehicles equipped with sensing technology, our work paves the way for the effective utilization of these sensors in urban settings, and we are confident that our results and findings will motivate further exploration in this field. We have made available all data collected during this research, consisting of over 300k sample points generated over a period of two weeks, along with all system configurations utilized in our experiments, and we are more than happy to respond to any additional inquiries regarding this study. This work introduces the multivariate functional singular spectrum examination (MFSE) framework, which expands upon the singular spectrum analysis (SSA) methodology to accommodate multivariate data across various dimensional domains. By leveraging a multivariate approach in equilibrium space, MFSE offers a solution to the dimensionality issue plaguing SSA. We demonstrate the effectiveness of MFSE by applying it to multivariate functional data, including tensors and matrix-valued functions, obtained from various real-world and simulated datasets. Our results indicate that MFSE surpasses the performance of SSA, especially in datasets with complex structures. Furthermore, MFSE is shown to be robust in identifying features and structure when compared to SSA, using an alternative transformation and a symbol-based representation. The MFSE framework is made available as an R package named 'MFSE', along with a detailed tutorial for its implementation. Deep learning-based automatic essay scoring systems are increasingly common in higher education institutions, tasked with evaluating vast numbers of students across different courses. These systems are designed by publishers to be form-stable, providing consistent ratings in response to varying student abilities and essay content. However, our research reveals a contradictory finding - after training on a substantial dataset - these systems exhibit an unanticipated and undesirable trait: they become excessively reactive to minor changes in essay content, resulting in significantly inconsistent scores. Notably, this behavior is observed even after incorporating important factors such as coherence and grammar, which are known to influence human scoring. A thorough analysis of several popular datasets through the lens of natural language, combined with insights from stability theory and machine learning, sheds light on the underlying causes of this stability-inconsistency duality. These explanations, in turn, give rise to novel concepts for mitigating the instability and hyper-reactivity in AES systems. Specifically, we propose two distinct approaches: first, incorporating a stability-augmented adversarial training framework; second, developing an interpretability-driven method that leverages pre-trained language models to filter out irrelevant content from the scoring process. Ultimately, our research offers a critical examination of the limitations and implications of relying on machine learning-based essay scoring throughout the education sector. Furthermore, we highlight the significance of addressing the dual challenges of stability and hyper-reactivity in this domain. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is equipped with a plasma source that utilizes a helicon to create and sustain a plasma within a cylindrical chamber. This source is analogous in design to the plasma sources employed in the ICER device at the French research facility CRIT, albeit with several key differences. A significant distinction lies in the application of the RF power where it is applied directly to a plasma-producing source in ICER as opposed to injection into a vacuum gap in IShTAR. As a result of these variations, the plasma properties in IShTAR are comparable to those in ICER despite their differing configurations, thereby validating the functionality of the IShTAR plasma source when operating in helicon mode. Additionally, the achieved plasma parameters in IShTAR of $0.1$ MW of RF power and pressures of $10^{-3}$ Pa are characterized through the use of a combination of diagnostic tools, including a Langmuir probe, a faraday probe, optical emission spectroscopy, and a system for analyzing gas composition, and show density and temperature values of $10^{19}$ m$^{-2}$ and $3$ eV respectively. Furthermore, the relationship between plasma properties and various operating parameters has been explored, and it has been found that there is a linear relationship between plasma density and applied power, alongside an inverse cubic relationship between plasma density and pressure, and an inverse quadratic relationship between plasma temperature and pressure. Optimal operating conditions within the plasma source have been identified as an RF power of $0.1$ MW and a chamber pressure of $2.5\times 10^{-3}$ Pa, and it has been confirmed through the use of gas-balance measurements that approximately $90\%$ of the sputtered material from the source is recovered within the chamber, and the remaining $10\%$ is released into the surrounding environment as gas. Overall, the characteristics of the IShTAR plasma source have been fully validated in helicon mode, and it is now suitable for use in life-time and material studies of plasma-facing components within fusion devices. Furthermore, the source is currently being modified to accommodate the application of additional sources, in order to meet the required plasma parameters for future research in this field. Lastly, the results presented in this paper are also relevant to the ICER device, and could provide a solution to the current difficulties encountered in achieving the desired plasma densities within that device. This system differs from standard chemical pesticide models as it incorporates the natural cycle of reproduction and toxin production in beneficial microbes. This study focuses on a microbial pesticide system model, which incorporates the reduction in pest population due to infection by the beneficial microbes and their toxins, to explore how this mechanism limits the spread of pest populations. We address the issue of stability around the equilibrium point and through numerical simulations, we examine the impact of the model's variables on the system's behavior, as well as the effects of contamination on the model's predictors. These analyses provide valuable insights into the dynamics and controllability of the system, which could be applied to optimal control strategies in real-world applications. Focusing on a Mitochondrial Hypoxia Pathway model for toxin production, we found that infection can act as a driving force for spatial pattern formation and isolate the mechanisms responsible for this phenomenon, creating opportunities for improving beneficial microbes through genetic modifications. These enhancements aim to increase the variable's sensitivity, potentially leading to more effective pest control. Our findings also demonstrate the feasibility of controlling pest populations through the optimal placement of beneficial microbes in areas where populations are highest. Our research on the model's variables has shown that increasing their values moves the system further from the edge of stability, reducing the risk of system failure due to contamination. While deep learning-based methods have significantly improved image analysis accuracy, they can be prone to saturation with high-resolution images. This issue is particularly common in medical imaging, especially when working with high-magnification images. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a novel nucleus segmentation approach that utilizes two different resolution levels in its network architecture. The proposed system, called W-Net, consists of a coarse-layer stage that generates a preliminary mask and refines it through a series of high-resolution layer expansions. The refined mask is then combined with the original image at the corresponding resolution level. This merged image becomes input for the next stage, where the same process is repeated. The output from each stage is combined, and the resulting mask is then merged with the images from each level, producing a final nucleus segmentation result. Experiments conducted on a dataset containing 2000 nucleus annotations at 20x magnification revealed that W-Net outperformed alternative methods, including U-Net, FCN, and R-FCN. The results showed a significant improvement in evaluation metric scores, particularly the Dice coefficient, Jaccard exclusion, and mean absolute error. To facilitate reproducibility, the model, dataset, and associated codes are available for download at the specified link. The research demonstrates that using two-stage convolutional networks can yield superior nucleus segmentation results, even with high-resolution images. Furthermore, the proposed W-Net architecture may find applications in image analysis tasks beyond nucleus segmentation. To validate the obtained results, the study conducted an experiment involving human annotators who assessed the accuracy of W-Net annotations in relation to their own markings. The findings showed a high level of agreement (0.933) between human annotators and W-Net, as evidenced by a recent paper presenting a different approach to evaluating nucleus segmentation results. The research also explored the relationship between resolution and annotation accuracy, revealing that W-Net's performance improves with higher magnification levels, including 40x, 60x, and 100x. To further enhance nucleus segmentation, the study explored the integration of W-Net with nucleus candidate detection. Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by inflammation, can contribute to the high cytokine levels seen in severe cases of COVID-19.  Pyroptosis is primarily initiated through the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation which can be triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection. Research has shown that some anti-inflammatory medications are capable of halting the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation, thereby delaying pyroptotic cell death. Our study aims to create a single-cell mathematical model that captures the NLRP3 inflammasome's formation and cell death due to pyroptosis, in addition to the effects of these treatments on the model's dynamics. This model will be used to explore factors contributing to pyroptosis's rapid development and how it responds to anti-inflammatory treatments in monocytes similar to those found in the lungs of patients with severe COVID-19. Furthermore, this model will be used to evaluate how the timing of these treatments in relation to infection affects the resulting outcomes. Ultimately, this research may facilitate the identification of key variables and their interactions that could be targeted through interventions or treatments in the fight against pyroptosis. This model and our findings may also provide valuable insights for further experimental studies. It is essential to note that a comprehensive understanding of SARS-CoV-2's host cell interactions is still in the process of being defined, therefore this study assumes a given set of cellular conditions that are influenced by the virus's presence. Given the complexity and the single-cell nature of this model, it is crucial to analyze it through the lens of dynamical systems in addition to ordinary differential equation (ODE) modeling. By using this dual perspective, we are able to explore its behavior both analytically and numerically. This study is an initial attempt at creating a single-cell model that captures the host cell's death due to pyroptosis and the effects of anti-inflammatory treatments in response to SARS-CoV-2 infection. This model is relatively simple yet is capable of producing cell death due to pyroptosis within a timeframe that is consistent with the known facts about COVID-19. A blockchain-based smart contract is an automated transaction program, utilized in various cryptocurrencies, that is prone to errors if developed without a thorough review. To address this issue, a sophisticated validation tool has been created for the Tezos blockchain, allowing developers to scrutinize their smart contracts through a command-line interface or an interactive web application. This evaluation tool employs a refinement-type-based approach to examine the contracts' behavior, guaranteeing that their ultimate transactions meet the predetermined protocols. By leveraging type inference, developers can assess the correctness of their contracts directly from the command-line interface or an interactive web application. This project's validation tool is an innovative advancement in the field of blockchain validation tools, offering a balance between practical application and theoretical soundness. This research paper provides a detailed explanation of the validation tool's design, along with an overview of its implementation and a discussion of its underlying theoretical concepts. This validation tool is an open-source project, with its source code available on GitHub under the permissive MIT License. Theoretical branes in string theory correspond to high-energy manifestations of symmetry, specifically non-reversible symmetry known as anti-commutative (AC) algebra. This study reveals the AC algebra underlying spacetime, proving it invariable and essential to maintaining the fundamental principles of general covariance and semi-reversibility. We demonstrate that the AC algebra is linked to the irrationality of specific mathematical values, such as the golden ratio and the square root of two, which are universal constants governing the structure of branes. Our analysis also shows the brane's structure is connected to the irrational nature of spacetime, supporting the concept of an irrational universe. This research provides the mathematical foundation for the relationship between branes, symmetries, and the universal constants that dictate their architecture. Ultimately, our findings validate the idea that the universe's irrational nature is reflected in its fundamental, indivisible components, which are branes themselves. This study is an expansion of our earlier work presented in the article "The Brane's Hidden Signature: Unveiling the Universal Constants Governing Spacetime" (arXiv:2301.00511). The brane's structure is an intricate, multi-dimensional construct based on the golden ratio, alpha numbers ($\alpha_i$), and the quadratic formula's symmetric and anti-commutative components. These building blocks, tied to the fundamental constants of the universe, are derived from the Chebyshev polynomials and the binomial theorem applied to the variable $x^2$. The results suggest that this technique has the potential to improve elastography imaging. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of natural deduction with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each logical pseudocode is comprised of a combination of imperative algorithm written in pseudocode and the underlying natural deduction principles. This framework enables the exploration of various imperative system expressions through natural deduction's application of rules, which can be achieved by modifying the imperative algorithm to include additional control flow elements, such as loops and function calls, following the established pattern. Four concrete examples are provided within this discussion, including a sequential search algorithm, a matrix multiplication algorithm, a recursive binary search algorithm, and an example drawn from natural language processing, to illustrate this notion in practice. A formal equivalence framework is introduced in the second part of this research, which is centered on the lambda calculus and its corresponding imperative evaluation procedure. Within this framework, the exploration of lambda terms is enabled through the use of natural deduction with cut operations in a controlled manner, which is guided by a controlled application of rules, here referred to as "logical pseudocode" or "LPP. A specific parameterized search language is introduced in the LPP framework, which provides a universal expression for encapsulating the controlled exploration of complex data structures and the controlled application of rules, offering a versatile expression that can be both executed and proven. This research offers a novel, unified approach that treats imperative algorithms and logical proofs as equivalent expressions, offering both theoretical contributions and practical benefits, such as the possibility to prove properties of algorithms in a natural and intuitive manner by translating the algorithms into the corresponding natural deduction formulas, and also addressing potential security threats, like code injection, by developing a formal specification for the algorithm that includes control flow elements, which can be used to create an interpreter that only executes the approved parts of the code, thus providing an effective solution to the problem of simultaneous execution and analysis of programs. We introduce a novel hierarchical framework for solving large-scale stochastic chase-evasion games of imperfect information in discrete space. Our approach divides the game into two nested components: a high-level macro-strategy, characterized by dynamic systems with reachability objectives, and a collection of low-level epsilon-approximate subgames. Within this framework, we establish a soundness theorem linking the behavior of the overall game to that of the macro-strategy. To demonstrate the practical utility of our framework, we conduct a series of experiments showing its potential for scaling down complex chase-evasion games without sacrificing strategic depth. Interestingly, our experiments reveal that some epsilon-approximate variants may offer superior performance compared to their precise counterparts, raising the intriguing question of subjective game size. The concept of a likelihood function was initially proposed having cyclic invariance properties, which would imply that the method is objective. However, in 1973, Edwards revealed a counterexample showing this assumption is flawed. Edwards' example, although well-known, remains understudied. This article delves into a comprehensive examination of this example, including both its historical context and technical details. A nontransitive likelihood scenario was discovered, which can be understood through a simple analogy involving tournament tables. A category of nontransitive likelihoods, characterized by Edwards' example, has been defined as "cyclic" and a new, distinct category of "nontransitive" likelihoods has been discovered. Edwards' example is compared to a more recent counterexample from 2001, and it is demonstrated that these two examples are unrelated. A discussion on implications and potential research directions is also presented. Edwards' example can be represented through a straightforward statistical model, which provides a clearer understanding of its underlying structure. A discussion on alternative models is also presented, which highlights the distinction between model-based and Bayes-factor approaches. A new term, "nontransitive likelihood," is proposed to describe these situations in a more concise manner. A in-depth examination of the relationship and differences between these two types of likelihoods is also provided. A discussion on potential solutions to mitigate the issues caused by nontransitive likelihoods is presented, which include the use of prior distributions and alternative estimation methods. A discussion on the limitations of frequentist statistics and the potential for new approaches is also presented. Recently, deep learning techniques have gained popularity for enhancing low-dose CT images, particularly due to their impressive performance, including the extraction of valuable imaging information at higher doses. Although several methods have been successfully applied in simulated and real-world clinical settings, most are limited by their inability to switch between different CT scans of varying doses without retraining the model. This is particularly problematic in multi-dose CT scanning protocols that have become more prevalent in recent years. This paper proposes a cycleGAN-based model that can restore low-dose CT scans with minimal computation and zero-labeled data, and incorporates an adaptive instance normalization (AdaIN) module to enable seamless switching between different CT scans of varying doses without additional training. This improved model achieves restored images at normal-dose CT scans just as effectively as the original CycleGAN model, yet it boasts significantly reduced parameters and computation when compared to the baseline method, while also facilitating the easy swapping of restored normal-dose CT scans for different low-dose scans without retraining. This enhanced model was evaluated using 240 abdominal CT scans from two independent datasets and compared to the original CycleGAN model in terms of image quality and computation requirements. According to the results from two independent experiments, the proposed AdaIN-Switchable CycleGAN model yields restored images with PSNR values 0.42~0.57 dB and SSIM values 0.0013~0.005 higher than the baseline method, while featuring model sizes that are 6.8 times smaller with comparable computation requirements. This innovative model has the potential to revolutionize multi-dose CT scanning protocols by enabling the conversion of low-dose scans to normal-dose scans without retraining or additional data, thereby facilitating the straightforward swapping of restored normal-dose CT scans for different low-dose scans. This breakthrough model offers a versatile solution for real-world clinical applications and paves the way for the exploration of other switching modules that could be adaptable to diverse imaging modalities and scanning protocols. When learning multiple tasks in a single environment, reinforcement learning agents often face the challenge of catastrophic interference, where their performance deteriorates significantly when switching between tasks. This issue is particularly pronounced in model-based multi-task reinforcement learning due to the shared representation of the task models and action policies. To mitigate this interference, we propose a novel modular multi-task reinforcement learning framework, where each task has a distinct world model and action value function, all of which are encapsulated within a shared policy network. When transitioning between tasks, this framework is designed to minimize the number of parameters affected, thus reducing interference. Our proposed method surpasses existing approaches and matches the state-of-the-art methods in multiple benchmark scenarios, including both single-task and multi-task scenarios, as well as scenarios involving a significant gap between tasks. Notably, our method exhibits a marked improvement over alternative methods in multi-task settings, achieving a 50% reduction in error when compared to the next best method. Our method also holds the record for few-shot learning performance in multi-task reinforcement learning tasks, demonstrating an 18% improvement over the next best method in a scenario with a significant gap between tasks. Our method is also amenable to efficient parallelization, enabling a 2.5 times increase in the number of tasks that can be learned within a fixed computational budget. We synthesize the life stories of four logicians from the 20th century, Alan Turing, Alonzo Church, Kurt Godel, J.B. Rosser, Stephen Kleene, Emil Post, Rudolf Carnap, Alfred Tarski, and Nicolas Bourbaki. Our account is presented in four chapters corresponding to these logicians. Godel's discovery of a fundamental property about first-order logic served as a significant milestone in the development of modern computer science and philosophy of science. After World War II, the Amsterdam Conference saw important contributions from Godel, Tarski, Carnap, and Church, among others, though one author, J.B. Rosser, made a crucial advancement in the theory of Turing machines that allowed for unbounded computation resources to be circumvented. Following the Amsterdam Conference, the development of theoretical computer science and related fields continued to evolve, marked by important milestones such as the Kolmogorov complexity theorem and the undecidability theorem, ultimately laying the foundation for Nicolas Bourbaki's constructive topology. Two appendices provide a historical context for the Amsterdam Conference and a formal proof of the unsolvability of the decision problem using Godel's incompleteness theorems, as well as a discussion on the Church-Turing thesis.

In chapter one, we explore the early lives and contributions of Alan Turing, Alonzo Church, Kurt Godel, J.B. Rosser, Stephen Kleene, and Emil Post.

In chapter two, we delve into the pre-war achievements of Rudolf Carnap, Alfred Tarski, and Nicolas Bourbaki, before shifting to the Amsterdam Conference in 1946-1947 and the post-war era.

In chapter three, we examine the life stories of Stephen Kleene and Alan Turing in greater detail, as well as the development of computer science and the philosophy of science in the mid-20th century.

In chapter four, we analyze the discovery of the property about first-order logic by Kurt Godel and the contributions of Kurt Godel, J.B. Rosser, Rudolf Carnap, and Alfred Tarski at the Amsterdam Conference in 1946-1947.

Two appendices are included: one provides a historical context for the Amsterdam Conference in 1946-1947, while the other offers a discussion of the Church-Turing thesis and a formal proof of the undecidability theorem using Godel's incompleteness theorems. This thesis is an extension of Peter J. Taal's undergraduate thesis

This paper introduces a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to circumvent the limited periodical context of WaveNet's causal convolution. By extending the model's context window without increasing parameters, we address this constraint. To optimize the model for low-frequency components, we modified the convolution's kernel expansion to be pitch-dependent. Experiments demonstrate that QPNet achieves superior quality and naturalness when compared to existing TTS methods. Furthermore, our findings indicate that QPNet effectively generates quasi-periodic waveforms and outperforms state-of-the-art models in subjective evaluations. The model's effectiveness is attributed to its ability to process context windows several times larger than its parameter count, enabling the generation of complex quasi-periodic signals. To facilitate reproducibility, the QPNet model and associated code have been made available on GitHub. This research presents a novel web-based framework called MADARi, which addresses both spelling and morphological annotation in Arabic. This hybrid approach tackles the intricate nature of Arabic language, which is frequently overlooked in other systems. Each word in Arabic depends on its root and pattern for meaning, rendering the need for a combined system in Arabic unavoidable. To achieve this, MADARi utilizes a root-based approach and offers both an annotation and a correction module. When annotating a word, the system suggests possible roots and patterns, which are then confirmed or adjusted through a morphological analyzer. This analyzer enables the detection of inflected forms and allows users to navigate from the surface level to the root and pattern level. MADARi's annotation module is underpinned by a sophisticated algorithm that identifies and corrects morphological errors. To validate the effectiveness of this system, a set of spell-checking and morphological annotation tests were conducted. The results show MADARi's performance surpasses that of other systems, with a spell-checking accuracy of 85.3% and a morphological annotation score of 83.5%. To facilitate community involvement, MADARi provides an annotation tool and a dataset comprising over 250,000 words, which can be accessed through its official website. Furthermore, the system's annotation module is available as an open-source project on GitHub. To ensure the reliability of its annotations, MADARi employs multiple confirmation steps with the system's developers. To avoid the introduction of new errors during confirmation, a confirmation interface with a "revert button" is used. To further verify the system's performance, a set of usability and community-based tests were conducted. These tests were repeated over a period of three years, with participants demonstrating a clear preference for MADARi over other available systems. To ensure the system's scalability, a set of stress tests were conducted. These tests involved the annotation of up to 500 words at a time and demonstrated the system's ability to handle large datasets efficiently. To facilitate the exploration of annotated datasets, a search function with filtering capabilities is provided. This enables the extraction of words based on their root, pattern, lemma, or a combination of these features. To further enhance the system's usability, a set of predefined filters is available, including filters for extracting words from specific genres, such as children's books, which can be downloaded from the system's website. Planets within the habitable zones of G-K stars, rich in water and organic molecules, undergo efficient absorption of visible light as they orbit their host star. This interaction with stellar radiation has far-reaching implications for their atmospheric and surface conditions through photochemical processes that shape molecular distributions, temperature profiles, and aerosol formations. The effects of host star type and spectral evolution on these processes are significant, leading to altered reaction kinetics and resulting consequences for the planets' atmospheres and potential for life. To address these complex phenomena, a new computational tool has been developed to simulate the chemical and photophysical changes in temperate exoplanet atmospheres under various conditions, considering multiple reactions and the planetary system's internal heat, as well as the influence of stellar radiation and the planet's spin. By leveraging this model in a comprehensive analysis of temperate exoplanets with stars of spectral types A to M, it has been observed that water photochemistry is primarily governed by visible light, leading to a complex network of reactions that produce both useful biomarkers, such as oxygen and organic molecules, as well as hazardous substances like nitrogen oxides, ozone, and cyanides, all of which are sensitive to changes in host star type and the resulting changes in atmospheric conditions. The model also reveals that the spectral characteristics of these planets are shaped by a combination of chemical species including neutral molecules, ions, and aerosol particles that form in response to extreme temperatures, as well as the coexistence of different gas phases that can vary based on the planet's distance from its host star, resulting in the production of several key biomarkers such as CH4, CO2, H2O, H2S, NH3, O2, and CH3OH that are influenced by the planet's orbit and host star type, producing distinct spectral patterns that serve as indicators of life on exoplanets, and providing a new framework for life detection through the analysis of visible and near-infrared spectra of temperate exoplanets, which can be further improved by hosting a bio-signature library and analyzing data from multiple telescopes. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that by employing the model in a maximum likelihood estimation algorithm and a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method, it is feasible to derive a comprehensive understanding of the atmospheric composition and conditions of a temperate exoplanet based on the analysis of visible and near-infrared spectra, which in turn enables the prediction of chemical species, temperature profiles, and aerosol formations in the planet's atmosphere, providing a solid foundation for future research

Specifically, we establish a direct correspondence between linear shadows
and the bicategory of typed string diagrams within the realm of Frobenius algebras.
Our framework also accommodates the graphical language of bimonads and weak Hopf algebras,
and we show that these are equivalent to certain bicategorical structures on string diagrams.
Our approach enables us to create an isomorphism between the category of linear shadows

Our research is an exploration of the intersection between the worlds of shadows and diagrammatics. 
Our findings can be seen as an expansion of the principles outlined by David Joyal in his talk at LEAD 2016.

A critical aspect of acoustic design involves identifying the structural framework that produces a desired sound, typically in the form of an acoustic wave. In this research, an unexplored area within structural acoustic design is tackled, where the objective is to reverse engineer both the structural matrix and the acquired sound wave to achieve a specific acoustic outcome. Although it may seem more complicated than designing the structural matrix directly, we demonstrate that this inverse process benefits from the ability to modify parameters freely across both the structural and acoustic domains, resulting in fewer constraints and potential solutions. However, the ability to accurately pinpoint the desired structural matrix depends on initial conditions and the uniqueness of the solution, which may not always be guaranteed due to the continuous nature of structural frequency parameters. As a result, the solution obtained through this inverse method may correspond to an alternative structural frequency parameter, leading to the need for the structural matrix $\Lambda$ to be a rational number to ensure a unique solution. In this research, an efficient algorithm is developed to solve this complex problem, and the results are verified using a designed enclosure that produces a desired sound wave. The fact that the desired structural matrix $\Lambda$ corresponds to a rational number $\Lambda = 5.25$ is a key reason it can be manufactured with ease, as shown by the images provided. The code developed in this research is written in MATLAB and is compatible with MATLAB Live, allowing for real-time visualization of the designed structural matrix $\Lambda$ through 3D plotting. The designed acoustic wave is then validated through numerical simulation using COMSOL, a leading multiphysics simulation software. The solution obtained through this inverse method is shown to match the desired structural matrix $\Lambda$ when the frequency parameter $\Lambda$ is equal to $5.25$. However, when the frequency parameter $\Lambda$ is set to $5.25$ in the forward problem, the solution obtained does not exactly match the desired acoustic wave, indicating that the two problems behave differently. This formula has a particularly insightful form when considering near-equilibrium situations, and it reveals a fascinating, quasi-probabilistic distribution function. Characterizing colorectal polyps histopathologically for inflammatory cell distribution is crucial for determining their potential for cancerous transformation. While computer vision can facilitate and accelerate this process, training reliable models requires substantial amounts of high-quality, annotated histopathological data. In this study, we introduce UniToPatho, an Italian-language dataset comprising 1426 H&E stained colon polyp images, collected from 121 different patients. Each image is labeled with information regarding the polyp's location, type (hyperplastic, adenomatous, inflammatory, or non-adenomatous), and the distribution of abnormal cells within the adenomatous polyps. To further enhance the training of deep learning models, we present two primary tasks: classifying polyps as hyperplastic or adenomatous, and grading the cell distribution in adenomatous polyps on a scale from 1 to 5. UniToPatho is the first dataset of its kind to incorporate Italian-language clinical reports, obtained through a natural language processing approach, enabling the extraction of relevant information from medical notes. To make the dataset freely available for the broader research community, we introduce an initial evaluation of state-of-the-art deep learning models and establish several challenging benchmarks for classification and grading tasks. Notably, our results demonstrate a notable gap between the performance achieved on the UniToPatho dataset and that reported in literature, suggesting a need for further investigation into the influence of linguistic and cultural aspects on the generalization of computer-aided diagnosis methods in colorectal polyp analysis. UniToPatho is currently the largest Italian-language dataset of its kind and is available for download at the specified URL. We are committed to expanding the dataset through ongoing collaborations with pathologists and endoscopists from various medical centers across Italy. We analyzed the isotopic composition of hydrogen and water in pyroxene minerals from recent chondrite falls in Benenitra (2018) and Chelyabinsk (2013), as well as three older chondrite finds in Antarctica. Our research indicates a smaller than expected isotopic gap between pyroxene and olivine within the same chondrite, particularly in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk, which could be caused by the underrepresentation of large metal-rich clasts commonly found in type 3 chondrites. These large clasts typically reside in veins composed of metal and troilite and are characterized by their high water and hydrogen content, as well as unique metal isotopic signatures. When comparing the isotopic composition of metal in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk to that in Antarctic samples, we found a 2 to 3 times greater water and hydrogen content in the former group, which is consistent with the underrepresentation of large metal-rich clasts in type 3 chondrites. This finding provides new evidence that large metal-rich clasts were missing from the inner solar system, where they failed to accrete due to the influence of viscous disk processes that broke apart and disrupted small solid bodies in the accretion process. As a result, the water and hydrogen content in the inner solar system remained underrepresented, leading to the observed differences in isotopic composition when comparing Benenitra and Chelyabinsk to Antarctic samples. This discovery also sheds light on the formation of the Earth, which is believed to have originated from a similar inner solar system location. As such, the Earth's water and hydrogen endowment should also reflect the underrepresentation of large metal-rich clasts, with implications for its formation theory. Additionally, this research provides new insights into the Earth's water and hydrogen budget, which is composed of approximately 1.5 times the amount of water found in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk, as well as about half the hydrogen content in the metal in Benenitra and Chelyabinsk, with possible consequences for the planet's differentiation and the origin of its distinct isotopic signatures in hydrogen, water, and mantle rocks. Furthermore, this research offers a new explanation for the Earth's large water inventory in comparison to other terrestrial planets, which is based on its unique formation process in the inner solar system where it underwent a prolonged period of accretion through a highly viscous disk that broke apart and disrupted small solid bodies in the accretion process. Speech translation bypasses the written intermediate step between listening to spoken language and speaking a different language. This task is complicated by the presence of multiple source and target languages. For instance, if someone is speaking English and you need to respond in Spanish but didn't learn any English, the task becomes significantly harder. Until now, it had been assumed that each combination of source and target languages required unique skills. However, our research reveals that a single neural network can accomplish all speech-to-speech translations with ease, even across vast linguistic families, provided it can learn from labeled data for each language pair. We demonstrated the efficacy of this single-firm approach by achieving superior results on six pairs of languages, including English and Spanish, in comparison to industry standards. Our novel system also excelled in zero-shot voice translation, where the target audience is unknown, at both automatic and human evaluation levels, outperforming a leading speech-to-text and subsequent text-to-speech model by a considerable margin. Our model's capabilities can be extended to any new language pair without the need to redesign it, thanks to its zero-shot adaptation ability. Our code and comprehensive evaluation have been made public for further research. We assess the applicability of three different methods for calculating electromagnetic multipoles: Cartesian primitive multipoles, irreducible multipoles and spherical multipoles. Our findings suggest that the spherical multipoles provide the most accurate description of electromagnetic scattering behavior, as demonstrated with an example of an amorphous silicon sphere. These multipoles are utilized to model the optical force exerted on particles of varying materials and sizes, showing good agreement with established theories and confirming the utility of spherical multipoles even for particles larger than the wavelength of light. A supplementary program, titled'multipol', is also introduced, enabling computations of spherical multipoles for Scattering Type Meshes, thereby extending the capabilities of the established'meshforce' program. The accuracy of this method is validated by comparing its results with both experimental data and closed-form expressions for the optical force. The'multipol' program is further designed to be adaptable to various applications, as exemplified with an exploration of the optical force distribution within a dielectric sphere, in addition to its exterior. Furthermore, this method is employed to investigate the electromagnetic scattering and optical force experienced by particles in multiple configurations, showcasing its usefulness for cross-sectional patterns, along with an examination of its efficiency and potential for further optimization. The'multipol' program is made available for download at the website of the University of Oxford, specifically at https://www.chemistry.ox.ac.uk/research/groups/neutron-scattering/software/multipol. Additionally, a corresponding library for the open-source high-performance computing framework 'HACC' has been created and can be accessed via https://github.com/roberthiggs/hacc-libs. The'multipol' program offers a groundbreaking capability for accurately modeling the optical force and electromagnetic scattering within complex systems, extending far beyond the commonly applied long wavelength approximation. This breakthrough is expected to significantly contribute to a deeper comprehension of mesoscopic particle dynamics, as well as its influence on scattering and optical force computations, and has paved the way for its application in various fields, including condensed matter, biological and biomedical sciences, materials science and chemical physics. Our technique notably enables us to find the leading coefficients of certain 'Schur shifted' symmetric functions, even though some of these have no direct link to Weyl characters. Some 'Schur shifted' symmetric functions, after applying our method, reveal new insights and might have use in other mathematical fields like algebraic geometry and geometric representation theory. Lastly, we've established a connection between our 'Schur shifted' symmetric functions and Capelli operators in the Drinfeld-Jimbo Weyl algebra, which in turn links to Chmutova-Mutovski's formula for such operators. Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we maintain a minimal part for generating right-handed neutrino masses and analyze its implications on WIMP dark matter and the Higgs vacuum stability. By introducing a minimal $SU(2)_L$ bi-doublet and a standard model singlet, we successfully resolve the little hierarchy problem while stabilizing the Higgs vacuum for a suitable range of the new scalar's mass parameter. Furthermore, we find that a WIMP dark matter mass region of approximately 1.6~keV to 1.7~GeV is formed by the interplay of the scalar's mass parameter and the $B-L$ symmetry breaking scale. A thorough analysis of the direct and indirect detection of WIMPs has revealed specific, constrainable multi-GeV mass windows, which could be explored by current experiments as well as upcoming ones such as HESS and CTA. Additionally, we identify a particular easy-to-reach, scoto-seesaw model for the 1.6~keV WIMP, which presents a fundamental, theoretical value for the WIMP-nucleon direct detection cross-section of approximately 6.44$\times 10^{-41}$ ecm$^2$, along with an apparent, indirect detection signature in the $e^+e^+$ channel at a signal count of roughly 3.44 in 1 year of signal collection with the LHCb. This model also offers a 7$\sigma$ beyond-the-standard-model contribution to the 1 GeV scale, effective Higgs four-point coupling $\sim 1.38$. This analysis provides a comprehensive understanding of the simplest scoto-seesaw model's phenomenological features and its capacity to yield a robust, theoretical prediction for WIMP properties. This implies that future standard model effective field theory-like, high-scale colliders such as CLIC or FCC-ee/FCC-he will be capable of verifying the model's underlying, fundamental characteristics through the analysis of WIMP and Higgs properties alone. This research also highlights the significance of investigating WIMP and Higgs physics in conjunction at any given scale, as demonstrated by this simple scoto-seesaw model, which can be scrutinized in depth via existing and upcoming experiments at both colliders and dark matter direct and indirect detection facilities. This study on the simplest scoto-seesaw model has the potential to serve as a benchmark for the analysis of more intricate models incorporating right-handed neutrino masses via the scoto-seesaw mechanism. Radiologists rely on low-quality or mislabeled images for training due to the vast amount of medical image data required. To address this, we propose an innovative approach that utilizes a limited set of high-quality image diagnoses in conjunction with mislabeled image data. Our method incorporates a novel contrastive learning technique called adaptive contrast learning, which enhances the representation of medical image features by accounting for both high-quality image-quality and medical label information. We pair this with a novel medical image editing framework called adaptive unpaired editing, which leverages a dataset of high-quality images with accurate diagnoses to fix the quality and inaccuracies in medical images. We experiment with two distinct medical image editing tasks: enhancing underexposed chest X-rays and correcting mislabeled heart vs lung localizations on X-rays. Our results show that our proposed methods outperform existing editing and image-to-image translation models, yielding more accurate diagnoses for edited medical images. Our code is available at https://github.com/ikostadinov/med-edit. Our research demonstrates the potential of medical image editing to complement weak supervision, addressing the quality issues commonly encountered in medical imaging datasets. We hope that our contributions will inspire further research in this area. We introduce Swift, a novel C++ library for computing potential fields in 2D by employing the methods of weighted averages and differential integration. Swift takes advantage of the success of AstroSWIFT, a Python implementation of these techniques, and builds upon its foundation. Building from AstroSWIFT's foundation, Swift focuses on accelerating and optimizing computational performance for complex planar domains using multi-core processors and thread-based parallelization. In a benchmark against AstroSWIFT, Swift demonstrates significant improvements in computational speed, showing a greater than 10-fold enhancement in scalar mode and a benchmarked rate of approximately 1.7 10^9 evaluations per second. Furthermore, Swift exhibits excellent scalar efficiency when compared to PySWIFT's C++ counterpart, PySWIFT_C, and shows a greater than 4-fold improvement in performance when compared to it. This acceleration in computational performance combined with a C++ interface makes Swift an ideal choice for integrating Swift with C++-based applications and for potential use in future GPU and machine learning accelerator evaluations. This library is an important step in the swift development of applications that leverage its unique capabilities for gravitational wave events such as neutron star mergers.

Abstract for updated paper: We present an updated evaluation of the planar Swift library in its current form. This evaluation includes an increased number of test cases covering 25 diverse geometries in comparison to the initial 7. Furthermore, we have made significant improvements to the underlying code resulting in a greater than 5-fold performance enhancement. This updated evaluation confirms the previously observed performance gains of up to 1.7 10^9 evaluations per second. In addition to performance enhancements, the code has been optimized for ease of use and a simplified API. We have also successfully integrated the Swift library with the GIMIC merger disk simulation code. This demonstrates the potential for Swift to be used in conjunction with other merger simulation codes. However, we have encountered performance bottlenecks with certain applications such as the GIMIC code, specifically in scenarios involving complex geometries and large particle counts. As a result, we have identified areas for further optimization and improvement, including the exploration of GPU acceleration, vectorized computations, and direct numerical integration methods. Despite these limitations, the Swift library remains an essential tool for the evaluation of Newtonian potentials in planar domains, and we anticipate continued development and refinement of this library in the future. This updated evaluation adds to the previously reported findings and provides a more comprehensive overview of the Swift library.
